content.rendered:
By David Walters (a bit long for me, but plays you might not get the chance to see ever again)

Fog and Ice, the title of an evening of three one-acts (Ile and Fog by Eugene O’Neill and The Brink of Silence by Esther E. Galbraith), is now playing on Theatre Row (410 West 42nd Street) through February 28.

I always feel a responsibility when watching a period piece. I watch it as its self, how it stands on its own and speaks to me today; I look to see how it fits into and reflects the times when it was first produced; and, what it says about the growth of a writer, where it comes in the writer’s timeline of work, where it foreshadows what’s to come, and what it is saying about the writer at this point in their career.

Each of the three plays have within them themes of isolation, fear, and what it means to be alive, each character answering in their own way.

——-

Ile (a dialect pronunciation of the word oil, referring to whale oil), which was first performed in 1917 (when the US joined WWI), addresses pride and ego fighting to keep their heads above water in the face of self sacrifice.

It’s based on real life tale floating around the town of Providence that O’Neil overheard of a whaler captain, Captain Keeney (John Long), who brought his wife, Mrs. Keeney (Charlotte Cohn), on a two plus year journey hunting whales and put an organ on board in the stateroom so she would have an outlet. Having stayed behind many a year, she romanticized what whaling was like. Now coming face to face with the harshness, the constant cold, meager rations, and gruffness of her husband, she begs and pleas for him to return home even though the hold is near empty. With the crew also near mutiny he first falters in his decision, but ignores her and the crew’s request and continues the journey despite the obstacles. This decision sets her adrift in a sea of insanity and wrecks his future marital happiness as his willfullness and personal pride triumph.

No question that the mental breakdown of Mrs. Keeney throughout Ile foreshadows Mary Tyrone’s in Long Days Journey Into Night. In some ways it’s like finding early sketches by the artist hidden beneath their masterpiece.

With: Jesse Castellanos, Charlotte Cohn, Simon Feil, John Long, and Steven Rattazzi.

——-

Fog was written in 1914 and sets adrift two men (poet Simon Feil and businessman Steven Rattazzi), a Polish peasant woman and her dead child in a lifeboat without oars having survived the sinking of their steamship, Starland. The woman is covered asleep in the bow clutching her son and the two men sit aft discussing their plight, their lives, and the meaning of life. It is pre-dawn and bodies can only be barely made out in the dimness for the first third of the play as a dawn slowly creeps in. There is so much fog though that nothing can be seen (including an iceberg until they bump up against it).

The poet, with a socialistic bent on life, tells how the boy may have been lucky as his life would have been nothing but drudgery anyhow, and his death was a gift that, “saved him many a long year of sordid drudgery.” The businessman, calling the poet a “reformer,” can only talk about the discomfort of the keening of the woman over her dead child and his hope that she doesn’t wake and continue the ear splitting agony.

They do hear a search boat through the fog and the poet suppresses the businessman’s calls as that would only bring the ship to them where it would strike the iceberg and sink. Sacrificing their lives is more important than jeopardizing the crew of the rescue boat.

The lifeboat is surprisingly found despite the dense fog and its rescuers attribute the cries of the little boy as guiding them safely through the fog. Knowing that the boy had been dead for longer than the cries were first heard, both lifeboat passengers are humbled by the realization.

The dead boy and his crying after death parallels the death of O’Neil’s brother Edmund who died young.

With: Jesse Castellanos, Simon Feil and Steven Rattazzi.

——-

The Brink of Silence, also written in 1917, is the tale of two Englishmen, Cole and Macready (John Long and Simon Feil), in a windowless stone hut at a whaling station in Antarctica. Cole, an explorer had led a failed expedition, attempting to cross the continent, where everyone died except him. He had left his crew and ship frozen in the ice to go and find help. When he did stumble back into life in South America, long after his deceased crew had been found, he discovered that he had also been presumed dead, his expedition perceived to be a disaster, his wife was set to remarry and no one was missing him, not even his son who he never really knew due to his travels. Since there was nothing left of his life, he was planning on living the rest of his days in and on the silence of the ice shelf. His only lament was that he would never be able to go on an expedition with his son and pass along his work.

Macready tries to counter this doomsday thinking and urges him to leave with him back to England when the next whaling ship arrives and start life anew. When a group of explorers, having just crossed the continent, does arrive, the leader of the expedition is a surprise to them all, and though he does not change Cole’s mind about his choice to remain, it only makes him more satisfied with this choice.

Not much is know about playwright Esther E. Galbraith. This play was written as an assignment and was very well received. She has written several other works, but was never widely produced. The title of the play, Brink of Silence, symbolizes the character choice, the continent, and the little we know of Esther

With: Jesse Castellanos. Simon Feil, John Long and Steven Rattazzi.

——-

All three plays do stand on their own in the world of today as the sense of isolation and loss will always be part of our story. Well worth a look as seeing these pieces on the boards is a rare glimpse into the author’s timelines, and not often played.

The set design by Brian Dudkiewicz and lighting by Max Stroeher add immensely to the feeling of each piece endowing them with cold, ice, and the vastness of the ocean and Antarctica.

——–

Fog and Ice, an evening of three one-acts, two by Eugene O’Neill and one by Esther E. Galbraith. All three directed by Jerry Heymann.

With: Jesse Castellanos, Charlotte Cohn, Simon Feil, John Long and Steven Rattazzi.

Associate director, Charlotte Cohn; Scenic Designer Brian Dudkiewicz; Costume designer Julia Squier; Lighting designer, Max Stroeher; Sound designer andy Evan Cohen.

Runs 75 minutes without intermission.

Tickets can be bought HERE.

As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

title.rendered: A Pianist of Uncommon Sovereignty: Marc-André Hamelin at the 92nd Street Y

content.rendered:
In an evening of breathtaking range, Canadian virtuoso Marc-André Hamelin delivered a program that was nothing less than a tour through the entire kingdom of the modern piano

Some pianists perform a concert, while others inhabit one. On the night of February 18, 2026, Marc-André Hamelin belonged emphatically to the second category. Seated at a gleaming Steinway on the stage of the David Geffen Stage at the Kaufmann Concert Hall — the storied concert room of The 92nd Street Y — Hamelin offered not merely a recital but an act of sovereign imagination, traversing two and a half centuries of musical thought with a command so total it seemed, at moments, almost suspiciously effortless.

Interpretive Intelligence

The program itself was an act of intellectual audacity: a labyrinthine journey from Haydn‘s crystalline classicism to the fevered Romanticism of Rachmaninoff, with illuminating stops at Zappa, Wolpe, Oswald, and Medtner along the way. Moreover, what made the evening truly remarkable was not the range itself — formidable as it was — but the absolute consistency of interpretive intelligence and communicative warmth Hamelin brought to every bar of every work on the program.

First Half: From Enlightenment Wit to Expressionist Fire

Haydn — Sonata in D Major, Hob. XVI:37

Hamelin opened with Franz Joseph Haydn’s sparkling Sonata in D Major (Hob. XVI:37, 1780) — and immediately, one grasped the intelligence of the program’s design. His Haydn was all wit, elegance, and affectionate command. The opening Allegro con brio unfurled with luminous clarity of voicing, every ornamental figure placed with absolute precision, every dynamic shade calibrated to perfection. The figurations were executed not with the rote fluency of the technically proficient, but with the living spontaneity of someone who clearly loves this music with his whole heart.

Marc-Andre Hamelin. Courtesy marcandrehamelin.com

Cheerful and Propulsive

The central Largo e sostenuto was a master class in the expressive possibilities of restraint — his tone darkened and deepened, the aching dissonances of D minor voiced with a tenderness that made the return of the sunlit major key feel, for a suspended moment, genuinely surprising. The concluding Presto ma non troppo arrived like a gust of exuberant air, cheerful and propulsive, warm and spirited. Each movement was, in sum, fresh and performed with complete aplomb — honoring the sophistication of Haydn’s oeuvre with both intellectual respect and human warmth.

Zappa — Ruth Is Sleeping: A Rock Star Meets the Second Viennese School

The transition to Frank Zappa‘s Ruth Is Sleeping (1993, arr. A. Askin) was, in retrospect, both startling and inevitable. Zappa, who in his final years turned his formidable creative energies from rock provocation toward concert works of genuine harmonic sophistication, left in this Synclavier-born piece a work whose language — bristling with tritones, sharp-nine chords, and tightly clustered dissonances one associates with Berg and Webern — sits unmistakably in the orbit of the Second Viennese School.

Virtuosic Interpretation

Hamelin, who champions the work on his Hyperion Records album Found Objects / Sound Objects (October 2025), performed it here in a solo transcription, with splendid results throughout. The complex harmonic architecture was navigated with a structural clarity that made the demanding seem luminous, the rhythmic energy relentless but never mechanical. This was a virtuosic interpretation of an extraordinarily challenging work, and it confirmed what the cognoscenti have long known: Hamelin’s fearlessness as a programmer is matched, note for note, by his fearlessness as a performer.

Wolpe — Passacaglia: The Geometry of Exile

If Zappa brought the Second Viennese School’s atmosphere into the hall, then Stefan Wolpe’s Passacaglia (1933) made that relationship explicit. Wolpe composed this stark and monumental work in Jerusalem, where he had fled after becoming an early Nazi target. Built from a simple series of expanding intervals and eleven derivative rows, the entire edifice rises from this germinal material with the rigor of a cathedral constructed from a single cornerstone.

Marc-Andre Hamelin on stage at the 92Y. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Color, Ritual, and Psychological Atmosphere

The contrapuntal opening was rhythmically incisive and tonally severe, carrying within it the Expressionist atmosphere of early twentieth-century German art. Furthermore, there were atonal admixtures — structures that dissolve traditional tonal gravity while retaining expressive clarity and acoustic beauty — reminiscent of the deeply personal sound-worlds of George Crumb, where atonality functions not as system but as color, ritual, and psychological atmosphere. Hamelin brought to it all the energy of a man untangling a particularly beautiful and complex knot, and the long, martial, monorhythmic final section arrived with the force of a historical reckoning.

Oswald — Tip: An Iceberg of Musical Memory

By brilliant contrast came John Oswald’s Tip (2021), commissioned by Hamelin from his fellow Canadian. A kaleidoscopic mosaic of quotations from the core pianistic repertoire — woven together with wit and structural intelligence akin to the cleverly designed miniatures of Peter Schickele — the work conjures, from the briefest gestures, an entire universe of musical association. Throughout, one caught fleeting shadows of Debussy, Chopin, Satie, Beethoven, Scott Joplin, Gershwin, and Vince Guaraldi. Hamelin performed it with a natural, charming expressiveness that made the piece feel less like an intellectual exercise and more like a genuine act of affection toward the history of the keyboard, and the audience responded with a delight that bordered on astonishment.

From Romantic Twilight to Symphonic Storm

Medtner — Improvisation & Danza festiva: The Last Romantic

Following the intermission, Hamelin offered a pair of works by Nikolai Medtner — the Improvisation in B-flat Minor (Op. 31, No. 1) and the vivid Danza festiva (Op. 38, No. 3) — and in doing so paid tribute to one of music’s most stubbornly magnificent figures. Medtner, the last of the great Romantic composer-pianists, held fast to that tradition deep into the twentieth century, championed throughout his career by Rachmaninoff himself.

Not Merely Velocity but Poetic Lightness

Hamelin’s Medtner was ravishing. The Improvisation — a memorial to a young pianist friend — unfolded as free-flowing variations on a brooding theme, and Hamelin lavished it with a tonal warmth and singing legato that recalled the finest late-nineteenth-century Romantic tradition. The passages of lightning-fast, airy filigree — delicate, gossamer phrases requiring not merely velocity but poetic lightness — were executed with serene mastery, seeming to float above the keyboard. The Danza festiva, by contrast, was a village celebration in sound, complete with clangorous bells and athletic dancing, shot through with a scherzo-like wit that Hamelin dispatched with magisterial ease. The scherzo sections were particularly picturesque and challenging — and completely tamed.

Rachmaninoff — Étude-Tableau & Sonata No. 2: Magnificent Summits

The concert’s final chapter belonged to Sergei Rachmaninoff, and it was magnificent. The Étude-Tableau in E-flat Minor (Op. 39, No. 5, 1917) arrived with unabashed passion and ferocious chromatic density. Rich in bold harmonicism, melodic power, and bravura, the work’s dense textures were navigated with structural clarity that never allowed the lyricism within to be overwhelmed by the sheer mass of sound. In turns turbulent and transcendent, it seemed to bear the entire weight of a civilization on the verge of irreversible transformation.

Bravura and Intellect

Then came the Piano Sonata No. 2 in B-flat Minor (Op. 36, 1931 revision) — and here one must simply say: it was an experience of the kind that justifies concert-going as a way of life. The opening Allegro agitato struck the hall with devastating force. Those accented chords like hammer blows, the primary theme in the left hand’s tenor register, establish its motive of descending chromatic tones with quiet inevitability. Hamelin played it with bravura and intellect, the full orchestral range of the piano’s dynamic palette deployed in service of structural argument never lost beneath the sonic splendor.

L-R Sergei Rachmaninoff, by George Grantham Bain, Public Domain. Claude Debussy portrait (1908) by Otto Wegener. Public Domain.

Unfettered Streams of Consciousness

The Non allegro — Lento was ravishing: pensive, luminous, transcendent, its harmonic and melodic elements hovering in the air with an almost sacred quality — a pavane, a sonic orison, music that seems to stand entirely outside of ordinary time. Unfettered streams of consciousness flowed through the movement, melodic poetry of the highest order. And then the finale — L’istesso tempo — Allegro molto — arrived with a cascade of fortissimo chords tumbling downward like a controlled avalanche, the whole extraordinary structure brought to its thunderous close in a way that felt simultaneously inevitable and almost unbearably exciting.

The audience rose immediately and entirely, their sustained ovation filling the Kaufmann with the warmth that can only be earned. Hamelin had earned it magnificently and expressed thanks with a final tribute to Debussy and his own composition, “The Music Box.”

A Portrait of the Pianist

What this recital demonstrated most powerfully was precisely the quality that makes Marc-André Hamelin singular among pianists of his generation — not merely the formidable technique (though that is extraordinary), nor the astonishing breadth of repertoire (though that too is unmatched), but the sovereign intellectual curiosity that animates everything he does.

Born in Montreal and based in the Boston area, Hamelin has assembled a discography of more than 90 albums as an exclusive artist for Hyperion Records. As a composer, he has written more than thirty works — including the Toccata on L’homme armé commissioned by the Van Cliburn International Piano Competition, and the Mazurka commissioned by the Library of Congress. He teaches on the faculty of the New England Conservatory of Music. Among his honors: seven Juno Awards, eleven Grammy nominations, the Jean Gimbel Lane Prize from Northwestern University, the Paul de Hueck Career Achievement Award from the Ontario Arts Foundation, the Lifetime Achievement Award from the German Record Critics’ Association, Officer of the Order of Canada, Chevalier de l’Ordre national du Québec, and member of the Royal Society of Canada.

Exceptionally Interesting, Challenging, and Thoroughly Enjoyable Concert Experience

What I enjoyed most about this concert was the extraordinary range of styles and genres Hamelin performed with equal aplomb. This shows not only his artistic genius, interpretive flexibility, and broad abilities, but also provides an audience with an exceptionally interesting, challenging, and thoroughly enjoyable concert experience. To attend a Hamelin recital is to be reminded, with every passing bar, that the piano repertoire is not a canon but a cosmos — and that there exists, at its center, a musician uniquely equipped to be its guide.

A Pianist of Uncommon Sovereignty: Marc-André Hamelin at the 92nd Street Y

THE 92ND STREET Y, NEW YORK, NY

David Geffen Stage at the Kaufmann Concert Hall 1395 Lexington Avenue, New York, NY 10128 Tel: 212-415-5500

Official Website   |   Current Concert Season   |   Purchase Tickets   |   Donate & Support 92NY   |   Marc-André Hamelin Official Site

excerpt.rendered: Marc-André Hamelin’s sovereign recital at the 92nd Street Y was a revelation of pianistic genius — Haydn to Rachmaninoff, with Zappa, Wolpe, Oswald, and Medtner illuminated en route. Seek out this peerless artist and others in the 92NY’s dazzling 2025–26 season: this is precisely why concert halls and the human spirit exist.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

This production is the third I have seen in the past few months where there is a wall-clock whose time has nothing to do with the play.  It takes us awhile to figure that out, and part of the figuring process is to consider why the clock is there in the first place.  Is it telling us that the location is so down on its luck that there is not enough money for new batteries or that the story is stuck in a time warp?  There are no answers for either query in Jacob Perkins‘ play “The Dinosaurs” now at Playwrights Horizons.

Instead we get mystery piled on mystery.  There is a clever sort of pickleball set up as the women show up for their regular AA meetings.  One by one we meet Jane (April Matthis), Rayne (Keilly McQuail), Joan (Elizabeth Marvel), Jolly (Kathleen Chalfant), Janet (Mallory Portnoy) and Joane (Maria Elena Ramirez).  Yes indeed: Jolly, Joan, Jane, Janet and Joane – all the “J” women are the regulars at this meeting,  It makes for some snappy dialogue as even the regulars get their names mixed up.  Chalfant does an outstanding job of being the elder with holes in her delivery.  She knows what she means – why doesn’t everyone?

Photo by Julieta Cervantes

Once we get through the very funny warm up we proceed to the meat of the gathering, and this is where the AA structure is called upon to support these women in staying on their sober path.  Stories are timed.  Tasks are delegated.  Rules are repeated.

The stories of today are revealed a bit like a jazz combo where each musician takes the lead for a few minutes.  Perkins deliberately lets almost every woman grab the spotlight, and these actors are a fine fine ensemble.  Monologues are timed as they are in real meetings.  When each woman’s time is up everyone moves on with thanks and grace.  Time becomes fluid.  The past and the future flip flop.  Their paths are strewn with stumbling blocks and regrets.  This, however, does not stop them from showing up each week and offering as well as expecting support.

What is missing here is the connection that each has to the group.  That connection is given lip service but does not dig deep into the underbelly of what makes this group of women click.  Why DO they keep coming back?  It must be more than their 5 minute stories.  Not that these stories are dull because in the hands of these very fine actors each one become a jewel.  In the end, however, the stories do not stick, they do not build.  Granted that may be exactly what some of these meeting are like.  But the premise of any play is “Why today?” Why are these stories being told (and from the sound of it not for the first time) today?

Audiences need a hook, a little zip in our Ovaltine, a little “I got you,” a little “Me too.” We want to be pulled in.  That is why we go to the theatre.  To be pulled out of our lives and into another life.

As it is, with this play we are left to our own devices.  We remain on the outside looking in.  What we really wanted was to be in there close to the dinosaurs slinging muck.  Instead, we were benched.  Along with the clock.

THE DINOSAURS – by Jacob Perkins, Directed by Les Waters

WITH Kathleen Chalfant, Elizabeth Marvel, April Matthis, Keilly McQuail, Mallory Portnoy, and Maria Elena Ramirez

Creative team is dots (Scenic Designer), Oana Botez (Costume Designer), Yuki Link (Lighting Designer), and Palmer Hefferan (Sound Designer)

THROUGH March 1 at Playwrights Horizons.  Tickets HERE

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

11 to Midnight, a nostalgic and upbeat production currently taking stage at Orpheum Theatre, drops us into a city apartment where a group of friends are noting their dreams for the new year with unlimited wine and endless energy. This dance production by viral creators Cost n’ Mayor and Hideaway Circus reminds me of the 2010’s, but we could be in any city in any year.

An ensemble of dancers–wearing holiday colors and sparkling sequins–are all cast from their dancing and performative presence on social media platforms such as TikTok. Together, they bring the ultimate energy, creating this joyful, bright environment where the audience can relax in their seats and feel as though they too are counting down the minutes til a fresh start. Post-it notes are stuck to the walls around us, in the orchestra. Celebratory tissue paper and glittering ribbons stream into the front rows of the theater during the group’s street-dance big numbers. Audience interaction plays a large part in this show. The woman in front of me was asked to hold one of the New Years Eve partygoer’s phones as the cast filmed a TikTok dance. This woman was clearly elated, as she couldn’t help but to move herself to the music and wave up to the cast as they smiled out to us and directed each other for their group video.

While this show drops us into a married couple’s (Austin & Marideth Telenko) apartment as they host that final hour where everyone is reflecting on their past year while looking into the next, we’re given snippets of their own brief courtship that began perhaps during a past New Year’s Eve that began just like this one. The friends indulge in a seemingly constant flow of wine. Two friends may have found love, but their story is left, unfinished, and forgettable. Despite the constant wine-pouring, we never actually see the actors consume from the bottles; rather, those fun, effective sound effects of clinking glasses and glugs simulate the party beverages. The fun choreography and impressive comrade among these dancing stars emulates a positive energy that both adults and kids can appreciate.

While 11 to Midnight leaves all that energy and excitement on the dance floor, I do feel the piece’s tremendous lack of purpose and connection. I don’t have any complex emotions throughout this production; really, I spend the evening just taking in the excitement of those on stage, purely because of  the energy the dancers are tossing us. They’re giving it their all, but I still feel as though I’m receiving nothing. If you’re looking for a show with exactly two things: energy and dancing–then this is the entertainment for you. But if you want a complete storyline and depth–even an opportunity to connect with these characters to which the dancers give face, you may leave Orpheum Theatre feeling very underwhelmed.

Without the depth and originality this production lacks, it makes up a little bit with the lighting and sound effects. Lighting significantly adds to the movement of this performance, but, again, these creative aspects add to the moment of the experience–not its story. The inclusion of so much movement made me realize that I didn’t recall there being any dialogue unless the dancers were singing along with the music blasting, guiding their choreography.

For a stage full of objects and furniture, I thought it was interesting and a smart choice to use sound effects and lighting for objects not included in this living space set: the pop of wine bottles being opened, the glug glug glug of it pouring, the opening and closing of doors. These creative choices are what I’ll remember most about 11 to Midnight, but, maybe if I were someone more invested in and inspired by the world of TikTok dancers, I’d be very, very eager to sit in that audience again.

Created by Josh & Lyndsay Aviner and Austin & Marideth Telenko.

Choreography by Austin & Marideth Telenko; Directed by Lyndsay Magid Aviner.

FEATURING: Austin & Marideth Telenko, Brendon Chan, Kati Simon, Ache Richardson, Makenzie Olsen, Tyson Hill, and swings Kristalyn Gill and Jake Urban.

CREATIVE TEAM: Arnel Sancianco (Scenic Design), Barbara Erin Delo (Costume Design), Jeff Croiter and Sean Beach (Lighting Design), Ben Scheff (Sound Design), and Jeremy Chernick (Special Effects).

Original compositions and soundscapes by Jacob Aviner, Spencer Novichm, and Steve Toulmin.

11 to Midnight is playing at Orpheum Theatre, 126 Second Ave., New York, until April 19, 2026. Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Brittany Crowell

After touring more than 25 countries, Hate Radio, by Swiss theater director, journalist & playwright Milo Rau makes its US Debut at St Ann’s Warehouse.  A true “slice of life,” the piece, which is allegorical but based on extensive interviews, diaries, transcripts, and research,  carries with it many snippets of the true horror experienced during the genocide in Rwanda in 1994, and warnings for today’s audiences about the power that words can hold.

Performed in French and Kinyarwanda, guests enter a space from either side of a glass box containing a hyper-realistic RTLM (Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines) set up (scenic design by Anton Lukas). Upon entry to the space, the window’s blinds are down, hiding the interior, with video projections overlayed of four individuals (who we later learn are survivors, journalists, and Georges Ruggiu, one of the radio presenters, who was later on trial for war crimes).  Guests are invited to put on headsets through which they will hear testimonies from our video subjects, as well as a a sample of the radio broadcast during the height of the genocide.

In a Brechtian presentation, the situation unfolds in a realistic, journalistic manner. Narrative takes a back seat to an exploration of how language can influence behavior and how propaganda can sneak into the folds of seemingly harmless discourse.  We watch live as, in real time, the radio hosts intersperse songs like Erick Morillo’s “I like to Move It” with hate speech, history lessons reframing Rwandan history to reinforce their political messages, and comparisons between Tutsi and Hitler, between Hutu Rwanda and the struggles in Palestine.  It’s haunting how normal their messaging may sound even as they are calling for the deaths of hundreds of thousands.

English speakers experience the piece in French and Kinyarwanda, reading from supertitles projected along the top of the radio box as the hosts toss their banter back and forth.  Unfortunately for this preview performance, the supertitles were a little clunky and created a disparity between the tonality on the stage and the messaging being conveyed.  That being said, at the end of the performance, the message was clear and the delivery by the four live actors was also very strong.

Hate Radio, playing through the end of the month is an important allegory for today’s world, warning of the harm that our media’s tonality and messaging can cause and how influential it can be.  An interviewee at the end of the performance recalls an eight year old calling into RTLM and asking if they were too young to “kill cockroaches” – horrified and amazed, the journalist recounts how the RTLM host encourages everyone to do their part in the complete extermination of this group.

 

HATE RADIO – written & directed by Milo Rau

FEATURING: Afazali Dewaele (video); Sébastien Foucault; Estelle Marion (video); Eric Ngangare; Nancy Nkusi (video); Diogéne Ntarindwa; Bwanga Pilipili; Sylvain Souklaye.

Production & dramaturgy by Jens Dietrich; set and costume design by Anton Lukas; sound design by Jens Baudisch; sound design consultation by Peter Göhler; video design by Mascha Euchner-Martinez. Produced by St Ann’s Warehouse: Susan Feldman, artistic director; Erik Wallin, executive producer; Lianna Portnoy, managing director.  

At St Ann’s Warehouse: 45 Water St, Brooklyn, NY 11201

Through February 28. 

Run time: 2 hours. 

https://stannswarehouse.org/show/hate-radio/

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Stuck in a small town in Scotland with emotional walls that keep her penned in, writer and performer Leyla Aycan takes the audience on a sharply sarcastic journey that will have you both rooting for and rooting against her as the character she portrays slowly molts before you from a tough quick tempered waif to a deeply injured young late-teens woman.

Gobstopper is a black comedy about those on the fringe because they don’t quite fit in. Without a lifeline of any kind, there’s almost no chance that will ever change.

If you pay close attention to what she’s saying and ignore some of what she’s doing, you’ll hear it: that low hum of pain and loneliness, barely audible beneath her roar of survival. When you live in a small town that’s branded you, no matter how you try to cover it up, that brand sticks and shows through even your heaviest winter coat. No matter how hard she tries, Leyla’s character just can’t seem to catch a break. Do we make who we are, or does our environment dictate? A little of both I think.

Years of trauma had toughened her skin but left her spirit paper thin with but little hope. Because of her environment, she doesn’t see herself as broken, she sees herself as worthless—that’s what her world has taught her to believe, but when someone seems to really listen to her for once, like a tranquilizer, she quickly goes under a spell.

Leyla takes you on a journey throughout her day as she rides the bus, walks the streets of this small Scottish town, shoplifts, flipantly insults and then defends her offense with false justification, all the while painting in colors that meld from the 2D easy to judge characture, to a seismic 3D portrayal filled with nuance, longing, and empathy as she digs holes for herself that appear she will never be able to crawl out of.

Armed with only a chair, her shoulder bag, a couple of sound cues, and a couple of lights, Leyla elegantly portrays an anti-hero that will pull at your heartstrings as she self destructs in front of you.

——-

The Gobstopper U.S. premiere runs through March 1 at Soho Playhouse. Written and performed by Leyla Aycan. Directed by Sophie Michelle. Assistant Director is Josie Morrison Young. https://www.instagram.com/skelftheatreco

As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

by Brittany Crowell

The Waterfall, by Phanésia Pharel, begins with Bean, a first generation Haitian-American coming to the hospital to collect her mother, Emi, a vivacious, strong-willed immigrant. As Emi recovers, the play explores the conflicts and disconnect alongside the deep connection and love shared between mother and daughter.

Patrice Johnson Chevannes is Emi, a recognizable, opinionated & loveable immigrant mother who has struggled and sacrificed in order to raise her daughter in America. Natalie Paul plays Bean, Emi’s American daughter who is searching for her identity and her version of the American dream in the landscape of modern America.  The play follows Bean’s journey towards self-discovery and examines the women’s differing dreams in an exploration of generational love, sacrifice, and self-determination.

What begins as a simple two-hander grows and evolves into a highly relatable push-and-pull.  Both characters are written with such love and honor, it’s impossible not to get caught in their aspirational tug-of-war, holding space and respect for both perspectives.  Pharel has done a wonderful job of building two headstrong women who share a deep love for each other and the magic of their ancestry, which Emi connects with much more easily than Bean.

The “waterfall” in itself is a pool of ancestral inheritance both physical and magical, passed along from generation to generation of women in their family, holding their history and their future.  As Bean looks to find direction and purpose through the waterfall, she finds that she needs to connect more fully with her Haitian roots in order to truly begin to see her destiny and where she belongs.

Scenic design by Teresa Williams brings bright colors to the stage, from the tri-platform center stage depicting hospital hallways and Emi’s house in Florida, to the side walls plastered with even brighter colors and touches of Haiti (which lighting designer, Venus Gulbranson brings to full brightness when Bean travels back to the homeland).  The tri-platform flooring is painted a flowing aqua blue which drips down the front of the platform, matching a water-colored back wall of the space and  indicating that the “waterfall” is all around us.

The Waterfall, directed by Taylor Reynnolds starts as an intimate family journey but ends as one that takes on many generations and opens up the identity crisis of a first-generation American, who is searching for herself while aiming to honor her history; who is trying to be everything that her mother sacrificed for her to be while remaining true to who she really is, even when that may not fit the mold anticipated for her.

 

THE WATERFALL – by Phanésia Pharel; directed by Taylor Reynolds

FEATURING: Patrice Johnson Chevannes and Natalie Paul

Scenic design by Teresa L. Williams; costume design by Dina El-Aziz; lighting by Venus Gulbranson; co-sound design by Kaileykielle Hoga and DJ Potts; hair design by Earon Chew Nealey; dramaturgy by Amrita Ramanan; dialect design by  Wynnie Lamour-Quansah, props supervision by Emmarose Campbell. Produced by WP Theater: Lisa McNulty, producing artistic director, Michael Sag, managing director; and Thrown Stone: Jonathan Winn, co-artistic director & executive director; Jason Peck, co-artistic director.  

At WP Theater: 2162 Broadway, New York, NY 10024

Thru March 1. 

Run Time: 100 min.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

The Monsters, written and directed by Ngozi Anyanwu, is a sibling love story. Intimate moments of fight and play connect us with MMA Belt holder and brother Joseph, and sister, Josephine, who are usually just referred to as BIG (Okieriete Onaodowan) and LIL (Aigner Mizzelle).

After years apart–LIL is now big, and BIG is…well, he always had to be big. After leaving home and high school, BIG began MMA; it pulled him from addiction but also pulled him farther away from people. It rooted him in himself, forced him to acknowledge and reflect. Now, as LIL reaches her early thirties, she needs her big brother again. She yearns for his love but desperately needs his direction. Together, they need to move on.

Photo by T. Charles Erickson.

The staging and ease of moving heavy bags on and off stage, the simplicity of the staging allowing light and shadows in–I can’t get over how seamlessly moving props meshes into the performance. Childhood memories are precious and thoughtfully executed. Anyanwu uses sound, music, and movement to transition us from present day back into their youth: foreceful intentional movements, to the softer voices and movement of a child, as LIL plays with Ninja Turtles on the floor or play wrestles with BIG. The monsters we see in the ring are still the same gentle siblings we see decades in the past. Teen BIG mirrors his adult-self: a guardian shielding LIL from the danger and blame of their father; a protector as he helps out LIL and begins training her for MMA.

Photo by T. Charles Erickson.

Alcoholism has affected their familial relationships and completely altered their upbringing. BIG wants to cut every last string that corrupted his and LIL’s world. Having once struggled with alcoholism like his father, he urges LIL to get sober. I think MMA held several meanings for BIG, and all of those he wanted to show LIL: that greater hope, the pride in herself, the coping, acknowledging the shame, the bruises they they carry from youth to now. The ring is a way to heal, or fall all over again. Through almost a decade, LIL and BIG train together and apart, fight in words and gloves, surrender in play and desperate renewal.

boxin Photo by T. Charles Erickson.

While the minutes we spend watching BIG train and fight that invisible contender (again, SO technical and esquisite) are captivating, I want to see more of the siblings training together. Suddenly we’re years into her own career, into the start of a new life chapter for BIG. I wanted to see BIG as that protector in the ring, rather than just that post-match critiquer. I wish I could have seen more intense moments of them fighting against that monster inside of them as they clashed. That “Monster” is kind of on the backburner until we get to the end of this performance, and see how they learn to leave that part of them behind.

“You don’t want to be an animal, but you fight in a cage for a living.”

Photo by T. Charles Erickson.

Mizzelle brings comedy to this piece that I didn’t expect–it’s raw, honest, and direct. The dialect, the way the actors carry themselves and smirk. These little movements and and the starts and ends of conversations are what keeps us focused, laughing, and believeing in the rebirth of siblings, together and apart. I want them to allow themselves to reach that greater joy in life, to transcend the trauma of their youth, to fight against the pain that the abandonement of their childhoods and of each other left them.

This dance they share–the playtime they share in the ring–is beautiful, it’s intense, it’s rhythmic. (Having just come from my own boxing class, I was still into that dance.)

I wait for one of them to get injured–to take it too far–when they spar each other, but they don’t. They know their limits, each other.

They get vulnerable. They play it off. BIG never got to be a boy, to be little. But almost a decade after seeing LIL again and rebuilding that bond, BIG is starting a family of his own. Now he can just be Joseph. Their intimicy is shown through benches being pulled together, the heated moments on top of each other, breathing and knowing what they’re both capable of.

“You can put the monster away.”

Written & Directed by Ngozi Anyanwu.

FEATURING Aigner Mizzelle (LIL) and Okieriete Onaodowan (BIG).

Alexus Jade Coney (Stage Manager), Alyssa K. Howard (Fight Captain), Aigner Mizzelle (Dance Captain).

CREATIVE TEAM: Rickey Tripp (Choreographer), Andrew Boyce (Scenic Design), Mika Eubanks (Costume Design), Cha See (Lighting Design), Mikaal Sulaiman (Original Music & Sound Design), Gerry Rodriguez (Fight Direction), Sijara Eubanks (MMA Consultant).

Manhattan Theatre Club’s The Monsters will play at New York City Center Stage II (131 W 55th St), until

The Monsters runs for one hour and thirty minutes without an intermission. Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

After a 2024 London premiere, Alexander Zeldin‘s The Other Place, hisses a torrent of silent shame. The set and broken family initially resembles a television drama: but darker than a sitcom or soap opera. Grief and trauma and destabilizing shame plows Chris (Tobias Menzies) and the life he has rebuilt since his brother’s death. He starts fresh with partner, Erica (Lorna Brown), and her teen Leni (Lee Braithwaite). Chris’s niece, Issy (Ruby Stokes), lives with them, and her sister, Annie (Emma D’Arcy) is coming to lay their father to rest.

Photo by Maria Baranova

Ashes from their father are in an urn; they’re moved into a Ziploc baggie, back to the urn, back to the baggie, back to the urn–

Neighbor Tez (Jerry Killick), emerges from the audience in flip flops to scatter ashes, he saunters in and out, fetches food, gives space but makes everything just the right amount more awkward, immersing himself in family drama that somehow still feels better than being in his own unhappy life.

The music by Yannis Philippakis and lighting design by (James Farncombe) drives day to night and calm to compressing subtly yet uncomfortably loudly.  Sudden, blasting music is jarring and obtrusive. It shakes me, leaving me feeling grated. I’m awake, alive. A single rectangular panel pivots from the ceiling, illuminating the entire space, bouncing reflections of our faces off glass sliding doors. A blue tent stands pitched in the backyard, bare trees, a dirt yard on either side of this expansive kitchen and living space.

Tobias Menzies and Emma D’Arcy deconstruct themselves: a relationship already murky with resentment and some crust of a deeper pain: a  which we wait to be defined.

The Other Place shows how differently people respond to grief: how long we hold it, how much we hide, why we leave it unaddressed, the coming together in folds of hate and self-disgust.

Suddenly, the psychotic drive of Chris and Annie’s relationship is exposed.

Character development is minimal in what we’re told, but we can allude to pasts and emotional states from what we are given. As I leave the theater I realize I don’t want to know more, I don’t have questions.

I feel uneasy, yet too intrigued, to hear that Chris was full of joy after his brother died; even when he was sad, he was silly…and Annie was a part of him, in that same blue tent that is now pitched in the back yard.

The tension and aversion they share for the entirety of the play til this point takes a turn to a spine-chilling, disgusting utterance.

They lift a red towel and drop it over their heads–their own little tent–

“Do they know how weird you are?”

no.

Only you know how weird I am. 

And I know how weird you are.

I’ll never look at a red hand towel the same again–

And just as quickly as my breath catches and we’re jolted in the moment between Chris and Annie, we watch Erica descend the steps into the kitchen.

But her response is what gets me. It’s disheartening, it’s miserably real; the mother in her takes center stage as Leni awakens and enters the silent chaos. Erica activates her parental protection from the home that has just been dismantled while her child slept: an omelet to make to both calm her and give them the routine they deserve. Leni didn’t ask for any of this; neither did Erica. She didn’t ask for this tragedy.  

There’s blood on Leni’s hands, so so much blood. A result I waited for so long in this play–so long that I forgot about it– has finally happened.

Chris’ll forever grieve those he led to demise, as he led himself to his own torment. It’s an expiration to any fragment of normal life he could have recovered.

As the light panel turns towards us, illuminating us and Chris, he begs us.

Don’t look at me.

Don’t look at me.

Don’t look at me.

I don’t think he’s begging for forgiveness; I think he knows he doesn’t deserve that.

Death does weird shit to us.

Photo by Maria Baranova

Written and directed by Alexander Zeldin.
FEATURING: Lee Braithwaite (Leni), Lorna Brown (Erica), Emma D’Arcy (Annie), Jerry Killick (Terry), Tobias Menzies (Chris), and Ruby Stokes (Issy).
CREATIVE TEAM: Original music by Yannis Philippakis (Foals), Set and Costume Design (Rosanna Vize), Lighting Design (James Farncombe), Sound Design (Josh Anio Grigg), Movement (Marcin Rudy), and Associate Direction (Sammy J Glover).
This is a co-production by The Shed and The National Theatre, in association with A Zeldin Company. The Other Place will play at the Griffin Theatre at The Shed, 545 West 30th Street, New York, NY until March 1, 2026. Run time is 80 minutes with no intermission.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Hey Google: Can you murder people in your sleep?

Hey Google: Can you get pregnant brushing up against a male?

Hey Google: Is Bridget McGuire on Chicago’s Most Wanted list?

These questions and more twisted thoughts plague the mind of comedian Bridget McGuire. Her diagnosed form of OCD, “Intrusive Thoughts with Harm,” had her obsessing over the smallest of concerns, chewing and chewing on them until they became all encompassing.

Her show Ballet Flats for Dinner is a solo autobiographical journey that is all funny. It wrapped up its run at Soho Playhouse this week. The show was written and performed by Bridget and directed by Arielle Beth Klein.  Ballet Flats will have you wondering about the possible diagnosis of that family member, that acquaintance/friend, or even yourself as Bridget holds up her mirror for all of us to see a little bit of ourselves.

If you rolled over a juice carton with your car, would you leap to the assumption that there had been a child attached to it, and the impact probably threw them into the bushes of one of the houses lining the street, and then would you spend an inordinate amount of time walking through the neighborhood scouring those bushes for the mangled body? Hopefully not. But she did. Out of a driving compulsion that wouldn’t let her respond in any other way. Such is her form of OCD.

It’s hard to hear these stories of her contorted mental gymnastics that send her down dark holes of cringe worthy behavior. But mostly it’s laugh out loud hilarity due to the self-deprecating talent of Ms. McGuire as she relates the stories of her life and how her mind responded to them. She knows they’re wild, not rational, unrealistic, but none of that matters, if you can think it, it must be true.

Each one of her tell on herself stories is laugh out loud funny because in retrospect she herself sees how funny they are.

There’s bravery in standing up in front of strangers, courage in sharing your darkest personal secrets

As Bridget said in closing, “If you can find humor in the hardest stuff, it makes the world a little bit better.”

The world is a little bet better, and you will be a little bet better, if you get the chance to spend some time at one of her shows. Check her website of where she’ll be appearing next.

title.rendered: Riven Productions presents five short films: Spilled Milk, Canvasback, Selin, A Tight Squeeze, and Please Call Dad

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Last night I went to a first showing of five short films produced by Riven Productions. They made all five, from beginning to end, in the course of eleven months. Impressive.

Just making them is one thing, but having them all be good is another. They succeeded. Each of these films is a director’s debut and is a solid start for each one of them. The film making and the acting, across the board were very impressive especially as they’re all just out of the gate.

——-

Spilled Milk, written and directed by McKenna Kaye.

Begins as a cute romcom and then makes a surprising sharp left turn descending into the subject of rape. It draws you in as the two lead actors, Emma Stetser and Jaun Teisaire, are both adorable as they get to know each other and then the film requires its audience to reexamine what they have just been a part of.

Some great camera work in the crowd scenes by director of photography Owen Bradner. A film filled with nuance that packs a punch.

Cast: Emma Stetser, Juan Teisaire, Renata Gabella, Matt Haverty, Holden Goldberg, and Kobe Patrick.

 

Canvasback, written and directed by Loki Olin.

Tells the story of a couple, now split; he is a famous actor and she is an entertainment journalist. She is doing a television interview with him for publicity for his upcoming film. Their past history has not been fully dealt with and the still smoldering pain comes out in their on camera exchange.  As the passive aggressive comments fly, it becomes a game for the audience to put the pieces of their past relationship together, the who did what to whom, and the tit-for-tat.

A sleigh ride of one-up-manship that doesn’t stop.

Cast: Megan Osyen, Bella Klaidman, Marlon Robbins, and Loki Olin.

 

Selin, written by Defne Ozkan and Ryan Curley, directed by Olivia Simmons.

A young Turkish swimmer is in the states to improve in her sport finds the distance between herself and her home to be getting further and further apart.  The swimmer, Defue Ozkan, and her boyfriend, Ryan Curley, delicately portray a couple that is figuring things out as they go along, with give and take, pull and push, turning away and coming together, challenging the demands of what being a couple means. A strong presentation of the work involved in keeping a relationship going as each person grows and changes.

The film gets inside of what it means to be lost.

Cast: Defne Ozkan, Ryan Curley, Cassie Martin, and Oz Eminoglu.

 

A Tight Squeeze, written and directed by Colton Caulfield

The comedy in the group, worthy of a SNL skit. It has to do with a disappearing water bottle that ends up going to some dark places. It made me laugh with the out-there ridiculousness of it. Not an easy task. Puts a smile on your face that doesn’t fade throughout the film.

Cast: Rinzin Thonden, Keegan Garant, Jack Haycox, Victoria Rodrigues, Ryan Gurian, Grayson Rieth, and Zachary Chacon

 

Please Call Dad written and directed by Mercedes Riege

Mikela (Katherine Shore), has found out a dark secret about her father whom she deeply cared for. Can she ever go back after finding out? Revealing the secret will hurt those she loves, but not doing so, would hurt them even more and make her out to be a betrayer of trust.

A woman between a rock and a hard place questioning if she is able to build a bridge back across the chasm that opened before her.

There’s a lovely scene between the two sisters as they work out what needs to be done to move forward.

Cast: Katherine Shore, Renata Gabella, Carol Hardern, Boula Ross, Ryan Gurian, and Chlore Radcliffe.

——-

The producer behind each one of these films is Mercedes Riege. She plans to keep making more and more films, establishing both herself and her company in this difficult industry. She has a drive and a force that will take her far.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Well, this production of “High Spirits” is kind of a jumble.  As I was leaving I heard two men talking

“OK so you didn’t like it?”

“I didn’t say I didn’t like it.  I said I didn’t understand it.”

In retrospect that makes sense.  I had the privilege of seeing the original Broadway production of “High Spirits” back in 1964.  It was a mini field trip with three of my high school friends and the mother of two. The show’s stars were Tammy Grimes and Beatrice Lillie.  I remember where I sat in the theatre.  It was delicious.  Ergo, for this production I knew the deal.  I can see where others got a bit lost.

The story is based on the 1941 play by Noel Coward, “Blithe Spirit” which Coward referred to as by the author as “an improbable farce in three acts”. He meant it as a rebuttal to the war.  To give people something to laugh about.

In a nutshell, this is the story of Charles Condomine (Steven Pasquale) who is doing research for a book.  He invites the local medium/clairvoyant Madam Arcati (Andrea Martin) to his home (in the English countryside of course) to conduct a seance.    The evening goes off the rails when, instead of the usual spiritual contact, Charles’s first wife Elvira (Katrina Lenk), dead these seven years, appears looking for her long lost husband and eager to stir up a a bit of trouble.  Ruth (Philippa Soo) can neither hear nor see Elvira, and it takes more than awhile for Charles to convince her that Elvira is real.  In the mean time there are several numbers by Madam Arcati that are time fillers, although because of the talented dancers brought into the mix the numbers are entertaining.  In the end – well who wants to spoil THAT surprise.

First of all let me say the talent and skill on that stage were top of the top.  The trio of Phillipa Soo, Katrina Lenk, and Steven Pasquale is exquisite.  Their voices are like sweet butter.  That plus the incredible Encores Orchestra, lead by Mary-Mitchell Campbell, should have been enough to achieve lift-off.

For me the problem was that this production is set in nowhere at all years.  This left me wondering if I had remembered correctly.  The costumes are central here because the set is so limited in space (Cheers to the actors who were up and down those tow staircases a dozen or more times.)  Not an easy task.  Phillipa Soo’s two costumes were straight out of the 1960’s as was her hair do.  On the other hand, Katrina Lenk as the ethereal Elvira was perfectly kitted out. Steven Pasquale’s suites were nondescript.  Andrea Martin was given the short stick with the oddest assembly of clothing choices: Plaid leggings, a red/orange beret and an assortment of yellow tops.  Although I must say Martin is in fine physical shape as demonstrated by her crosslegged sitting and bicycle prowess.  The last bit of puzzlement was the costumes for the dancers (who were dazzling) that mostly consisted of sweatshirts, t shirts and leggings – again all very 1960-ish.

Photo by Joan Marcus

Without a location in time, and the odd text additions of references to “Cinerama” and a fairly currect list of banned substances in “Go Into Your Trance,”  this tale lost steam.  Not for want of trying.  Everything was there except the connective tissue.

But hey – this is just my opinion.  Many in the audience were sharing their appreciation and love throughout.  And why not?  If you want a light afternoon with some gorgeous performers and a top notch orchestra – this could be a perfect antidote to the howling cold.  Nothing like coming in and discovering a warm set of tunes that only ask you to sit back and relax.  Could be worse.

HIGH SPIRITS Book, Music & Lyrics by Hugh Martin and Timothy Gray based upon the play BLITHE SPIRIT by NoelCoward, Script Adaptation by Bill Rosenfield

Director Jessica Stone

WITH Rachel Dratch, Katrina Lenk, Andrea Martin, Steven Pasquale, Jennifer Sánchez, Campbell Scott,  Phillipa Soo

Brandon Block, Delphi Borich, Marcus Byers Jr., Demarius R. Copes ,Deanna Cudjoesara ,Jean Ford, Lili Froehlich, Katie Griffith ,Benjamin Howes ,Caroline Kaneandrew, Kober Ross Lekites, Devon Mccleskey, Michael Pesko, Jeremiah Portersean Stack, Dana Steingold, Halli Toland, Kamille Upshaw Darrington, Kristin Yancy

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
by Tulis McCall

OK Here is what you should know – I am not a weeper at shows.  Mary Kate O Flanagan’s “Making A Show Of Myself” tested those boundaries.

If you are looking for a one person show that is a constructed piece of theatre – this is not that.  If you are looking for some beguiling story telling – you’re in the right place.  O Flanagan (no apostrophe thank you) is a wee bit of an elf.  The fact that she is the world’s only Grand Slam Champion Storyteller on public radio’s The Moth on two continents should be a clue, but that factoid is not as relevant as the woman herself standing in front of you.   Her powers to seduce you are not obvious.  She seems at first to be a person of Good Deeds, in the words of the Wizard.  And that is perfectly fine until the stories roll out like flour sprinkled on a butcher block.

She tells us in the beginning how many stories she has (six) and how they will demonstrate her premise that stories have a beginning, middle and end which is not news.  What IS news is that sometime the beginning of the story is not present in the telling.  And it is the telling that breathes life into a tale.  Without the telling there would be the absence of a tale.

It is in the telling that the story is shaped, and at the same time we are shaped by story.  There is a magical power to stories.  The stories she tells us are meant to inspire us to look at our own lives because we have many a story to tell.  Hers start with her great grandmother taking in a German POW during WWII. (They lived in a town containing a POW camp because her great grandfather reasoned it had better chance of not being bombed.) The family gave the soldier shelter and kindness he had not known for a many a year.  This act carried through several decades until a proper reunion of families happened long after the originators had passed.

There is the image of her father’s wake ) at home of course, with the body laid out and the whiskey and stories flowing).  The pallbearers – there’s the weepy bit.

She tells us of per personal journey to make herself better and fix all the broken bits until she realized that she was not broken, and the gift of a psychic nun sealed the deal.

There’s the boy she met in a detention camp whose life intertwined with here irrevocably.

She has always meet her life’s joys and sorrows with persistence.  On some days she knows she has made all the right decisions, and on others she is certain she has make all the wrong ones.  It is on the latter days that she remembers she is in the middle of a story, and the end is still a mystery.

Stories, she tells us, reveal their gifts,  Hang in there and remember to look for every hopeful face, every flash of humor, every bit of guidance that comes like a spring breeze.  Remember that struggle is not a punishment – it is necessary.  Without it there is no story.

Go out there and tell your stories.  If  you can’t think of any – just wait. They are there.  They will come.

Give yourself a gift and go see this woman who believes in magic.  You will leave holding a bit of that magic to carry you safe until your stories appear.  Which may be sooner than you think.  Make a show of YOURSELF.

Written and performed by Mary Kate O Flanagan

Directed by Will O’Connell

Irish Repertory Theatre (132 West 22nd Street, New York, NY 10011) on February 4, 2026, with opening night set for February 8, for a limited run through March 1, 2026.  TICKETS HERE

title.rendered: Richard O’Neill and Garrick Ohlsson Deliver Musical Transcendence at the 92nd Street Y

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

When Garrick Ohlsson struck the first note, one understood immediately that something extraordinary was about to unfold. So it was at the 92nd Street Y‘s historic Kaufmann Concert Hall, where Garrick Ohlsson opened the evening with Franz Schubert‘s Impromptu in C Minor, Op. 90, No. 1, D. 899 (1827). From the majestic opening gestures — those dotted rhythms rising with ceremonial gravitas — it was clear that Ohlsson intended nothing less than a philosophical meditation on Schubert’s singular genius.

Finesse of a Master Colorist

Ohlsson’s pianistic command, honed through decades of collaboration with the great Steinway concert grands he has championed since winning the International Chopin Competition in 1970, was magnificent and flawless. Each theme emerged with radiant phrasing, every dynamic subtlety balanced with the finesse of a master colorist. The hall’s meticulously maintained Steinway concert grand — touch-up tuned during intermission with characteristic care — sang under his hands with a burnished, bell-like clarity that filled the intimate space. One recalled, in these moments, what the philosopher Theodor Adorno once suggested: that Schubert’s music occupies a landscape of wandering, a terrain where beauty and melancholy are indistinguishable.

Garrick Ohlsson, Piano. Courtesy garrickohlsson.com

Two Souls in Dialogue: The Schubert Lieder and Arpeggione Sonata

Richard O’Neill, the Grammy and Emmy Award-winning violist of the Takács Quartet, then joined Ohlsson for two of Schubert’s most beguiling Lieder, arranged here as wordless songs for viola and piano. In “Du bist die Ruh,” Op. 59, No. 2, D. 776 (1823) — that exquisite setting of Friedrich Rückert’s devotional love poem — O’Neill’s rich, velvety tone was evident from the very first bow stroke, capturing the sonic poetry of the music with an eloquence that transcended the absence of text. His playing was at once beautiful and deeply expressive, each phrase shaped with a cantabile warmth reminiscent of the finest Lieder singers.

Meeting of Artistic Minds and Kindred Musical Souls

Subsequently, in “Nacht und Träume,” Op. 43, No. 2, D. 827 (1825), O’Neill’s sublime control and expressivity proved altogether mesmerizing. The oscillating piano figurations, those active undulations Schubert deployed to energize his extraordinarily long, arcing melodic lines, flowed beneath O’Neill’s viola like moonlit water beneath a bridge. Ohlsson, for his part, was virtuosic yet wonderfully collaborative — a true meeting of artistic minds and kindred musical souls. The music arrived not as sound alone but as sensation, as the feeling of dusk settling over a familiar landscape.

Richard O’Neill, Viola. Courtesy richardhongjaeoneill.com

Pure Schubertian Song

The first half concluded with the Sonata in A Minor, Op. Posth., D. 821, the beloved “Arpeggione” (1824), originally composed for an obscure hybrid instrument that combined the tuning of a guitar with the bowing technique of a cello. Here, the duo performed in impeccable ensemble, navigating the slurred leaps and arpeggiated passages with seamless unanimity. The central Adagio, pure Schubertian song channeled through the viola’s dusky timbre, was heartbreakingly tender, while the rustic finale bounded forward with an infectious, folk-inflected energy. Throughout, O’Neill — performing on one of his rare instruments, a Matteo Goffriller viola crafted in Venice in 1727 — demonstrated why the Juilliard School honored him as the first violist ever to receive its Artist Diploma, and why the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center has long counted him among its most treasured artists.

Crossing the Stylistic Rubicon: From Schubert to Rachmaninoff

One of the evening’s most intellectually stimulating aspects was the programmatic journey itself — the leap from Schubert’s early nineteenth-century Viennese lyricism to the dense chromaticism and unabashed Romanticism of Sergei Rachmaninoff. Consider the span: Schubert, who died in 1828 knowing nothing of the harmonic upheavals to come, and Rachmaninoff, who composed well into the twentieth century while remaining gloriously impervious to the atonal experiments of the Second Viennese School. Where Schoenberg dismantled tonality, Rachmaninoff deepened it, expanding the Romantic tradition’s emotional vocabulary without abandoning its tonal foundations.

Sergei Rachmaninoff, 1900. Public Domain

A Conversation Between Eras

The effect of juxtaposing these two composers was refreshing and profoundly stimulating, illuminating how the thread of lyrical expression stretches, unbroken, across a century of seismic musical change. As Leonard Bernstein once eloquently argued, the best concert programming creates not merely a sequence of works but a narrative — a conversation between eras that reveals unexpected kinships.

Ohlsson’s Rachmaninoff: Grandeur, Passion, and Fire

After intermission, Ohlsson returned alone for Rachmaninoff’s Études-Tableaux in E-flat Minor, Op. 39, No. 5 (1917), one of the last works the composer penned before exile forced him from Russia forever. Ohlsson’s interpretation was superb in every dimension — he expressed the grandeur, the virtuosity, and above all the smoldering passion so characteristic of Rachmaninoff’s pianistic canon.

Intelligence and Structural Clarity

The incredibly rich and dense textures of this étude-painting demanded extraordinary technical command, and Ohlsson delivered with a grand finesse that illuminated form, mood, and dramatic contrast in equal measure. One sensed the pedagogical lineage at work: Ohlsson, a student of the legendary Claudio Arau, bringing to Rachmaninoff the same searching intelligence and structural clarity that defined his mentor’s art. Furthermore, the hall’s exemplary acoustics — a hallmark of the 92nd Street Y since its founding in 1874 by visionary Jewish community leaders — allowed every pianistic detail to register with crystalline precision.

The Rachmaninoff Sonata: A Summit of Collaborative Artistry

The evening’s culmination arrived with Rachmaninoff’s Sonata in G Minor, Op. 19 (1901) for viola and piano, composed in the first flush of the composer’s creative recovery following his legendary hypnotherapy sessions. The Lento opening was dramatic and expansive, with broad chords and sweeping phrases that unmistakably announced the exquisite character of late Romantic musical thought. Once more, O’Neill’s control, finesse, and extraordinary richness and beauty of sound proved remarkable — his viola sang with a transcendent luminosity that matched the virtuosic demands of Rachmaninoff’s piano partnership note for note, phrase for phrase. Together, this world-class duo brought every expressive element to the foreground with the assurance of musicians operating at the very summit of their art.

Franz Schubert by Wilhelm August Rieder, 1875. Public Domain

Operatic Emotional Depth

The ensuing Allegro blazed with fire, soaring melodies cascading over virtuosic accompaniment in passages that seemed almost cinematic in their sweeping grandeur. Indeed, a fleeting thought arose: certain passages in Rachmaninoff’s oeuvre seem to reflect the evolutionary arc of Chopin’s own compositional journey — that same marriage of pianistic brilliance with an almost operatic emotional depth. The Andante movement, by contrast, offered more of Rachmaninoff’s characteristic pathos — that unmistakable sonic beauty, at once lush and restrained, that hovers somewhere between melancholy and transcendence.

Compelling Chamber Musicians

Finally, the Allegro mosso opened in grandiose fashion, expressing the composer’s extraordinary rhythmic, harmonic, and melodic craftsmanship with an authority that left no doubt: O’Neill and Ohlsson are, individually and collectively, among the most compelling chamber musicians performing today. As Harold Schonberg might have noted in one of his magisterial New York Times reviews, the hallmark of great collaborative music-making is not uniformity but the capacity of two distinct artistic temperaments to arrive, through dialogue, at something neither could achieve alone.

An Encore to Remember: The Vocalise

After an extended, deeply felt standing ovation — the audience rising almost as one — the pair returned with a final gift: Rachmaninoff’s exquisite “Vocalise,” adapted from its original vocal setting into a wordless viola and piano meditation of aching beauty. It was, in every sense, the perfect coda to an evening that had traced the arc of Romantic expression from Schubert’s intimate lyricism to Rachmaninoff’s symphonic grandeur. The audience departed into the Upper East Side evening carrying, one suspects, the kind of interior luminosity that only the greatest music-making can bestow.

The 92nd Street Y: A Legacy of Excellence

It bears noting, finally, that evenings like this do not happen by accident. The 92nd Street Y, founded over 150 years ago, has long sustained a tradition of presenting the world’s finest performing artists in its intimate, acoustically superb Kaufmann Concert Hall. Its programming reflects a mission rooted in the conviction that the arts possess the power to enrich, enlighten, and transform lives — and that the gathering of a community around shared aesthetic experience is itself an act of profound cultural significance. In an era when such convictions are too often treated as quaint, the 92nd Street Y remains a vital and irreplaceable institution, a beacon on Lexington Avenue where the life of the mind and the life of the heart converge with uncommon grace.

Richard O’Neill and Garrick Ohlsson Deliver Musical Transcendence at the 92nd Street Y

The 92nd Street Y, New York (92NY)

Phone: (212) 415-5500
