title.rendered: Sublime Schubert: A Radiant Immersive Masterclass by the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

content.rendered:
Outside, the thermometer had plunged to single digits—the kind of merciless February evening that sends even the heartiest New Yorkers retreating to their radiators. Nevertheless, those who braved the arctic chill and made their way to the DiMenna Center for Classical Music on West 37th Street were rewarded with something far warmer than any furnace could provide. The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony (PACS), under the baton of its visionary Music Director David Bernard, presented “Sublime Schubert,” a program of staggering beauty and intellectual depth that transformed the hall into a sanctuary of tonal radiance and communal warmth. Indeed, by the time the first pianissimo tremolo of the Unfinished Symphony sparkled through the room, every last shiver had been replaced by a quiet, collective gasp of wonder.

Maestro David Bernard describing Franz Schubert’s Symphonic Works in a concert entitled “Sublime Schubert’ with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Active Inhabitants of the Orchestral Soundscape

Maestro Bernard, with his characteristic geniality and pedagogical flair, opened the evening with warm welcomes and introductions, setting the stage for what would prove to be an extraordinary immersive experience. Moreover, his remarks served as a gentle overture of their own—contextualizing the music, illuminating the genius of Franz Schubert, and, most importantly, inviting the audience to participate not merely as passive listeners but as active inhabitants of the orchestral soundscape. Clearly, the truest engagement with music demands not distance but proximity—and proximity, in every conceivable sense, was precisely what this evening delivered.

Inside the Sound: The InsideOut Concert Experience as the Ultimate Quadraphonic Journey

What distinguishes a PACS concert from virtually any other orchestral event in New York City is the patented InsideOut Concerts® format, pioneered and perfected by Bernard himself. Rather than the conventional proscenium arrangement—with its implicit barrier between performer and listener—the InsideOut model disperses the audience among the musicians of a 100-plus-member orchestra. The result is nothing less than the ultimate quadraphonic stereo experience, a total immersion in orchestral polyphony that renders even the finest home audio system a pale imitation. Consequently, every fortissimo is visceral, every pianissimo intimate, and every harmonic overtone palpable as it travels through the air and, quite literally, through your body.

Music Education and Musical Rapture Need Not Be Adversaries

Bernard encouraged audience members to look around throughout the concert, take photographs, and observe the musicianship unfolding in every direction. Furthermore, he invited individual sections of the orchestra to hold up their instruments for identification. To illuminate key passages, the orchestra performed brief excerpts. This revelatory approach—part master class, part theatrical experience, part sacred ritual—recalls what Leonard Bernstein championed in his legendary Young People’s Concerts: the conviction that music education and musical rapture need not be adversaries but can, in fact, be exquisite allies. Just as cinema devised IMAX to intensify its art form, and theater devised site-specific productions to dissolve the fourth wall, so InsideOut stands as classical music’s answer—its own revolution of intimacy and immersion.

Additionally, Maestro Bernard enriched the immersive tapestry with yet another sensory dimension: a large projection screen displaying evocative scenes, historical imagery, and contextual text throughout the performance. This visual counterpoint served as a luminous companion to the orchestral narrative, offering audiences biographical vignettes of Schubert’s world, structural annotations illuminating thematic development, and atmospheric imagery that deepened the emotional resonance of each movement. Far from distracting, these projections functioned as a kind of visual programme note — a silent docent guiding the eye while the ear remained enraptured. The effect was holistic and transporting, transforming the concert into a genuinely multisensory experience that honored both the intellect and the imagination.

Unwavering Devotion to Craft

One of the most arresting aspects of sitting within the orchestra is the opportunity to watch the faces of both musicians and fellow audience members. The musicians, generally appearing dispassionate on the surface, are in truth burning with intense concentration, particularly during the more technically demanding passages. Yet when the music alights into a tender, Romantic venture—a lyrical second theme, a sighing appoggiatura—some musicians gently smile, a quiet acknowledgment of beauty passing through their hands and breath. The audience members, by contrast, are openly expressive, their faces registering wonder, contemplation, and at times a kind of luminous melancholy that only Schubert can provoke. It takes thousands of hours of preparation and an unwavering devotion to craft to perform orchestral music at this level, and those hours were manifest in every phrase the PACS delivered this evening.

A Young Man’s Torso, Perfectly Formed: The Symphony No. 8 in B Minor (“Unfinished”)

The evening began with Schubert’s Symphony No. 8 in B Minor, the celebrated “Unfinished,” and here Bernard made a decision both generous and symbolically resonant. He honored this work—written by a young man overflowing with melodic invention—by placing it in the hands of another young man: his son, James Bernard, who served as guest conductor for the performance. It was a gesture at once paternal and artistic, a passing of the baton (literally) mirroring the essential spirit of Schubertian fellowship and mentorship.

Guest Conductor James Bernard conducting Schubert’s “Unfinished” Symphony No. 8 in a concert entitled “Sublime Schubert’ with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music. Photo courtesy PACS

Thematic Metamorphosis

Before the downbeat, Maestro David Bernard offered illuminating commentary on Schubert’s compositional process. He demonstrated how the melodic and harmonic material from the symphony’s haunting opening theme—that unforgettable pianissimo introduction in the cellos and basses, followed by the sighing oboe-and-clarinet duet—served as the generative seed from which Schubert constructed the entire work. This process of thematic metamorphosis, a hallmark of the Classical-Romantic bridge, was rendered even more vivid when sections of the orchestra performed the germinal motif in isolation, allowing the audience to hear the symphony’s DNA before experiencing it in full orchestral bloom.

Luminous Orchestration

James Bernard took the podium with the aplomb of a conductor far beyond his years. His cues were clear and confident; his expression was articulate; his command of dynamics and articulation conveyed the kind of gestural authority that elicited an immediate, musical response from the players. The Allegro moderato first movement unfolded with a brooding tensile strength—the low strings providing a subterranean rumble. At the same time, the woodwinds sang their plaintive cantilena above, a dialogue of shadow and light that Schubert managed with an emotional directness that anticipates the Romantic era’s full flowering. The Andante con moto second movement, meanwhile, arrived like a consolation—its long-breathed melodies and luminous orchestration bathing the room in a glow of serene melancholy.

Guest Conductor James Bernard conducting Schubert’s “Unfinished” Symphony No. 8 in a concert entitled “Sublime Schubert’ with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Rich Orchestral Sonority and Virtuosic Command

David Bernard also noted the poignant historical context: Schubert never heard these works performed live. In his era, orchestral resources were scarce and expensive, and it was Beethoven—towering in reputation and influence—who commanded the forces necessary for premieres of large-scale works. Consequently, Schubert composed in a kind of magnificent isolation, and Bernard opined that this solitude may have emboldened the composer to write passages of exceptional difficulty—passages that only the most accomplished orchestras could realize. It is a bittersweet irony that the PACS, with their inimitable rich orchestral sonority and virtuosic command, were now bringing these works to vibrant, breathing life in exactly the manner Schubert himself never experienced.

Heavenly Length and Earthly Triumph: The Symphony No. 9 in C Major (“The Great”)

Before launching into the second half of the program, David Bernard returned to the podium to share additional insights into Schubert’s life and creative world. He spoke movingly of the Schubertiads—those intimate salon gatherings where the composer and his small circle of devoted admirers made music, recited poetry, and nourished one another’s artistic spirits. These evenings, Bernard explained, were the crucible in which much of Schubert’s chamber music was forged, and they offer an indispensable window into the mind of a composer who died at the devastating age of thirty-one, leaving behind a catalogue of over a thousand works of breathtaking lyrical beauty. As the great critic Harold C. Schonberg once observed in his magisterial survey of the great composers, Schubert possessed an inexhaustible melodic gift that seemed to flow as naturally and continuously as a mountain stream—and the “Great” C Major Symphony represents that stream at full flood.

A Thematic Wellspring

The Symphony No. 9 in C Major is, by any reckoning, a monumental work—Schubert’s capstone orchestral achievement, a composition of what Robert Schumann famously described as “heavenly length.” Bernard introduced the work by having the orchestra perform the celebrated opening horn theme once again, that noble, arching melody that serves as the thematic wellspring for the entire four-movement edifice. This holistic programming approach—showing the audience the architectural blueprint before unveiling the completed cathedral—gave the performance an extraordinary sense of narrative coherence and intellectual transparency.

Maestro David Bernard describing Franz Schubert’s Symphonic Works in a concert entitled “Sublime Schubert’ with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music. Photo Courtesy PACS

A Marvel of Sustained Lyricism

And then the symphony began in earnest, and it was magnificent. David Bernard’s conducting was its usual expressive, precise, and deeply artistic self—a masterclass in orchestral leadership. His rubato was judicious, his accelerandi thrilling, his pianissimi gossamer-thin and achingly beautiful. The first movement’s sonata-form exposition unfolded with grandeur and rhythmic vitality; the Andante con moto second movement was a marvel of sustained lyricism, with the oboe soloists and the strings trading phrases of devastating tenderness; the scherzo blazed with rustic energy and contrapuntal wit; and the finale—that titanic, surging Allegro vivace—built to a peroration of genuine orchestral triumph.

Richly Burnished Sonority

Throughout this demanding work, the PACS musicians prevailed with remarkable aplomb. The woodwind section displayed impeccable intonation and a singing legato. The brass, particularly in the horn passages that are the symphony’s lifeblood, projected with warmth and heroic resonance. The strings—from the shimmering tremolandi of the first violins to the muscular, propulsive eighth-note figures in the cellos and basses—delivered the kind of richly burnished sonority that has become a PACS hallmark. And the timpanist anchored the rhythmic foundations with precision and dramatic flair, particularly in the finale’s electrifying coda. Considering the symphony’s length and formidable technical demands, the orchestra’s sustained concentration and musical cohesion were nothing short of exemplary.

Maestro David Bernard conducting Schubert’s “Unfinished” Symphony No. 8 in a concert entitled “Sublime Schubert’ with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music. Photo courtesy PACS

A Holistic Vision: Bernard’s Gift for Musical Storytelling

What elevates a PACS InsideOut Concert from mere performance to genuine artistic event is Maestro Bernard’s extraordinary gift for musical storytelling. His spoken commentary throughout the evening was never pedantic or gratuitous; rather, it was illuminating, engaging, and suffused with a palpable love for the music and a sincere desire to share it with everyone in the room. He described his goal as providing the audience with a “holistic” view of Schubert’s music. This approach encompassed not only the sonic experience of the works but also their biographical context, compositional architecture, and emotional depth.

Artist Conversations

This pedagogical generosity recalls the great tradition of musical lecturing that stretches from the 92nd Street Y’s legendary programming—an institution whose decades of pre-concert talks, master classes, and artist conversations have done immeasurable service to music education in New York—to Bernstein’s televised explorations of symphonic form. And now, with its steadfast mission to enrich communal life through the arts, the PACS exemplifies the belief that great music thrives when it is not cloistered but shared, not merely performed but explained, contextualized, and brought into dialogue with its listeners’ lives. Bernard’s InsideOut Concerts operate in precisely this spirit, and the results—judging by the rapt attention and audible delight of this evening’s audience—speak for themselves.

The DiMenna Center: A Jewel Box for Immersive Music-Making

A word must be said about the venue itself. The DiMenna Center for Classical Music, located at 450 West 37th Street in the heart of Hell’s Kitchen, is New York City’s only acoustically optimized space dedicated exclusively to classical music rehearsal, recording, and performance. Opened in 2011 as the permanent home of the Orchestra of St. Luke’s, the Center has since welcomed more than 100,000 visitors and over 400 ensembles. Its warm, resonant acoustics and flexible seating configurations make it an ideal home for the InsideOut format, and the space’s intimacy ensures that every nuance of the orchestra’s playing registers with clarity and emotional impact.

Schubert’s Eternal Song: Why This Music Still Matters

Franz Schubert, who died in 1828 at the age of thirty-one, left behind a body of work of astonishing breadth and emotional depth—over six hundred songs, numerous chamber works, piano sonatas, masses, operas, and nine symphonies. He was, as Schumann recognized with prophetic clarity when he unearthed the “Great” C Major Symphony in 1839, a composer whose music bore within it “the core of everlasting youth.” It took roughly four decades after Schubert’s death for the world to recognize his full genius, and his influence ultimately rippled through the work of Brahms, Dvořák, Bruckner, and Mahler. If he was not the first of the Romantics—that distinction belongs more properly to Weber—he was, in the words of the great critics, the first lyric poet of music, a designation that rings truer with every passing generation.

Franz Schubert by Wilhelm August Rieder 1875. Public Domain

As Inevitable as Birdsong at Dawn

There is in Schubert’s music a quality of interior luminescence—a way of catching the fleeting impressions of consciousness and fixing them in sound that is akin to the stream-of-consciousness technique in literature. His melodies arrive not as constructed things but as natural phenomena, as inevitable as birdsong at dawn, and yet they carry within them a piercing awareness of transience that gives them their peculiar, aching beauty. To sit inside the orchestra and feel these melodies pass through you—through the vibration of nearby strings, the breath of a neighboring oboist, the resonance of a French horn bell pointed directly at you—is to experience Schubert’s music in the most intimate and revelatory way possible. It is, in a word, transformative.

An Invitation to Experience Music Anew

This was, from first note to last, an evening of solid musicianship and inspired artistry, replete with the PACS’s inimitable rich orchestral sound. Maestro David Bernard, commanding and eloquent at the helm, demonstrated once again why he has been called “the Johnny Appleseed of Classical Music”—a champion and evangelist for an art form that too many have written off as inaccessible or irrelevant. James Bernard, stepping confidently into the spotlight, proved himself a conductor of genuine promise and musical sensitivity. And the men and women of the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony played with the kind of devotion, precision, and heartfelt expression that honors not only the composer but the art of music itself.

Single-Composer Deep Dives

If you have not yet experienced an InsideOut Concert, do not wait. The PACS’s 2025–2026 season, “Immersions and Explorations,” promises more evenings of this caliber—programs built around single-composer deep dives that draw audiences into broader, deeper perspectives on the masterworks. Classical music, at its best, is not a museum piece but a living, breathing, communal act of beauty and meaning. The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony, under David Bernard’s inspired leadership, proves this truth anew with every performance.

Maestro David Bernard conducting Schubert in a concert entitled “Sublime Schubert’ with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music. Poster courtesy PACS

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

JUST DESSERTS: A Musical Bake-Off, now playing at AMT Theater, is just what the title suggests – a musical about a bake-off.  No not the Great British Bake-Off, with famous chefs and the weirdest, candied-fruit, nut-filled, 12-flavor concoctions you have ever seen (I love the GBB but I gotta be honest about the food).  No, our story is hyper-local.  In a true moment of Americana, five contestants have gathered to compete for the baking crown at the Jefferson County Fair.

Emma, (an excellent Tori Jade Lopez) a spunky, precocious, determined young woman, has Big Plans for her Future.  Equally determined is the three-time Jefferson County Bake-Off winner Mildred (vocal powerhouse Klea Blackhurst).  Not one to rest on her laurels, Mildred has come to Play.  Ditto Blackhurst.  She is assured, engaged and interesting, and when she opens her mouth to sing, you know you are dealing with the real thing.   On the shyer side, we have Lou (a gentle, reassuring JP Sarro, who risks fading into the background) a teddy bear nice guy with a secret, and the even shyer Jean (sweet voiced, versatile Gina Lamparella, who is clearly batting below her level in this show.)  Jean is a school nurse whose dedication to service has extended to the level of self-sacrifice when it comes to being at her sister’s beck and call.  Remarkably, Jean has gathered her courage to the sticking point, as it were (despite no sticky buns being on the bake-off menu), and is taking her first bold step in a long time.  In the middle is the brash and gregarious Brandy (a delightful Lauren Nicole Shirley.)  Brandy is indeed a fine girl – a little too loud, a little too bright, but with her own vulnerabilities and true heart.  She’s won some; she’s lost some, but she has not let that dim her light.  Running the show is Las Vegas heartthrob wannabe Zack (a funny, engaging Michael Hunsaker).  The local weatherman branching out to ‘show biz’, after a day of wrangling bakers and 4H Club distractions, he may want to rethink his plans.

The individual experience of these cast members varies widely, from Broadway to community theater, but they all bring real commitment to their performances.  I wish the writing matched their energy, but alas it does not.  The music is repetitive and mostly uninteresting, despite orchestrations that include actual harmony and depth (egad!).  The book itself reads like pre-teen literature, a bit on the nose, and lacking any real tension.  I am sorry to say that, because we all know how much work goes into bringing an artistic vision to fruition.

The elements are there, but the show just doesn’t level up.  It comes off as amateurish and under rehearsed.  It is also too long.  This absolutely should be 90 minutes, no intermission, which would also give the theater a little more time to sell some delicious treats after the show.

JUST DESSERTS: A Musical Bake-Off, Book and lyrics by Barbara Campbell, and music by Brad Ross.  Directed by Tom Wallace.

With Tori Jade Lopez, Klea Blackhurst, JP Sorro, Gina Lamparella, Lauren Nicole Shirley, and Michael Hunsaker.

Music direction by Matthew Lowy, lighting design by Melanie Leff, costume coordination by Adrian (Ria) Mellowes, sound design by Steven Fine.

Runs through February 22nd, 2026 at AMT Theater, 354 West 45 Street, NYC.  For schedule and tickets, go here, or go to www.amttheater.org/justdesserts.  Run time:  two hours with one intermission.

yoast_head_json.og_description: JUST DESSERTS: A Musical Bake-Off, now playing at AMT Theater, is just what the title suggests – a musical about a bake-off.  No not the Great British Bake-off - this one is hyper local. In a true bit of Americana, five contestants have gathered to compete for the baking crown at the Jefferson County Fair. I wish the writing matched the energy and pedigree of a lot of the cast, but alas it does not.  The music is repetitive and mostly uninteresting, despite orchestrations that include actual harmony and depth (egad!).  The book itself reads like pre-teen literature, a bit on the nose, and lacking any real tension.  I am sorry to say that, because we all know how much work goes into bringing an artistic vision to fruition.

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

title.rendered: Where Wonder Wears No Age: The Artistry Behind Broadway Magic Hour

content.rendered:
Jim Vines and Carl Mercurio conjure something rarer than illusion at the Broadway Comedy Club — they conjure shared joy

There exists a particular alchemy in live performance that cannot be bottled, streamed, or swiped into view — the moment an entire room holds its collective breath, and then, simultaneously, exhales in delight. That phenomenon, at once ephemeral and deeply lasting, is precisely what Jim Vines and Carl Mercurio achieve every weekend at The Broadway Magic Hour, their family-friendly magic show now flourishing in its second year at the historic Broadway Comedy Club on West 53rd Street in the heart of New York City’s Theatre District. Indeed, to witness this show is to understand that the finest theatrical magic has never been merely about deception — it is, and always has been, about revelation.

Jim Vines and Carl Mecurio in a scene from The Broadway Magic Hour at the Broadway Comedy Club in New York City. Courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

A Prestidigious Inheritance: The Legacy of Family Wonder

Consider, for a moment, the lineage to which Vines and Mercurio belong. Not merely the technical genealogy of stage magic — from Robert Houdin‘s elegant parlor mysteries to the grand spectacles of the modern illusionist — but, more importantly, the sacred tradition of adults who understand how to speak to children without condescension. Captain Kangaroo knew this secret. Sesame Street codified it. Fred Rogers, with his gentle cardigan and boundless patience, elevated it to philosophy. These luminaries grasped an essential truth that the finest children’s entertainers have always intuited: young audiences do not want to be talked down to — they want to be invited up.

Vines and Mercurio, consequently, operate in that noble tradition with a virtuosity that is both technically dazzling and emotionally generous. Their show is not a children’s program that tolerates adults; rather, it is a theatrical experience calibrated — with the precision of a Swiss chronometer — to captivate every sensibility in the room simultaneously. As the great children’s author Maurice Sendak once observed, children live in the same world adults do; they simply experience it with wider eyes. The Broadway Magic Hour opens those eyes wider still.

Jim Vines: The Prestidigitator as Poet

To watch Jim Vines perform sleight of hand is to witness a kind of visual lyricism — a bravura display of dexterity so refined that it transcends mere trickery and enters the realm of genuine artistry. His career credentials alone are formidable: the FISM North American Championship in Close-Up Magic, a celebrated appearance on Penn & Teller: Fool Us (Season 10, Episode 17) that drew the duo’s unequivocal praise, performances across eleven countries, and residencies at the world-famous Magic Castle in Hollywood. Furthermore, his original effects have been published in Genii Magazine and The Linking Ring, the prestige journals of the conjuring arts.

Jim Vines performing in a scene from The Broadway Magic Hour at the Broadway Comedy Club in New York City. Courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

Yet none of those accolades quite captures what makes Vines extraordinary in the intimate setting of a family show. His magic, at its core, is an act of generosity. When a young volunteer steps onstage — trembling with excitement, eyes wide as saucers — Vines treats that child as a collaborator, never a prop. His manner recalls the spirit of the great Roald Dahl dictum that children are not merely small adults but astonishing beings possessed of their own magnificent logic. Accordingly, when Vines invites a child to participate in an illusion, the moment belongs to the child. The applause, the gasps, the delighted bewilderment of the audience — all of it flows toward that young person standing in the spotlight, experiencing the transcendent sensation that they, personally, helped make the impossible happen.

Carl Mercurio: The Comedic Maestro of Misdirection

Carl Mercurio brings a complementary and equally essential brilliance to the partnership. A former corporate executive who abandoned the boardroom for the stage — a leap of faith that itself deserves admiration — Mercurio has spent more than twenty-five years honing a performance style that blends classical conjuring technique with the comic timing of a seasoned raconteur. He is a regular performer at Mohegan Sun Casino, City Winery, Smoke & Mirrors Magic Theater in Philadelphia, and the Chicago Magic Lounge — venues that demand both technical excellence and genuine charm in equal measure.

Jim Vines and Carl Mecurio performing with Magic Wands and a Child’s Sneaker in a scene from The Broadway Magic Hour at the Broadway Comedy Club in New York City. Courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

Moreover, Mercurio possesses that rarest of theatrical gifts: the ability to play the sage jester while being anything but. Throughout the show, his comedic interplay with Vines generates a kind of affectionate pandemonium. At one point, Vines attempts a particularly intricate illusion while Mercurio — ostensibly assisting — slyly sabotages proceedings behind his partner’s back, to the shrieking delight of every child in the room. This is slapstick elevated to art, reminiscent of the interstitial chaos of Abbott and Costello yet executed with the knowing wink of performers who understand that the joke, ultimately, is a gift. One thinks of the playful mischief in Dr. Seuss’s The Cat in the Hat: controlled mayhem designed to thrill children while reassuring adults that capable hands are guiding the narrative.

An Enchanted Afternoon: The Show Unfolds

The enchantment begins, notably, before the curtain ever rises. As the audience assembles — families, tourists, grandparents clutching small hands — pop songs about magic fill the room with anticipatory energy. Meanwhile, Vines and Mercurio themselves circulate among the tables, these two dapper gentlemen performing close-up card tricks that astonish adults and mesmerize children from the very first moment. It is a masterful touch that establishes intimacy and trust before the formal performance commences.

Jim Vines and Carl Mercurio in a scene with volunteers in “The Big Money Challenge?” from The Broadway Magic Hour at the Broadway Comedy Club in New York City. Courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

Once onstage, the duo’s complementary temperaments ignite a kinetic hour of escalating wonder. Card tricks give way to sleight-of-hand illusions; objects vanish and reappear with bewildering nonchalance; and throughout, a carefully curated soundscape of imaginative children’s music and perfectly timed sound effects enriches each sequence with additional layers of theatrical atmosphere. The show’s dramaturgy — its careful arc from intimate close-up mysteries to full-stage spectacle — reveals experienced showmen who understand pacing as intuitively as a conductor understands tempo.

Children Take the Stage — and Soar

The audience participation sequences constitute the show’s emotional crescendo. Multiple young volunteers are invited onstage throughout the performance, each one treated with warmth, respect, and conspiratorial delight. In one breathtaking sequence, a small boy is levitated — actually, physically, impossibly elevated above the stage — and the collective gasp that rises from the audience is not merely surprise but something closer to awe, that ancient and irreducible human response to witnessing the impossible. The child’s own laughter, pure and unguarded, ripples through the room like the most beautiful incantation.

Jim Vines and Carl Mecurio performing Levitation with a volunteer in a scene from The Broadway Magic Hour at the Broadway Comedy Club in New York City. Courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

In another memorable turn, a father gamely volunteers and risks a hundred-dollar bill in a trick that concludes, improbably and hilariously, with the currency materializing inside a Kiwi fruit. The sequence is a miniature masterpiece of narrative construction: tension, release, surprise, and joy, all compressed into minutes. All share his relief at getting his $100 back. Later, the duo performs full-audience card tricks whose collective result leaves both children and adults shaking their heads in genuine astonishment. These are not merely tricks; they are communal experiences — shared moments that, as J.M. Barrie understood when he wrote Peter Pan, depend upon the audience’s willingness to believe, and reward that belief magnificently.

Where Families Share Wonder: The Enduring Magic of Connection

What distinguishes The Broadway Magic Hour from lesser entertainments — and what secures its place in the proud lineage of programs that honor childhood’s imaginative sovereignty — is its profound understanding that the most powerful magic occurs not onstage but between people in the audience. A grandmother gleefully gasps at the precise moment her five-year-old grandson does. A father, briefly and beautifully, forgets to be a grown-up. A teenager who arrived with studied indifference departs with genuine wonder in her eyes. Children can hardly contain themselves when the duo asks them questions. These are the moments that Vines and Mercurio have been cultivating since they first met performing at Coney Island’s beloved Magic at Coney variety show over a decade ago — a serendipitous encounter that ultimately led, through years of collaborative performances across the tristate area, to the creation of this very show.

Jim Vines and Carl Mercurio performing in a scene, “Where did the Root Beer Bottle Go?” from The Broadway Magic Hour at the Broadway Comedy Club in New York City. Courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

Since its sold-out premiere at the Broadway Comedy Club in August 2024, The Broadway Magic Hour has earned recognition from Time Out New York as one of the city’s best off-Broadway shows for kids and families, and one of the best magic shows in New York City. That acclaim is richly deserved, yet it only partially captures what makes this show special, for what Vines and Mercurio offer transcends critical categories.

They offer something increasingly rare in our fractured, screen-saturated age: an hour in which families sit together, look in the same direction, and share authentic astonishment. In a world where, as Neil Postman once warned, childhood itself risks disappearing into the static of endless digital distraction, that is no small enchantment. It may, in fact, be the greatest trick of all.

How do They Do It? Jim Vines and Carl Mercurio present The Broadway Magic Hour at the Broadway Comedy Club in New York City. Courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

Where Wonder Wears No Age: The Artistry Behind Broadway Magic Hour

Show Information & Tickets

The Broadway Magic Hour with Jim Vines and Carl Mercurio

Venue: Broadway Comedy Club, 318 W. 53rd Street, New York, NY 10019

(Between 8th & 9th Avenues, Theater District)

Schedule: Select Fridays, Saturdays & Sundays — Weekend Matinees at 2:00 PM

Tickets: www.broadwaymagichour.com/tickets

Phone: (347) 915-3050

Email: broadwaymagichour@gmail.com

Jim Vines: www.jimvines.com

Carl Mercurio: www.carlmercurio.com  |  (646) 808-6383  |  MercurioMagic@yahoo.com

excerpt.rendered: The Broadway Magic Hour, starring Jim Vines and Carl Mercurio, transforms weekend afternoons into luminous shared experiences where children levitate, adults rediscover wonder, and families create memories that outlast any illusion. Award-winning artistry meets heartfelt comedy at the Broadway Comedy Club in Times Square. Unmissable family magic — book your seats before they vanish.

title.rendered: Forging an American Musical Identity by the ASO and Bard Festival Chorale

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

On January 30, 2026, the American Symphony Orchestra returned to its spiritual home—Carnegie Hall, specifically the Isaac Stern Auditorium—with a program whose ambitions matched the grandeur of the space. Titled Forging an American Musical Identity, the evening traced the complicated, often paradoxical genealogy of American concert music: European inheritances refracted through a restless New World imagination, Indigenous and African American sources long marginalized, and a late-19th-century nationalism that both aspired and deferred.

American Symphony Orchestra. Courtesy americansymphony.org

At the helm stood Leon Botstein, whose curatorial intelligence and pre-concert lecture framed the evening not as a museum tour but as a living inquiry. Botstein’s scholarship—brisk, humane, and enriched with anecdote—prepared the ear for discovery. He spoke of provenance and purpose, of how ideas travel, settle, and transform, reminding us that American music did not emerge whole but was forged—heated by history, hammered by contradiction, polished by aspiration. The program book, rich and generous, amplified this inquiry with essays that functioned as a vade mecum for listeners eager to go deeper.

Maestro Leon Botstein. Photo by Edward Kliszus

An Overture of Assertion: Dudley Buck and the National Air

The evening opened with Dudley Buck’s Festival Overture on the American National Air, a work that wears its intention proudly. Buck’s treatment of “The Star-Spangled Banner” is neither ironic nor bombastic; rather, it is confident, ceremonious, and grounded in a 19th-century symphonic rhetoric that sought legitimacy through craft. Under Botstein’s baton, the ASO’s strings sang with breadth, winds articulated with civic clarity, and brass crowned phrases with burnished authority. One sensed not mere patriotism but a composer asserting that American material could sustain symphonic argument.

Spirituals as Living Architecture: Burleigh and J’Nai Bridges

If Buck asserted, Harry T. Burleigh testified. His arrangements of spirituals—“Go Down, Moses,” “Behold that Star!,” and “Swing Low, Sweet Chariot”—were entrusted to J’Nai Bridges, whose performance radiated assurance and inward glow. Bridges shaped each phrase with poise and breath-led intelligence; pianissimo floated like prayer, fortissimo rang with uplift. What impressed most was communion: a sense that these songs were not presented but inhabited. The orchestra supported with restraint, allowing the spiritual architecture—call, response, ascent—to speak plainly and powerfully. Bridges’s voice conveyed a lovely, richly dramatic character, bringing the vocal narrative’s reflections and passions to life.

J’Nai Bridges, Mezzo Soprano. Photo by Arvin Prem Kumar

A Curious Centennial: Wagner in America

The program’s most curious artifact, Richard Wagner’s Großer Festmarsch (American Centennial March), arrived as both spectacle and question mark. Commissioned for the 1876 centennial, it bears Wagner’s unmistakable orchestral handwriting without his deepest imaginative urgency. Heard here, it functioned less as a masterpiece than as a historical document—a reminder of America’s lingering deference to Europe even while proclaiming independence.

Botstein resisted inflation; the ASO played with discipline and color, revealing the march’s pageantry while keeping its limitations audible. Wagner’s signature motivic thinking is present but strategically restrained, serving architectural clarity rather than psychological depth. The Großer Festmarsch is not Wagner thinking aloud, but Wagner speaking publicly. Its grandiose, dramatic denouement—precisely because it forgoes subtlety—lands with unapologetic theatrical force, proof that even when Wagner simplifies, he never thinks small.

Niagara Reclaimed: Bristow’s Monument

After intermission came the evening’s cornerstone: George Frederick Bristow’s Symphony No. 5, “Niagara”, a sonic portraiture of Americana of the late 19th century. Last heard complete in this hall at its 1898 premiere, the work returned as a valedictory monument—part Beethovenian ambition, part American panorama. The ASO’s inimitable string sheen carried the symphony’s long spans; winds painted a landscape; brass summoned grandeur without glare.

The Symphony No. 5 expressed idyllic, poetic, and scenic moments through gentle phrasing. Notable were descriptive sounds of pastorale beauty and bold, richly arranged brass writing. There were notable inferences from the 19th century with hymnody and dashes of Mendelssohn, Romberg, and Lehar.

The vocal forces—Anna Thompson, J’Nai Bridges, Freddie Ballentine, and Alan Williams—integrated seamlessly with the Bard Festival Chorale, prepared with incisive clarity by James Bagwell.

Anna Thompson’s soprano brought a luminous clarity to Bristow’s score, her tone floating with poise above the orchestral layers while retaining a firm, expressive center. The voice combined freshness and control, shaping phrases with elegance and precision, and lending the music an inward radiance that balanced the symphony’s broader gestures. Even in its most exposed moments, Thompson’s singing conveyed confidence and refinement, her line unfolding with natural musical intelligence.

J’Nai Bridges anchored the vocal ensemble with a mezzo-soprano of striking depth and presence, her sound rich, grounded, and emotionally resonant. She sang with commanding assurance, drawing warmth and gravity from the lower register while allowing the line to expand seamlessly into moments of heightened intensity. Bridges’s vocal authority lent the symphony a sense of human weight and inward strength, her phrasing both generous and keenly attentive to the music’s expressive arc.

Freddit Ballentine’s lyric tenor seemed to rise and surge like the symphony’s namesake, flowing with elegance before gathering dramatic force in moments of radiant culmination. Ringing climaxes carried emotional authority without hardness, the voice preserving suppleness and textual sensitivity even as Bristow’s music leaned toward its most expansive, affirmative gestures.

Alan Williams contributed a bass-baritone voice of resonant solidity and noble bearing, projecting with clarity and calm authority. The timbre carried gravitas without heaviness, grounding Bristow’s expansive vision of programmatic aural poetry in firm tonal assurance. Williams shaped his lines with restraint and purpose, offering a vocal presence that conveyed stability and breadth, reinforcing the symphony’s monumental character without overstatement. Williams anchored the ensemble with sonorous authority. The chorale’s diction and dynamic control brought Bristow’s texted finale into sharp relief, the Niagara metaphor unfolding as both natural wonder and spiritual ascent.

Anna Thompson, Soprano. Courtesy avaopera.org

The Room That Listens Back: Carnegie Hall

Carnegie Hall proved an ideal partner. Its acoustics—resonant yet precise—allowed tuttis to bloom and inner voices to speak. One felt the hall listening back, returning sound with generosity. Such conditions are not incidental; they complete the circuit between composer, performer, and audience.

Freddie Ballentine, Tenor. Photo by Dario Acosta

Legacy and Mission: From Stokowski to Now

This concert also paid homage to the ASO’s founding spirit under Leopold Stokowski—affordable access, adventurous programming, and the revival of neglected works. Under Botstein’s stewardship, that mission has matured into a distinctive model: thematic concerts that braid music with history, literature, and ideas. Here, lesser-known American voices stood shoulder to shoulder with the canon, not as curiosities but as necessary chapters.

Why the ASO Matters

The ASO’s concerts are not to be missed because they trust audiences—trust curiosity, patience, and imagination. They remind us that repertoire is not fixed; it is a living field awaiting cultivation. This evening affirmed that American musical identity is plural, contested, and rich—and that hearing it whole requires advocacy as much as virtuosity.

Alan Williams, Bass Baritone. Screen capture courtesy LA Opera on YouTube.

Forging an American Musical Identity by the ASO and Bard Festival Chorale

American Symphony Orchestra

Leon Botstein, Conductor and Music Director of American Symphony Orchestra

Bard Festival Chorale

James Bagwell, Director, Bard Festival Chorale

Members of the Bard Festival Chorale at the ASO’s Requiem and Revelation by the ASO at St. Bart’s in NYC. Photo by Matt Dine

Soloists

J’Nai Bridges, Mezzo-Soprano

Anna Thompson, Soprano

Freddie Ballentine, Tenor

Alan Williams, Bass

About the American Symphony Orchestra

American Symphony Orchestra
Address: Carnegie Hall, 881 Seventh Avenue, New York, NY 10019
Tickets: https://americansymphony.org
Donate: https://americansymphony.org/support/

Now in its 64th season, the ASO continues its vital work—reviving rare repertoire, championing American music, and inviting audiences into concerts where ideas sing as vividly as sound.

excerpt.rendered: The American Symphony Orchestra’s Forging an American Musical Identity illuminated both forgotten paths and familiar landmarks, uniting scholarship, passion, and superb musicianship. Tonight was orchestral programming with purpose—inviting listeners to rediscover America’s musical past and eagerly anticipate the ASO’s 2025–26 season.

title.rendered: An Evening With Laura Benanti at 92NY: A Cabaret of Wit, Memory, and Musical Grace

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

From the moment Laura Benanti stepped onto the stage of 92NY, the air seemed to lift. Applause arrived not as a courtesy but as a reunion—extended, affectionate, and unmistakably earned. The audience, visibly primed with anticipation, greeted her as one greets an old friend sorely missed. That affection would return at evening’s end, swelling again into sustained ovation and two warmly received encores.

Laura Benanti in An Evening with Laura Benanti at the 92nd Street Y, New York City, with Todd Almond, music director and pianist, Ann Klein, guitar, Cat Popper, bass, and Rich Mercurio, drums. Photo Credit Richard Termine

This was not merely a concert. It was a cabaret in the fullest, most civilized sense: a shared space of storytelling, music, memory, and intelligence, shaped by collaboration and guided by taste.

Laura Benanti in An Evening with Laura Benanti at the 92nd Street Y, New York City, with Ann Klein, guitar, and Cat Popper, bass. Photo Credit Richard Termine

Cabaret as Conversation

Cabaret, at its best, is not a parade of songs but a conversation between artist and audience, past and present, text and subtext. Benanti understands this instinctively. From the outset, she was humorous, candid, and irresistibly charming, using personal anecdotes not as digressions but as dramaturgy—giving each song context, immediacy, and emotional contour.

Her tone was light without being trivial, confessional without indulgence. She invited us in, and we followed gladly.

Laura Benanti. Courtesy Laura Benanti.com

Eliza Doolittle Revisited: My Fair Lady

Benanti opened with selections from My Fair Lady, slipping once more—effortlessly—into the role of Eliza Doolittle. What emerged was not impersonation but inhabitation. Through “Wouldn’t It Be Loverly,” “Just You Wait,” “The Rain in Spain,” “I Could Have Danced All Night,” and “Show Me,” she conjured an entire Edwardian world.

Her Cockney accent was richly shaded, her phrasing alive with intention. With subtle narrative brushstrokes, she allowed us to meet not only Eliza but also Henry Higgins, Colonel Pickering, Freddy Eynsford-Hill, and Mrs. Higgins—each character briefly illuminated, then gently set back into the flow of memory. It was a masterclass in characterization through song.

Todd Almond, music director, singer, and pianist for An Evening with Laura Benanti at the 92nd Street Y, New York City. Photo Credit Richard Termine

Sondheim, Memory, and the Shape of Loss

Benanti’s reverence for Stephen Sondheim is well documented, but here it felt intimate rather than ceremonial. Her performance of “Without You” from Company was spare, unsentimental, and quietly devastating—loss rendered not as melodrama, but as a fact of weather, inevitable and endured.

“I Remember Days” from Evening Primrose followed, sung with hushed intensity. Memory, that most Woolfian of currents, flowed through the room—not nostalgia, but recognition. The song hovered, suspended between then and now, reminding us how musical theater can hold time without fixing it.

Laura Benanti. Courtesy laurabenanti.com

Todd Almond and the Architecture of the Evening

At the piano was Todd Almond, serving as music director, arranger, composer, and performer. Stylistic fluency and emotional intelligence distinguish Almond’s musicianship. His arrangements moved seamlessly between Broadway lyricism, country-rock inflection, jazz idiom, and baroque parody, all while maintaining structural clarity.

When Benanti turned to Almond’s original songs—“Mother Is a Liar,” “I’m Always Gonna Love You,” and “Here Come the Good Man”—the evening deepened. These works, grounded in family life and emotional truth, allowed Benanti to sing not about experience but from within it. Her physicality in “Here Come the Good Man,” animated by movement and character, reminded us that she is as compelling an actor with her body as with her voice.

Almond’s solo moment—an uproarious meditation on love, marriage, and jealousy, underpinned by a sly J. S. Bach pastiche—was both musically sophisticated and joyously self-aware. It landed exactly where comedy should: precise, surprising, and human.

Laura Benanti and Todd Almond, music director, singer, and pianist, in An Evening with Laura Benanti at the 92nd Street Y, New York City. Photo credit Richard Termine

The Ensemble: Musicians in Dialogue

The musicians were not accompaniment but interlocutors.

Ann Klein on guitar brought tonal color and rhythmic nuance, her playing alternately supple and incisive. Cat Popper’s bass anchored the evening with warmth and authority, while Rich Mercurio’s drumming was alert, responsive, and tastefully restrained.

Together, the ensemble functioned as a breathing organism—listening, shaping, responding.

Transformation, Satire, and Theatrical Mischief

Benanti’s return in her now-famous Melania Trump persona—complete with blond wig and razor-sharp comic precision—was a reminder of her range. The spoof, delivered with accent and aplomb, walked the fine line between satire and performance art, culminating in a knowing rendition of “Everything’s Coming Up Roses.”

Laura Benanti as Melania. Screenshot courtesy of @colbertlateshow and @laurabenanti on Instagram

Later selections—“She Loves Me,” “Recovering Ingénue,” “Vanilla Ice Cream,” and encores including “Edelweiss” and “The Impossible Dream”—felt less like finales than benedictions.

Sound, Light, and the Art of Support

The evening’s sound and lighting design was exemplary—transparent, flattering, and precise. Nothing distracted; everything served. Such technical artistry often goes unnoticed precisely because it succeeds. Here, it allowed the room to breathe and the performers to trust.

92NY: A Living Institution

Founded in 1874, 92NY has long stood as one of New York’s great cultural conveners—a place where music, literature, dance, and civic life intersect. Its legacy includes not only excellence but continuity: a belief that art belongs at the center of communal life. This evening reaffirmed that mission with grace.

Laura Benanti front stage in An Evening with Laura Benanti at the 92nd Street Y, New York City, with Ann Klein, guitar, and Cat Popper, bass. Photo Credit Richard Termine

Conclusion: Art as Shared Experience

What lingered after the final applause was not merely admiration, but gratitude. Gratitude for artists who understand that performance is an act of generosity, for institutions that honor craft, and for evenings that remind us—quietly, insistently—why live performance still matters.

As one Romantic poet once suggested, music can become the atmosphere in which feeling learns to breathe. On this night, it did exactly that.

Laura Benanti. Courtesy Laurabenanti.com

  • Todd Almond – music director/piano
  • Ann Klein – guitar
  • Cat Popper – bass
  • Rich Mercurio – drums

excerpt.rendered: Laura Benanti’s luminous evening at 92NY reaffirmed the power of cabaret as storytelling, memory, and joy. With Todd Almond and a stellar ensemble, she reminded audiences why live performance endures. The 2025–26 season promises extraordinary artists.

title.rendered: Arturo Sandoval at the 92nd Street Y: A Masterclass in Joy and Virtuosity

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

There is a particular kind of evening that arrives in a concert hall when the musicians onstage cease to be performers and become, instead, conduits for something far older and more luminous than themselves. Wednesday night at the David Geffen Stage at Kaufmann Concert Hall, inside the storied 92nd Street Y on the Upper East Side of New York City, was precisely that kind of evening. Before Arturo Sandoval even set foot onstage, his ensemble—a cohort of world-class instrumentalists—launched into a blistering, virtuosic opener at breakneck tempo, trading improvised solos over the song’s form and exchanging crackling fours with drummer Daniel Feldman. The rhythmic dialogue was electrifying, each musician’s statement more incendiary than the last. The message was unmistakable: tonight, the bar would be set at the stratosphere.

Then, from behind the stage curtain, a hand appeared—a small wave, a welcoming grin—and Sandoval stepped into the light. At seventy-seven years old, the Cuban-born trumpet titan remains a force of nature: a ten-time Grammy Award winner, Emmy recipient, Presidential Medal of Freedom honoree, 2024 Kennedy Center Honors laureate, and a protégé of the incomparable Dizzy Gillespie. To catalog his accolades is to recite a litany of modern jazz’s highest distinctions. Yet none of that quite prepares you for what happens when the man raises his horn and plays.

An Ensemble Forged in Musical Fire

As the great critic and historian Gary Giddins once observed, the truest measure of a bandleader’s artistry lies not only in what they play but in whom they choose to play beside them. By that measure, Sandoval’s ensemble is a masterwork of curatorial intelligence. On tenor saxophone, Michael Tucker—a Grammy-nominated powerhouse from Berklee College of Music and the New England Conservatory—delivered solos of startling fluidity and harmonic depth, engaging Sandoval in fiery call-and-response and unison passages that recalled the golden dialogues of bebop’s founding era. Alongside him, baritone saxophonist Larry Bustamante, a New York City native whose pedigree includes the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra and the Mingus Big Band, provided a rich, anchoring bottom voice that lent the horn section its full-bodied resonance.

Arturo Sandoval at the 92nd Street Y in NYC. L-R: Lisandro Pidre, Piano; Roberto Vizcaino, Drums; Arturo Sandoval, Trumpet; Michael Tucker, Tenor Saxophone; Larry Bustamante, Baritone Saxophone; Keith Fiala, Trumpet; and William Brahm, Guitar. Photo by Edward Kliszus

On trumpet, Keith Fiala stood as both disciple and collaborator. A former touring member of Maynard Ferguson’s celebrated Big Bop Nouveau Band and longtime associate of Sandoval, Fiala brought a bright, muscular tone and precision to every passage. Meanwhile, guitarist William Brahm—a Los Angeles-based artist and 2019 Herbie Hancock Institute semifinalist who has toured with Sandoval since 2019 and performed with Gordon Goodwin’s Big Phat Band—wove sophisticated comping and luminous solo lines throughout the evening, his Stratocaster singing with a Jeff Beck–inflected lyricism. Pianist Lisandro Pidre, an Argentine virtuoso whose résumé includes performances with Dave Weckl and orchestral conducting in Mexico City, provided harmonic sophistication and an impeccable rhythmic feel, shifting between accompaniment and solo passages with the assurance of a seasoned auteur.

In the rhythm section, bassist Maximilian Gerl—a Berklee honors graduate from Dallas who has performed with Stanley Clarke, Makaya McCraven, and Veronica Swift—proved nothing short of astonishing. As the bebop tunes roared at dizzying speeds, Gerl navigated the changes on the upright bass with two fingers alternating across the strings, his walking lines powerful, precise, and impossibly locked in. One could scarcely tap a foot fast enough to keep pace, yet Gerl never wavered. Drummer Daniel Feldman drove the ensemble with an unerring pulse, alternating between explosive polyrhythmic fills and sensitive handwork that recalled the kinetic grace of the great Afro-Cuban percussionists. And on congas and percussion, Roberto Vizcaino—son of the legendary Cuban multi-percussionist of the same name, a two-time Latin Grammy winner, and currently a member of Chucho Valdés’ Royal Quartet—laid down rhythmic patterns of intoxicating complexity, his hands summoning the ancestral pulse of the clave with a master’s authority.

Arturo Sandoval, renowned Classical Musician. Courtesy arturosandoval.com

Bebop, the American Songbook, and the Latin Soul

LeRoi Jones—later Amiri Baraka—wrote in his seminal Blues People that the story of jazz is inseparable from the story of a people’s liberation, and Sandoval’s biography embodies that thesis with rare poignancy. Born in Artemisa, Cuba, in 1949, he overcame political oppression to bring his boundless gifts to the world stage, defecting with the help of Gillespie during a tour with the United Nations Orchestra in 1990. On this evening, that journey was palpable in every note. Sandoval delivered a masterclass in bebop for the audience, explaining the form’s virtuosic unison fire—its roots in the late 1940s and its architects: Gillespie, Charlie Parker, and Clark Terry. He characterized each of these titans with humor and affection, stepping into their caricatures with a raconteur’s delight and a historian’s reverence.

The program itself traversed a thrilling landscape. Latin works of incandescent rhythmic vitality—including “Sangu” from Sandoval’s latest album—ignited the hall with their syncopated drive and percussive brilliance. The unison bebop heads, performed at breakneck tempos, showcased the ensemble’s astonishing technical command and collective telepathy. And then there were the gems from the American Songbook: Ray Noble’s “Cherokee” tore through the hall like a benevolent gale, and Henry Mancini’s “The Days of Wine and Roses” became, in Sandoval’s hands, something transcendent. He began alone at the piano, exploring the melody with a Romantic, almost Satie-like tenderness and the harmonic richness one associates with the great Kenny Barron, before Gerl and Feldman joined him in a medium swing that built and blossomed like a garden in time-lapse. It was marvelous, moving, and deeply virtuosic.

Arturo Sandoval, trumpet, and Michael Tucker, tenor saxophone, on stage at the 92nd Street Y, NYC. Photo by Edward Kliszus

The Polymath at Play: Trumpet, Piano, Timbales, and the Human Voice

I have been fortunate to see Sandoval perform several times over the years. I recall a concert decades ago at The Blue Note jazz club in Greenwich Village, expecting an evening of magnificent trumpet. What I received instead was a revelation: Sandoval rotating from trumpet to piano to timbales and cowbell with equal aplomb, a polymath in full flight. Wednesday night confirmed that the passage of time has only deepened his mastery. As Leonard Feather might have wryly noted, Sandoval at seventy-seven is more dangerous than most musicians half his age—his fingers faster, his musical vocabulary richer, his sense of drama more refined.

He moved between instruments throughout the evening with the ease of a man walking through the rooms of his own home. His trumpet playing remained fearsome—traversing registers from the instrument’s deepest, warmest tones to stratospheric high notes, delivered with dazzling technique and a tessitura that defied belief. At the piano, he conjured expressive, richly textured voicings. On the timbales, he channeled the percussive fire of his Cuban heritage. And then came the singing. Sandoval confessed, with characteristic self-deprecation, that he never liked his singing voice—but that at sixty-five, it had finally matured. He proceeded to deliver Charlie Chaplin’s beloved “Smile”—nodding to Nat King Cole’s iconic rendering—with a tenderness that hushed the room and elicited, true to the song’s title, many smiles. Perhaps this performance represented the grace and comfort of a great artist’s elder years, especially when one loves music as deeply as Sandoval and his fellow artists and audience so clearly do.

His scat singing was equally revelatory. Initially drawing affectionate chuckles, Sandoval soon clarified that scat was no mere novelty but a serious musical discipline that excited the imagination and imposed few limits—an insight that the pioneering vocal improvisers from Ella Fitzgerald to his mentor, Gillespie, would have endorsed wholeheartedly.

Arturo Sandoval. Trumpeter, Composer, and Pianist. Courtesy arturosandoval.com

The Raconteur: Humor, Heart, and the Art of Connection

What separates Sandoval from so many other virtuosi is his extraordinary gift for human connection. He is, quite simply, a charming raconteur with a wealth of anecdotes and a laid-back, self-deprecating cleverness that makes you feel as though you are conversing with an old friend over café con leche. He joked about the challenges of learning English after arriving from Cuba at forty, noting with infectious wit that English words are too vague and their rules too capricious. At the same time, Spanish, by contrast, is more logical, with sounds and words that behave themselves. This riff culminated in a hilarious bilingual exchange between Sandoval, Vizcaino, and Feldman that had the audience roaring.

He spoke candidly about the trumpet’s unforgiving nature—this brass object, he called it, with the comic timing of a man who has spent a lifetime taming it—and about how the piano, by contrast, is a forgiving instrument that he neglected in his youth because, in Cuba at the time, boys simply did not play the piano. Despite that early admonishment, his pianism tonight was sublime. Sandoval reminded the audience, with genuine humility, that the music they enjoyed was the product of many thousands of hours of practice by the individuals onstage. It was a gracious, democratic moment: the maestro insisting that the glory belonged to the collective.

A Stage Beautifully Lit and Lovingly Managed

A brief word must be said about the production values at Kaufmann Concert Hall. The lighting design was thoughtfully executed, shifting hues to set moods that mirrored the music’s emotional arc—warm ambers for ballads, cooler blues for the Latin passages, saturated tones for the fiery bebop numbers. Sound engineering was equally well managed, balancing the ensemble’s dynamic range without sacrificing intimacy. The 92nd Street Y continues to demonstrate why it has earned its reputation as one of New York’s finest concert venues.

An Evening to Remember: Why Arturo Sandoval Still Matters

In the end, what Sandoval achieves transcends technical virtuosity—though his technique remains among the most prodigious in the history of the instrument. What he achieves is something that the philosopher and musicologist Theodor Adorno would recognize as art’s highest aspiration: the capacity to make the complex accessible, the intellectual visceral, and the beautiful urgent. He makes music fun, important, interesting, and deeply human. His concert was a vivid reminder that jazz, at its best, is not a museum piece but a living, breathing, joyously present art form.

As the final notes faded into the rafters of Kaufmann Concert Hall, the standing ovation that erupted first from those dancing in the audience was not merely for the astonishing musicianship on display. It was for the spirit—generous, exuberant, unquenchable—that Arturo Sandoval continues to bring to every stage he graces. He is, in every sense, a national treasure, and his ensemble a sterling reminder that the art of jazz performance remains alive and magnificently well.

Arturo Sandoval at the 92nd Street Y: A Masterclass in Joya and Virtuosity

The 92nd Street Y, New York

The 92nd Street Y, New York, is a world-class cultural and community center that has harnessed the power of arts and ideas to enrich, enlighten, and change lives for over 150 years. Presenting more than 80 concerts each season across chamber music, solo recitals, jazz, the American Songbook, and family programming, 92NY remains one of the most vital cultural institutions in the world.

excerpt.rendered: At seventy-seven, ten-time Grammy winner Arturo Sandoval remains a blazing force of virtuosity, humor, and heart. His electrifying concert at the 92nd Street Y showcased bebop fire, Latin rhythms, and tender balladry, supported by a world-class ensemble. Seek out Sandoval live and watch for his upcoming album—this is jazz at its most joyous and vital.

title.rendered: Hans Litten: The Jew That Cross-Examined Hitler

content.rendered:
By David Walters

The staging is clumsy, the set is a hindrance to the action, the script is sluggish, and the acting is hit and miss.

BUT NONE OF THAT MATTERS!

Let me repeat, NONE OF THAT MATTERS, and should not in the slightest keep you away from attending Hans Litten: The Jew that Cross-Examined Hitler.

Because what you will witness is a piece of history that will resonate with what we are presently living and eye-witnessing today in our country. It will give you pause.

It seems that history does indeed repeat itself. While watching this play, every time you hear the word Hitler and what he is doing in Germany in the ’30s, the name Trump will scream out at you. Every time you hear the words “storm troopers” or “SA” your thoughts will stop in their tracks because the word ICE will immediately take their place.

When Hitler was first solidifying his base, he was still under the rule of law (or pretended to be). He would tell falsehoods about his plans and what his organization was doing or planned to do. The first enemy he created to vilify was communists and with the help of Goebbels propaganda, he put all of the difficulties people were having squarely on them, that they would destroy what it meant to be German, and even though their support within the country was small, they became the scapegoat for everything. One day some of Hitler’s henchmen, his private army, the SA, purposely went into a communist meeting hall in order to create trouble. They were attacked and then subsequently held up by Hitler as victims. Lawyer Hans Litten, in defending the communists, subpoenaed Hitler and put him on the stand as ultimately responsible for what happened, purposely sending his men in to cause trouble. Hans won.

This isn’t just the story of the trial though, this is the story of Hans Litten’s life, how he came to be a lawyer, what he stood for, and what happened to him after Hitler did come to power (Think personal retribution for losing. Hmmm, do we know anyone else like that?). It’s a compelling story of a man standing by his convictions despite the full knowledge of where those convictions would lead him.

Today Germany honors Hans with buildings, streets, and a legal prize named after him.

Watching this story will personally challenge you about your convictions and what you stand for.

The factual subject matter of this play rises above everything in its prescience of what is happening right now in this country.

——-

Hans Litten: The Jew that Cross-Examined Hitler was written by Douglas Lackey and directed by Alexander Harrington.

Cast: Stan Buturla, Zack Calhoon, Robert Ierardi, Whit K. Lee, Barbara McCulloh, Dave Stishan, Marco Torriani, Mark Eugene Vaughn, Daniel Yaiullo

Creative: Scenic design, Alex Roe; Costume design, Anthony Paul-Cavaretta; Lighting design, Alexander Bartenieff; Sound design, Abirami Senthil; and Kevin S. Foster II, Wig design.

Now playing at Theatre Row, 410 West 42nd Street. Tickets can be bought HERE.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Standing in front of the agreed upon location in Brooklyn, surprisingly the bookstore was closed. And the safety gate locked. But a small light could be seen glowing around the corner in the far back of the store.

A bit befuddled we peeked around the corner and saw a light shining in a side door. Cautiosly creeping in from the cold we were welcomed in the back entrance of the establishment and shown to a long table set up in the children’s section at the back of the bookstore, where the light had been eminating, surrounded by two rows of chairs. On the table were laid out 27 objects. We were given permission to look at and handle any of them. Some of the objects included: a postcard, a baseball glove, a green flag with an E on it, a dilapidated bible, a Hummel figurine, a little white stone, and a well read and marked up copy of The Catcher in the Rye.

All of this was the set (back of the bookstore included) as well as the subject for the play Edward by Ed Schmidt, the delightfully human tale of a normal man (Edward O’Connell) who lived a normal life, the marks that life left on him, and the marks that he left on it. Each of the objects on the table were a trigger for Schmidt to launch into one part of Mr. O’Connell’s experience and what that object meant in one aspect of his life. Taken together they came together like a puzzle, one piece at at time, that painted a rich picture of a life lived.

Each performance is a different experience as the audience members decide which order the objects are examined and how they were related to O’Connell’s life. The play is performed for one night only in a different location, either an independent bookstore or a private home somewhere in the city.

The story setup is that before he died, O’Connell (born in 1939) placed all of these objects in a box as no longer needed and offered it to a library rummage sale. In getting rid of stuff, little did he know how each object was a small selfie of part of his life.

What tales can the objects we’ve saved as we go through our lives tell about us? I came home and looked at the small things around my home and asked myself that question, smiling when the answers came to mind.

Ed Schmidt is writer, creator, director, and actor of this revelation in theater. Theater comes in many forms and this is an intimate uncovering of a story, released in small segments, that, put together, share the essence of a life lived in the United States.

Although sitting together in the children’s section in the back of a bookstore naturally brought the audience into a comfortable shared experience, Mr. Schmidt’s delivery is personable and warm, revealing O’Connell’s life in appetizers that together make a complete meal. Each bite keeping us intrigued about what the next object would reveal.

This would make a wonderful date night, not only for its uniqueness, but as it also reveals so much about our humanity.

——-

Edward is playing at bookstores in all boroughs. Tickets are $40 and can be had HERE, if available. Seating is limited.

If sold out they will soon be adding more shows at more bookstores throughout the New York City area. If you’re not able to get a ticket, put your name on the mailing list for when new shows will be scheduled.

Running time is 95 minutes.

I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.
