title.rendered: Falling Out: Where Heartbreak Finds Its Harmony in the East Village

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

In the storied basement of FRIGID New York’s intimate Under St. Marks theatre, something remarkable is unfolding—a musical so deeply felt, so exquisitely rendered, that one leaves the smoky confines of this imagined downtown dive bar transformed. In its World Premiere, Falling Out: A New Musical, with book, music, and lyrics by the prodigiously talented Josée Weigand-Klein, represents precisely the kind of theatrical alchemy that makes Manhattan’s off-off-Broadway scene an essential crucible of American theatrical innovation.

Gavin Cole in a scene from the World Premiere of the Musical “Falling Out” presented by Frigid New York at Under St. Marks in Manhattan’s East Village. Photo by Seana E. Rogovin

Indeed, as Shelley once mused that poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world, so too are the creators of intimate musical theatre the unheralded architects of our emotional landscape. Moreover, this production, directed with immersive brilliance by Anthony Logan Cole and musically shaped by the formidable Calvin Hitchcock, achieves that rare theatrical feat: it makes the particular universal, transforming personal heartbreak into collective catharsis.

Amelia Grace Beckham in a scene from the World Premiere of the Musical “Falling Out” presented by Frigid New York at Under St. Marks in Manhattan’s East Village. Photo by Seana E. Rogovin

The Dramaturgical Architecture: An Immersive Journey into the Heart

From the moment the audience enters what appears to be a semi-legendary open-mic night at “The Lounge,” one senses the meticulous craftsmanship beneath this production’s seemingly casual façade. The conceit is delightfully clever—patrons settling in as performers take turns at the microphone, only to discover that these fragmentary performances weave together into a profound narrative of loss, redemption, and the terrifying beauty of human connection.

Patrick Dinnsen in a scene from the World Premiere of the Musical “Falling Out” presented by Frigid New York at Under St. Marks in Manhattan’s East Village. Photo by Seana E. Rogovin

Moreover, Weigand-Klein’s score demonstrates a polyglot musical sensibility that draws upon pop, rock, folk, and Broadway traditions while remaining distinctly her own. Her melodic invention recalls the accessible sophistication of Benj Pasek and Justin Paul, yet her harmonic language is emotionally direct, reminiscent of Jason Robert Brown’s most affecting work. The songs move with an organic fluidity between intimate confession and soaring ensemble, each number advancing both character and theme with economical precision.

Matthew Liu in a scene from the World Premiere of the Musical “Falling Out” presented by Frigid New York at Under St. Marks in Manhattan’s East Village. Photo by Seana E. Rogovin

Virtuosic Performances: A Company of Extraordinary Gifts

The production’s success rests upon the shoulders of a genuinely remarkable ensemble. Amelia Grace Beckham, making her New York City theatrical debut as Alex, brings a luminous vulnerability to the role of a woman navigating the wreckage of a failed relationship. Her voice possesses both sparkling clarity and emotional depth, and her journey from a tentative open-mic performer to an empowered artist unfolds with the inevitability of a genuine character arc. Additionally, her interpretation of “A Lonely Number” achieves a transcendent poignancy that lingers long after the final note fades.

L-R: Amelia Grace Beckham, Photo by Sam Pickart. Gavin Cole, Courtesy reallygavincole.com, performing in the World Premiere of the Musical “Falling Out” presented by Frigid New York at Under St. Marks in Manhattan’s East Village

Opposite her, Gavin Cole delivers a revelatory performance as Rock, the troubled musician whose celebrity masks overpowering wounds. Cole navigates the character’s arc from guarded cynicism to hard-won honesty with remarkable subtlety, and his vocal work—particularly in the confessional “Questions” and the achingly beautiful “Thing Called Love”—demonstrates both technical mastery and interpretive intelligence. The chemistry between Beckham and Cole crackles with authenticity, their duets on “Shatter” and “Don’t Wanna Write This Song” achieving a synergistic power greater than either voice alone.

Amelia Grace Beckham, Matthew Liu, and Patrick Dinnsen in a scene from the World Premiere of the Musical “Falling Out” presented by Frigid New York at Under St. Marks in Manhattan’s East Village. Photo by Seana E. Rogovin

Consequently, the supporting ensemble proves equally indispensable. Matthew Liu, a Juilliard-trained polymath, singer, violinist, and MC, anchors the proceedings as the Narrator with sardonic charm and impeccable musical instincts. Ashley Margaret Morton brings both comedic timing, piano skills, vocal artistry, and genuine warmth to the Therapist; her duet with Beckham on “City Streets” sparkled with witty interplay. Meanwhile, Patrick Dinnsen renders the Ex with nuanced complexity, while Alex Crossland infuses the Bandleader with infectious energy.

L-R: Ashley Margaret Morton, Courtesy ashmorton.com. Matthew Liu, Courtesy backstage.com, performing in the World Premiere of the Musical “Falling Out” presented by Frigid New York at Under St. Marks in Manhattan’s East Village

Musical Craftsmanship: Songs That Illuminate the Soul

What distinguishes Weigand-Klein’s score is its dramaturgical intelligence. Each song emerges organically from character and situation, advancing narrative while deepening emotional resonance. “Can You Sing Me a Song” establishes the production’s thematic preoccupations with elegant simplicity, while “To Always Love You” achieves a devastating beauty through its juxtaposition of past hope and present loss.

Subsequently, the climactic “Don’t Wanna Write This Song” stands as the musical’s moral and musical fulcrum, where heartbreak is not healed by forgetting but transformed through authorship—pain given shape, conflict given conscience, and art revealed as a resilient, self-authored truth.

Gavin Cole and Ashley Margaret Morton in a scene from the World Premiere of the Musical “Falling Out” presented by Frigid New York at Under St. Marks in Manhattan’s East Village. Photo by Seana E. Rogovin

The instrumental work throughout deserves special commendation. This company of actor-musicians moves seamlessly between keyboard, guitar, electric guitar, electric bass, drums, and violin, their collective virtuosity in service of the material rather than display. The arrangements by Weigand-Klein, Hitchcock, and Gideon Klein support the songs’ emotional trajectories with subtle sophistication, the orchestrations achieving remarkable variety within their instrumental constraints.

Production Values: Intimacy Elevated to Art

Director Cole’s staging demonstrates a masterful understanding of immersive theatre’s possibilities. The production unfolds in and around the audience, transforming spectators into participants in the open mic’s communal ritual. Transitions flow with cinematic fluidity, and the ensemble’s physical storytelling amplifies the emotional stakes without sacrificing naturalism.

Alex Crossland in a scene from the World Premiere of the Musical “Falling Out” presented by Frigid New York at Under St. Marks in Manhattan’s East Village. Photo by Seana E. Rogovin

Similarly, the design team contributes work of remarkable refinement. Mikaila Baca-Dorion’s scenic and projection design creates atmosphere without overwhelming the intimate space, while Zach Pizza’s lighting design sculpts mood with painterly precision. Emerson Wachnik’s sound design strikes a difficult balance between acoustic presence and dynamic range essential to musical theatre in close quarters.

L-R: Patrick Dinnsen, Courtesy pdinns on Instagram. Alex Crossland, Courtesy Alexander Crossland on Facebook, performing in the World Premiere of the Musical “Falling Out” presented by Frigid New York at Under St. Marks in Manhattan’s East Village

FRIGID New York: A Legacy of Downtown Excellence

That Falling Out premieres at FRIGID New York seems altogether fitting. Founded in 1998 as the Horse Trade Theater Group, this venerable institution has spent over a quarter-century nurturing precisely this kind of adventurous theatrical work. The company’s 2015 Obie Grant recognition merely confirmed what downtown audiences had long known: FRIGID provides an essential incubator for independent theatre artists seeking to develop work outside commercial constraints. Indeed, their eight annual festivals—including the Fire This Time Festival, Estrogenius, and Queerly—have launched countless careers while maintaining an unwavering commitment to artistic diversity and experimentation.

Ashley Margaret Morton in a scene from the World Premiere of the Musical “Falling Out” presented by Frigid New York at Under St. Marks in Manhattan’s East Village. Photo by Seana E. Rogovin

A Theatrical Experience Not to Be Missed

As Wordsworth wrote of poetry, so might we say of this musical: it is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings, recollected in tranquility. Falling Out offers precisely the theatrical nourishment audiences crave after the holiday season—a meditation on love, loss, and renewal that reminds us why we seek out live performance in an age of digital distraction. The production runs through February 1, 2026, and represents an unmissable opportunity to witness the birth of a significant new work by artists of genuine vision and talent.

Ashley Margaret Morton and Matthew Liu in a scene from the World Premiere of the Musical “Falling Out” presented by Frigid New York at Under St. Marks in Manhattan’s East Village. Photo by Seana E. Rogovin

excerpt.rendered: Falling Out at FRIGID’s Under St. Marks delivers heartfelt storytelling through Josée Weigand-Klein’s luminous score and an extraordinary cast who transform heartbreak into hope. This immersive world premiere—running through February 1, 2026—offers the perfect antidote to winter’s chill: warmth, music, and the redemptive power of human connection.

By Kendra Jones

“Why do you walk like that?”

“Because I’m fucking fancy.”

We’re in the dark, listening to a phone conversation between Anne Gridley’s mother and a man named Pavol; from their conversation observed only through an audio recording, we wouldn’t know that either Anne or her mother, Teresa, have the rare degenerative neurological disease, Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia (HSP). But, as we all sit before this stage knowing the show’s title, Watch Me Walk, and its autobiographical narrative, we know that there’s an underlying reason Anne’s mother notes that she thinks she found the perfect man for Anne, if only just a fantasy.

I watch Anne Gridley walk back and forth across the stage for what seems like minutes–at least twelve times and back and forth in each direction; the theater is silent aside from the dull thud of her cane and the soft drag of her Doc Martens. It’s a spectacle, it’s a sort of social experiment, it’s shameless vulnerability; Gridley wants us to watch her walk. She wants us to immediately see her: the part of her that we are quick to judge or make assumptions. Gridley gives us a straight-forward, witty, and sharp window into her life as a human with an untreatable disease. Gridley’s performance is a visual stab at America’s healthcare system, the perceptions we have of disabled people, and the falls that encourage us to walk again.

Anne immerses us into her research, discoveries, and candid appearance through experimental theater and costuming and stage props. Watch Me Walk does the work it needs to do. It shows Anne in the way she sees herself and guides us through her own self discovery of her disability, her limitations, her ability to still occupy space in her life which she’s crafted into her own free form dance.

Photo by Maria Baranova

I’m reminded of a young writer I teach, who’s been drafting a journalistic piece about her own experience with rare disorders–this young girl’s experience being one of the 5% with an FDA-approved treatment. I think of the stories she tells me of the young children and adults she’s met that don’t have a treatment, how they avoid living in fear. Anne’s on stage, calculatedly serving us a glossary of her walk–she is anything but ashamed.

Foot drop! Spasticity! Clonus! Hyperreflexia! Dropsy! Crip Time! 

Fall.

Photo by Maria Baranova

This evening is a reminder of how crucial awareness of rare diseases are, how America defines them, and how we as a population see them. Alex Gibson & Keith Johnson play several roles throughout this piece, supporting Gridley on stage, although she can carry the show herself. They most notably represent Adonis: an ideal male specimen.

 

Photo by Maria Baranova

While Gridley is off-stage, Alex Gibson leads the audience in a sing-along: “The Ha Ha Ha History of Disability.” This number gives us a separation from Gridley, as we sing along to these lyrics almost behind her back: a sarcastic history of how “well” disabled people have been treated over centuries, across the world. The audience painfully sings out “ha-ha-ha” after each line; the hesitation, the uncertainty and wavering confidence in our voices as we shouted out those three sounds of laughter as we listen to Gibson lead the choir.

While this production brings to light the questions, perceptions, and injustices that come with disability, Anne uses the stage to and show her own emotional roller coaster that settles on her family. In turn, she is investigates her ancestry. The deaths of her parents, her grandparents, her distant relatives, illuminates inheritance. Not the kind that we get after family dies, but the kind we’re born with. The kind that sometimes we only come to realize, learn, and connect the dots after our loved ones have passed on, but it’s the conditions we’ve always had. And in Anne’s case, even thought she hadn’t walked with a gait her entire life, she was born with the same disease shared by both her mother and grandmother. Connecting the dots between Anne’s ancestors and their health seem to serve as a way to cope and ground herself.

Photo by Maria Baranova

One of the most memorable pieces of Anne’s performance is when she reads recollects the moment her mother died, and then died again. Our breaths are caught in our chests, and suddenly we hear her mother’s voice over the speakers. She’s describing how Anne danced. Anne, as a child, dancing a free form, spontaneous rain dance on their porch. Now, in front of us all, she attempts to dance that rain dance as her mother describes it on tape.

Anne moves her body, arms up, swaying, questioningly–as if asking the sky if she’s doing it as her mother remembers;

Her mother’s voice: “that’s… what I think of when… I think of Anne and movement.”

…The things we inherit.

 

The World Premiere of Watch Me Walk is presented by Soho Rep and playing at the Peter Jay Sharp Theater at Playwrights Horizons, 416 W 42nd Street (between 9th and 10th Ave, until February 8 as part of the Under the Radar Festival.

Full performance schedule and tickets can be found at sohorep.org. Soho Rep offers general admission seating. All seats are the same price and available on a first-come, first-served basis, without price tiers or pre-assigned seating. However, to better accommodate a range of access needs, audience members can now select from different, equally priced ticket types at sohorep.org.

Written and performed by Anne Gridley.
Directed by Erik Ting.
FEATURING: Alex Gibson & Keith Johnson.

CREATIVE TEAM: Asli Bulbul (Choreography), Jian Jung (Scenic Design), Lux Haac (Costume Design), Kate McGee (Lighting Design), Tei Blow (Sound and Video Design), Noah Lethbridge (Original Songs), and Thomas Jenkeleit (Props Supervision).

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

There is not much music in Joe White’s moody and brutal Blackout Songs, but there are plenty of blackouts. The American premiere of this 2022 British drama features two blackout drunks who are as addicted to each other as they are to the bottle. Told in a series of, yes, blackouts, the one-act explores the sometimes fine line between love and codependency while measuring the importance of what is usually taken for granted in a relationship: the existence of memories.

White has set up several ground rules for the telling of his tale. The characters’ names are not divulged until near the end of the play, so they are introduced to the audience only as Him (Owen Teague) and Her (Abbey Lee). This distancing effect underscores the difficulty of truly getting to know and sympathize with a person in the grip of alcoholism. The audience never witnesses either character actually taking a drink. Instead, the uncontrollable impulses leading up to a swig set up each scene, while the occasionally bloody, occasionally coital results of a binge are revealed in the aftermath.

White’s riskiest trick is that the play progresses in the way a hardcore alcoholic might perceive it. Time is uncertain. A pause between scenes could indicate the passing of an hour, a week, or a year. Truth is relative. Do the characters actually mean what they say to each other, or are they toying with the other’s emotions, or merely fooling themselves? Memory is vague. A line of dialogue from Her might later be said by Him, reflecting how a couple can forget which of them actually started a fight or uttered a callous remark. Indeed, where a memory play is dependent on its narrator to propel the action, this is just the opposite, a loss-of-memory play that does not so much move forward as it does slip back upon itself or blur reality altogether.

When Him and Her first interact, it is anything but a meet-cute. Huddling near the coffee urn at an A.A. meeting, she is on pins and needles, while he is stammering, suffering from tremors, and wearing a neck brace for reasons he cannot recall. Still, she is drawn to him, and it will turn out that this opening scene perhaps falls out of sequence, that maybe they have been intimately involved with each other already. Who can remember?

As their attraction grows, the third member of their relationship is never far away, and the playwright’s ear for the meddling effect of drinking proves to be disturbingly on point. “Medicine” becomes the couple’s code word for liquor, and that is just the least worrisome symptom of their shared sickness. He describes taking a sip as being like “someone’s fingers in my hair…someone, stroking my head.” When she responds by actually stroking his head, he finds it is “not quite” as soothing. In listing the reasons he would never forget her, he includes, “Your throat when you drink.” Their connection to religion falters when there is wine to be stolen from a church. “My first drink was communion. I was twelve,” she fondly recalls.

Director Rory McGregor sets a quick pace for his actors, though, given the play’s less-than-lovable duo, it’s a race to the inevitable tragic finish before the audience tires of the falling off the wagon, then climbing back on, only to tumble again. In her U.S. stage debut, Lee, a successful Australian fashion model turned film actress, understands the assignment, showing flashes of wit and compassion despite her character’s dazed existence. As Him, Teague gives a literally sobering performance, finding a self-assured manner when off the bottle, then crumbling under the weight of his compulsions.

 

Blackout Songs – By Joe White; Directed by Rory McGregor

WITH: Abbey Lee (Her) and Owen Teague (Him)

Scott Pask (scenic design), Avery Reed (costume design), Stacey Derosier (lighting design) and Brian Hickey (sound design & original music). Regular People, Linden Productions, and The Cohn Sisters at The Robert W. Wilson MCC Theater Space, 511 W 52nd St. blackoutsongs.com. Through February 28. Running time: 100 minutes

title.rendered: Bob Marley: How Reggae Changed the World

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Not only capturing the spirit of Bob Marley, Duane Forrest also freely gives of his spirit in his soulful presentation of Bob Marley: How Reggae Changed the World now playing through February 1 at Soho Playhouse.

This is a dual presentation as it’s not just about Bob, Duane freely gives of himself, his personal history, and the connection that he had at a young age with the music of Marley. As he shares the history of reggae and its birthing, he shares his personal journey and the history of Jamaica and its people. Duane’s choice of songs flow effortlessly and directly comment on his storytelling. No Woman No Cry, Falling in Love, Jammin’, Redemption Song are but a few of Bob’s classics that Duane plays or creates a mashup of. He talks about where each song came from, and what it is truly talking about. You will listen differently to the songs after this experience.

And if you know and love these songs, this show is a winner for you. the audience is encouraged to sing along as this is an interactive show. That’s what reggae is, communal, empowering, spreading tones of love. Reggae wants to take us all to Zion, where “The rich are no longer rich, the poor are no longer poor, we all have enough.”

Duane’s personality is as inviting and giving as reggae is and you can’t help but like him. Only a dozen of us were in attendance on a cold snowy afternoon and we all left feeling that we wouldn’t have wanted to be anywhere else but there, listening to Bob’s music and on the receiving end of what Duane has to give. This production is musical storytelling that is a delight as it both entertains and educates, resonating deep inside in the same way that the beat of reggae does.

The beginning of the year in New York is inundated with great theater from around the world brought to you by Under the Radar (January) and Soho Playhouse’s Fringe Encore Series (January and February) making it nearly impossible to see all of the great, and I really mean great, offerings due to the quantity of presentations scheduled. Soho Playhouse Fringe Encore is put together by its directors traveling the globe to all the theatrical fringe festivals throughout the world (good gig) and bringing the best of the best to New York for you to see. Every year I see things that blow me away, deeply challenge me, surprise me, put a smile on my face, and make me happy for what live theater can do.

——-

Bob Marley: How Reggae Changed The World was written and performed by Duane Forrest. Music by Bob Marley and Duane Forrest.

this U.S. premiere runs thru February 1.

Tickets can be purchased HERE.

Two other plays that can be seen at Soho Playhouse:

Puttana

and Her Children

content.rendered:
By David Walters

“If I call you a whore you won’t get offended. I mean, that’s what you are, right?”

 Puttana (whore) is nine microphones, two stools, a large teddy bear, a pile of clothes, and the audience wearing green lit headphones that turn the seats in the darkened theater into a field of fireflies.

This is an old old story, biblical in its telling of blaming the victim, justifying the perpetrator, turning the physical body into a commodity, that, like a taxi ride, once the destination is reached, the transaction is over and each goes their separate ways with little thought of the other. Unless, the ride becomes an addiction.

Life takes her from daughter, to student, to prostitute, and him, the husband, father, and provider looking for a connection, with a live blow up doll, that he no longer has in his life. Is it real if he pays for it or just a temporary fantasy?

Puttana (whore) is both a visual and an audio play. Using audio techniques that change the actor’s voice, Puttana is a full frontal, pull the curtain back expose’ of the humanity and inhumanity of sex for purchase. The experience utilizes red light, and, in film what is called fast cutting, to look and listen inside the mind of what a character is experiencing and thinking. The headphones that the audience wears throughout the show utilizes 3D spatial audio, “designed to replicate the experience of being surrounded by an orchestra.” What it really does is bring you inside the minds and emotions of the five characters that actress Beatrice Elena Festi expertly portrays. It’s jarring, revealing, and prescient to how this will all end.  How its always ended.

The beginning of the year in New York is inundated with great theater from around the world (Puttana is from Italy) brought to you by Under the Radar (January) and Soho Playhouse’s Fringe Encore Series (January and February) making it nearly impossible to see all of the great, and I really mean great, offerings due to the quantity of presentations scheduled. Soho Playhouse Fringe Encore is put together by its directors traveling the globe to all the theatrical fringe festivals throughout the world (good gig) and bringing the best of the best to New York for you to see. Every year I see things that blow me away, deeply challenge me, surprise me, put a smile on my face, and make me happy for what live theater can do.

——-

Puttana (whore) was written by Maura Pettorruso. Conceived and directed by Mirko Corradini.

Performed by Beatrice Elena Festi.

Music composed by Michele Calla. Sound designed by Sebastiano Cecchini.

https://www.compagniateatroe.it/teatro-adulti/puttana

Puttana (whore) U.S. premiere runs through January 25. Produced by Teatroe ETS and playing at Soho Playhouse.

Tickets can be purchased HERE.

content.rendered:
Review by Brittany Crowell

Can humans be defined by a set of data points? Data, a new play by Matthew Libby, directed by Tyne Rafaeli, begs the question while setting up its moral quandary – an ethical dilemma that hits a little closer to home than folks might have anticipated.

 Maneesh (Karan Brar), a first generation American, is following in his brother’s footsteps and has become a data analytical prodigy.  Just out of undergrad, his senior thesis and thoughtfulness of practice have caught the eye of the data analytics team at Athena, a large-scale, Silicon Valley tech company, and he is recruited from UX engineering to join the team on a top secret project – which comes with a pile of ethical questions as well.

The topic – immigration – the conundrum (and this is only a slight spoiler) – that he has been recruited to generate an algorithm that will help the Department of Homeland Security vet potential immigrants based on available online data, determining if they would be a positive and productive addition to America.

This topic is made even more timely (and important) in the wake of ICE raids across the nation and the killing of Rebecca Good and Alex Pretti by federal agents in Minnesota. While the nation responds to these senseless murders by a government agency, Data begs the question – How does one respond to a corrupt system? Can you change it from within, or do you have to (metaphorically) burn it down?

The play takes a little too long to show its cards, revealing this ethical dilemma at just about the halfway point of the 100 minute piece, however, it spends the second half exploring these questions with a cast of characters carrying different backgrounds, approaches, and responses.

The ensemble cast is led by Karan Brar (Maneesh) who gives a subtle yet energized performance as the newcomer to the tech company. Sophia Lillis (Riley), plays a woman trying to make her way in the tech world with anger and desperation humming beneath the surface; Justin H. Min’s calm portrayal of Alex, the head of data analytics, gives a new definition to the tech bro and quietly terrifies audiences with his earnest performance; and Brandon Flynn brings a mix of comedy and tragedy with his heartbreaking portrayal of Maneesh’s UX colleague Jonah. 

The story unfolds on a ‘Severance’ inspired set made up of a large metal room with fluorescent walls (designed cleverly by scenic designer Marsha Ginsberg).  Original music by Daniel Kluger along with Amith Chandrashaker’s lighting design jet the audiences from scene to scene during adrenaline-inducing scene changes & costumes by Enver Chakartash help to tell the story and showcase the transitions between the characters.

Data, playing now through March 29th, begs the question: what does positive and productive actually mean?  Who are the systems governing us actually serving, and how do we impact them?  Sure to give you something to discuss on the cab ride home, this is an important piece for right now – so make your way to the Lucile Lortel this winter to catch it.

 

DATA – by Matthew Libby; directed by Tyne Rafaeli

FEATURING: Karan Brar; Brandon Flynn; Sophia Lillis; Justin H. Min

Scenic design by Marsha Ginsberg; costumes by Enver Chakartash; lighting by Amith Chandrashaker; sound design & original music by Daniel Kluger. At the Lucille Lortel Theatre: 121 Christopher Street; through March 29.  90 minutes. www.datatheplay.com

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

“Ulysses” by James Joyce may be more famous for the stir it caused than its content.  Published by Sylvia Beach – owner of Shakespeare and Company in Paris in 1922.  It was banned in the U.S. because of explicit sexual content and, even worse, the stream-of-consciousness prose that James introduced.  It took another 10 years for the ban to be reversed.

This production by Elevator Repair Service is a noble and gargantuan project.  This cast and tech crew pull off astonishing feats of storytelling as they maneuver the tale of Leopold Bloom (Vin Knight), Stephen Dedalus (Christopher-Rashee Stevenson), and Molly Bloom (Maggie Hoffman).  We are told in advance by our host, Scott Shepherd, that “not much happens in Ulysses, apart from everything you can possibly imagine. And it all happens on a single day: mostly Thursday, June 16, 1904.” We are off to the races. Dee Beasnael, Kate Benson, and Stephanie Weeks become the center of the Ensemble that buoys us up and into the world of Dublin, 1904.

The events of the day spin out in what seems to be no particular order.  We follow Leopold Bloom from pillar to post.  Pub to post office.  Practical, daily exchanges to assignations’ correspondence.  Stephen Dedalus is a man whose powers of observation serve to overwhelm him.  Molly Bloom,, although famous for being herself, does not surface with her famous “Yes” monologue until the production is winding down and puling into the station.

I wish I could give you a concrete example of what happens, but most of this production is filled with moments that explode into one another.  You fasten your seatbelts and you takes your chances.

I have  not read “Ulysses” in its entirety.  I tried several times and felt like I was thrown off a wild beast whose elusive behavior was larger than I could handle.  Perhaps if I were a James Scholar I would have fared better watching this production.  As it was, I floated from moment to moment, following the lead of these excellent actors who pursued their paths with skill and determination.  An added element here is the time travel.  The script speeds up (adding a welcome bit of humor), slows down, reverses and leaps forward.  Forget about the brilliant Guiding Clock upstage.  Although a well  intentioned and executed, it becomes part of the overall mayhem soon enough.

I was never attached to the this production’s story or the outcome, and this may be exactly what James intended.  The text flies through these characters’ actions, thoughts and feelings as if James were being pursued by a bear.  All we can do is hang on to his coattails.  He drops us into a one situation after another and pulls us out without notice.  He may have created this book as an elaborate ruse just to see how the rest of us would react.

And why not?  Whatever Elevator Repair Service intended with this piece, it was executed with precision, style and grace.

 

ULYSSES Created by Elevator Repair Service; Text: Ulysses by James Joyce, Co-Direction and Dramaturgy by Scott Shepherd Directed by John Collins

WITH Dee Beasnael, Kate Benson, Maggie Hoffman, Vin Knight, Scott Shepherd, Christopher-Rashee Stevenson, and Stephanie Weeks.

The production includes scenic design by dots, costume design by Enver Chakartash, lighting design by Marika Kent, sound design by Ben Williams, projection design by Matthew Deinhart, and prop design by Patricia Marjorie.

And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. title.rendered: Shelter in Place: A Heartwarming Theatrical Triumph at the Players Theatre

content.rendered:
Greenwich Village’s Latest Theatrical Gem

In the manner that Percy Bysshe Shelley once observed that poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world, so too does independent theater serve as the unheralded conscience of our cultural moment. Nestled in the bohemian heart of Greenwich Village, where Eugene O’Neill once paced these very streets, and Bob Dylan first strummed his folk hymns at the legendary Café Wha? below, the intimate Steve and Marie Sgouros Theatre at 115 MacDougal Street has become the crucible for a production that reminds us why we still gather in darkened rooms to witness the eternal human comedy unfold.

Ego Actus and Feldman Productions LLC present Shelter in Place, playwright Henry Feldman‘s tender and uproariously funny examination of family dynamics, generational obligations, and the courage required to finally claim one’s own happiness. This production, running through January 25, 2026, represents everything that makes off-Broadway theater indispensable: intimacy, authenticity, and the ineffable magic that occurs when gifted performers inhabit a well-wrought text.

The Distinguished Legacy of Ego Actus Theatre Company

Founded by the indefatigable Joan Kane, Ego Actus has established itself as a paragon of independent theatrical excellence in New York City. The company’s productions have garnered an impressive 61 award nominations, winning 21 awards—a testament to their unwavering commitment to provocative, accessible theater. Kane, inducted into the Indie Theatre Hall of Fame and named one of the People of the Year for her contributions to the New York theatre scene, brings to this production the same dramaturgical precision and emotional intelligence that earned her Best Director honors at the United Solo Festival.

Moreover, the collaboration with Feldman Productions LLC extends this legacy of excellence. Henry Feldman’s personal genesis for this work—born from the crucible of Hurricane Ike in 2008, when the bureaucratic refrain of ‘shelter in place’ echoed through Houston while his family navigated loss, love, and the relentless demands of the sandwich generation—infuses every scene with hard-won authenticity. As William Wordsworth proclaimed, poetry springs from ’emotion recollected in tranquility,’ and Feldman’s script achieves precisely this alchemical transformation of lived experience into theatrical gold.

The Cast of Shelter in Place playing at the Sgouros Theater, 115 MacDougal Street., NYC. L-R: David Cagen, Alyssa Simon, Jared Ritter, Haley Watkins, Martin Revere. Courtesy @davidgcagan on Instagram

Joan Kane’s Masterful Direction: A Study in Theatrical Intimacy

Joan Kane SDC approaches this material with the sensitivity of a chamber musician—every beat calibrated, every pause pregnant with meaning, yet never losing the spontaneous combustibility that distinguishes live theater from mere recitation. Her direction demonstrates what is often observed of the finest theatrical work: that it operates on multiple registers, engaging the intellect while ambushing the heart.

Kane’s staging transforms the modest Sgouros Theatre into the Pelican Bay Bed and Breakfast with remarkable verisimilitude. Furthermore, the mise-en-scène achieves that rare theatrical accomplishment: an environment so completely realized that the audience forgets they are watching a play and becomes a witness to genuine human revelation. The director’s blocking demonstrates masterful spatial intelligence, utilizing every inch of the intimate playing space to create moments of both comedic chaos and quiet emotional resonance.

An Ensemble of Extraordinary Talent

The production’s cast embodies theatrical ensemble work—individual brilliance in service of collective illumination. Each performer brings not merely technical proficiency, but that ineffable quality Virginia Woolf identified as the ‘luminous halo’ surrounding human consciousness.

Martin Revere delivers a tour-de-force performance as George Bennett, the octogenarian father whose entrance alone—complete with cane, walker, high white socks, sandals, and a loud Hawaiian shirt—elicits waves of recognition laughter from the audience. Additionally, Revere’s comedic timing proves impeccable; his ersatz suicide attempts ( his inventive concept model Barbie doll in a wheelchair with a dagger in her chest representing his son’s ex-wife, a hangman’s noose dangling with bathetic impotence, standing in buckets of water while fumbling for an extension cord) achieve that delicate balance between the absurd and the poignant that defines great comedy.

Martin Revere as George Bennett in a scene from Shelter in Place. Photo by Maria Passannante-Derr

As Frank Bennett, the beleaguered owner of the bed and breakfast, David Cagan brings six decades of theatrical experience to bear on this portrait of a man caught in life’s eternal squeeze play. Cagan’s Frank is simultaneously neurotic and noble, a former physics professor who abandoned academia to pursue his wife’s dream of running a Florida B&B, only to find himself abandoned in turn for a pool boy named Thor. Cagan’s work with Stag & Lion Theatre Company and his memorable turn as “Carloz with a Z” in Diva Therapy under Kane’s direction demonstrate his versatility and commitment to the collaborative theatrical process.

Alyssa Simon infuses Dr. Heidi Murphy—America’s TV therapist seeking refuge from her own romantic catastrophe—with a delicious combination of professional composure and private vulnerability. Heidi’s gradual warming to George provides the production’s romantic through-line, handled with refreshing subtlety rather than sitcom predictability.

The young Jared Ritter embodies Sam Bennett with the boundless energy and earnest optimism of youth, undaunted by cynicism. Ritter captures the specific charm of a twenty-year-old in love, desperate to orchestrate his parents’ reconciliation so that his own romantic prospects with the delightfully named Barbie might proceed unburdened by his ‘broken family’ status. Ritter’s rapport with both Cagan and Revere creates the intergenerational male bonding that forms the production’s connective emotional tissue.

Haley Watkins rounds out the principal cast as Mildred Bennett, the ex-wife whose entrance—propelled by her latest romantic disaster—catalyzes the play’s final act complications. Watkins navigates the difficult task of making a potentially unsympathetic character both comprehensible and, ultimately, redeemable.

Special mention must be made of Danny Siebert as the voice of Gilbert and Rebecca Lovett as the Radio Weather Announcer, whose unseen presences provide the production’s atmospheric tension. This ever-approaching hurricane serves as an objective correlative for the emotional storms raging within the Bennett family.

L-R: Martin Revere, Haley Watkins, Jared Ritter, David Cagen and Alyssa Simon in a scene from Shelter in Place. Photo by Maria Passannante-Derr

Technical Artistry: The Unsung Heroes of the Stage

The production’s technical elements achieve that ideal state of theatrical design: complete service to the narrative while demonstrating consummate artistry. Set designer Evan Frank has created a bed-and-breakfast interior that breathes authenticity, from its practical details to its symbolic possibilities. The space must accommodate comedy, romance, conflict, and reconciliation—and Frank’s design proves equal to every demand.

Cat Fisher‘s costume design demonstrates her characteristic blend of character revelation and period accuracy. Frank Bennett’s Florida retiree ensemble—those immortal high white socks with sandals—achieves instant character establishment while maintaining the visual vocabulary of authentic Gulf Coast casual.

Bruce A! Kraemer’s lighting design employs what theater practitioners term chiaroscuro effects—the interplay of light and shadow—to underscore the production’s shifting emotional landscape. As the hurricane approaches, Kraemer’s lights pulse with increasing urgency, creating a crescendo of visual tension that elevates this intimate production to international-caliber technical standards.

Sound designer Ian Wehrle crafts an immersive soundscape that transports the audience to Hurricane Country. As patrons assembled in the intimate theater, gentle Hawaiian beach music set the Florida ambiance, while the subtle sounds of surf and wind foreshadowed the approaching storm. The emergency weather radio—an authentic prop secured by Amy Lesser—punctuates the action with increasingly dire warnings, its mechanical voice providing darkly comic counterpoint to the human drama unfolding onstage.

Prop designer Lytza Colon, a passionate multi-talented visual artist from the South Bronx who has served as props master for Theater for the New City‘s award-winning Street Theater Summer Program since 2008, has assembled a collection of objects that anchor the production in tactile reality. Special acknowledgment goes to Reese Cutler, 3D printing specialist, for the custom-made hotel key fobs, and to the Theater for the New City Prop Collection for purses, wireless phones, and sundry other items that complete the world of the play.

Casting director Robin Carus has assembled an ensemble whose chemistry transcends mere professional competence. Production stage manager Dana Vincent-Robbins ensures that the complex choreography of entrances, exits, and comedic business proceeds with clockwork precision, while assistant stage manager Max Kilsheimer supports the production’s technical demands with quiet efficiency. Graphic designer Ken Oppriecht has created visual materials that capture the production’s spirit of comedic warmth.

Jared Ritter and Haley Watkins in a scene from Shelter in Place. Photo by Maria Passannante-Derr

Thematic Resonance: The Sandwich Generation and the Search for Self

Shelter in Place examines what sociologists term the ‘sandwich generation’—those caught between the obligations of aging parents and the demands of their own children. Frank Bennett represents the ‘platinum card member’ of this demographic cohort, having suppressed his own desires in service to others for so long that he has forgotten how to want anything for himself.

The approaching hurricane serves as what T.S. Eliot termed an objective correlative—an external circumstance that embodies and externalizes the characters’ internal states. Just as John Keats celebrated the season ‘of mists and mellow fruitfulness,’ Feldman finds in nature’s fury a mirror for human emotional turbulence. The shelter-in-place order that confines these disparate characters to a single location creates the classical unity of place, forcing confrontation and, ultimately, transformation.

In this admixture of family dynamics examining dialogue, honesty, love, loyalty, and ambition, the production achieves what many praise as theater’s highest function: holding a mirror to humanity while simultaneously offering hope. The denouement proves both charming and heart-rendering—everyone seems to get what they need most, though perhaps not in the manner they expected.

The Historic Sgouros Theatre: A Jewel of Greenwich Village

The Steve and Marie Sgouros Theatre, a 50-seat black-box space within the historic Players Theatre complex, provides the ideal setting for this intimate family drama. Built in 1907 as a carriage house for police horses and converted to theatrical use in the late 1950s, the venue has witnessed the artistic development of Natalie Portman and Britney Spears (both of whom appeared in Ruthless! in 1992) and has served as a Greenwich Village cultural landmark for over six decades.

David Cagan and Alyssa Simon in a scene from Shelter in Place. Photo by Maria Passannante-Derr

A Production Not to Be Missed

As Andrea Alton PR has rightly emphasized in promoting this production, Shelter in Place represents precisely what theatergoers need after the holidays—a journey into hope and love, a reminder of springtime and renewal even as winter holds the city in its grip. The collaboration between gifted production people, writer-director Joan Kane, and these remarkable actor-artists has produced something vital, important, and at times heart-rending.

Working with well-conceived scenes, the performers prove sympathetic and vital as they portray not only human frailty and loss but hope and love. The cast expresses individual and group talent, energy, and artistry in equal measure. This is, quite simply, a show that demands to be seen.

Shelter in Place performs through January 25 at the Sgouros Theater, 115 MacDougal Street, NYC 10012. Performances run Thursdays, Fridays, and Saturdays at 7:00 pm, with Sunday matinees at 3:00 pm. Running time is approximately 110 minutes without intermission. For tickets and further information, visit EgoActus.com/plays/Shelter-in-Place.

excerpt.rendered: Shelter in Place delivers heartwarming comedy and profound emotional truth at the intimate Sgouros Theatre in Greenwich Village. Joan Kane’s masterful direction guides a stellar ensemble through Henry Feldman’s tender exploration of family, sacrifice, and self-discovery. This not-to-be-missed production runs through January 25, 2026—a perfect antidote to winter’s chill.

title.rendered: Sitting Around Baker’s Table: An Edward Allan Baker Showcase

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Red Door Productions is a young group just getting their feet wet in the theatrical world. They’ve come together to present two one-acts by Edward Allan Baker, who passed in 2021 leaving behind a large body of work, that in his words is about, “People born to brick and asphalt, who don’t have bad days, they have bad years.”

The two one-acts are A Dead Man’s Apartment and Face Divided. Same type of brick and asphalt people, but two different genres, one of farce and the other bitter reality.

Dead Man deals with an absurd test that, in looking to leave her marriage and find another mate, Nickie (Jamie Ragusa) spends considerable time with the possible candidate, Lonnie (also married, looking to leave his relationship) (Simon James Gibson). They don’t have sex, just build intimacy with talking, kissing, holding, and long walks. When she thinks this might be the one, before breaking it off with her husband (“Nothing but a shadow that can piss.”), she brings in her daughter (sharply played by Isabella Candillier) and her brother (an imposing Penny Bittone) to run the chosen one through the final gauntlet challenge of family (because you don’t just marry a person, you also marry their family). Lonnie has to decide whether he can or even wants to jump this final hurdle.

Face Divided is a traumatic event taking place in a Providence, Rhode Island hospital emergency room. While Debbie’s (a complexly raw Violet Levinson) toddler daughter is in ICU, brought in by her due to falling down the basement stairs, she is being kept in a waiting room, unable to see the child, until her husband, Freddie, (Josh Cromwell) arrives. They are a young married couple, just scrapping by, living on dreams and odd jobs, being dragged into an adulthood that neither of them really wants to embrace. When Freddie does show its revealled that he’s already been at the hospital for some time as there is concern that it was not a fall, but parental abuse. It’s not a black and white issue though for either, as the impulsiveness and irresponsibility of youth strongly binds the parents to each other despite the traumatic.

Eddy’s writing is very strong in this piece, providing the actors buckets of characterzations and behaviour for them to completly soak themselves with. And they do.

This is a young company with raw visable talent that may have a future for themselves.

——-

A Dead Man’s Apartment, written by Edward Allan Baker; directed by Marcel Simeoneau.

Performed by: Simon James Gibson, Jamie Ragusa, Isabella Candillier, and Penny Bittone.

Face Divided, written by Edward Allan Baker; directed by Kristen Russell.

Performed by: Violet Levinson and Josh Cromwell.

Running through January 25 at 8 PM (doors open 7:30 PM) at Studio 17, 13 W 17th St, 3rd floor.

Tickets can be had HERE.

80 minutes no intermission.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Let me tell you something.  You know how you fantasize about what you would say to an icon?  Of course you do.  You might be cool and charming and tell that person in a few extraordinary and well thought out phrases how much their work means to you.  You would not gush.  Heaven forbid.  You would not use phrases like, “I am your biggest fan,” which would be even worse.  Your palms would not sweat.  You would make a classy impression on your beloved icon  and move on with the said icon watching you long after you had dropped out of their orbit.

Well, kiddo, all that pretty much flew out the window when I was on the other end of Ian McKellen’s gaze.  This is made intimately possible thanks to the set of tight nifty goggles that each audience member wears in order to experience An Ark.  We are supervised by the excellent ushers because the success of this production depends on these goggles being fitted correctly.  (If  you wear prescription glasses they will make this work anyway.)

Credit Tulis McCall

We are in a large room with nothing to adorn it but an enormous white ball hanging above the center. What interests us most are the four empty wooden chairs we see through our goggles.

Credit Marc J. Franklin

It all sounds complicated, and I haven’t even mentioned the part where you have to check all your belongings and take off your shoes.

All of the palaver is of no matter, however, when McKellen steps into your sight line.  He looks right at you – not through you – because of the magic goggles that you wear.  He is followed by the other three actors: Golda Rosheuvel, Arinzé Kene, and Rosie Sheehy who enter and take their seats.  They, too, look you in the eye.

It’s that looking thing to which I never got used.  Unsettling and intriguing.  The entire experience is reminiscent of the ViewMasters we played with as kids that made 3D pictures.  And before that were the Stereoscopes from the 1800’s that caused women to faint and men to get puffed up.  “There is nothing new under the sun.”  Even Ecclesiastes knew that.

In this case, the direct eye contact is so engaging that the text takes second place in the overall experience.  It is a narrative about all the stages of life.  We hear the exquisite moments and the tragic ones as well.  Beginning to end.  Simon Stephens is telling us “Here we are, all of us, together in this steam of life.  Remember that – especially when the world is being picked apart by self centered and mean people.  Remember that.”

And we do, in our own  way, but not to the extent that we get connected to the story, such as it is.  As beguiling as these actors are – and they are an exquisite ensemble – they are not provided with much of a hook to pull us in and hold us close..

The connection feels so tenuous that at the conclusion of the performance a few people clapped and most did not.  No one knew quite what to do.

This is a media format in its infancy.  It may fare better with a more nuanced future presentation.

Myself, I still lean toward sharing the theater with actors in the flesh.

And now I AM ready for my closeup, Sir Ian.

 

AN ARK – The first play created for and in mixed reality

Written by Simon Stephens, Directed by Sarah Frankcom, Conceived and Produced by Todd Eckert

WITH Ian McKellen, Golda Rosheuvel, Arinzé Kene, and Rosie Sheehy

Production Design by Rosanna VizeVolumetric Captureby 4DViews

Through March 1.  Tickets may be found HERE.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Nicole Itkin

The Broadway revival of Tracy Letts’ Bug at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre feels like a relic of the past. 

Lonely Agnes (played by Carrie Coon)  is living in a crowded motel room. When her friend R. C (played by Jennifer Engstrom) introduces Agnes to Peter (played by Namir Smallwood), Agnes quickly falls in love with Peter. In her loneliness, she begs him to stay in the motel with her. 

Soon, Peter starts talking about bugs. Bugs, bugs, bugs. Everywhere. At first, Agnes can’t see them. She looks and she looks–nothing. But, before long, Agnes falls into his paranoia around bugs: she, too, comes to believe that the bugs are government surveillance in the form of living organisms.

From Peter’s first few lines, it is clear that he is paranoid and delusional. It is clear far too soon that Peter cannot be trusted. And my sole instinct is to scream at Agnes to kick him out, to get him away from her, to run. Instead of a descent into paranoia that feels inevitable, the descent here feels predictable. 

The relationship between Agnes and Peter is meant to be a bedrock of the show, but their relationship feels like it is floating out in space. As Agnes declares her love for Peter, she states that she is confused by why she cares so much for him, confused because she barely even knows him. She admits that they have essentially exclusively spoken about bugs, very little else. That was my question precisely—why does she adore him? Does she really? Without a real belief in the depth of their attachment, their need and desire for each other, it is difficult to understand their future descent, to understand why where one goes, the other does as well. 

The show discusses how beliefs can turn into delusions can can turn into a loosening grip on sanity. It asks at what point we start believing and how we decide we should stop. It asks us how far trust can take us. At its heart, it is about belief. But, unfortunately, from the beginning of the show–I struggle to believe anyone. Which makes the realization that I shouldn’t believe anyone feel easy to accept, not at all a struggle.  

Letts writing is superb. The dialogue and plot create space for significant tension. Unfortunately, very little of that tension actually exists on stage. 

A great show, but a flawed execution.   

 

Written by Tracy Letts

Directed by David Cromer.

Cast: Carrie Coon, Namir Smallwood, Randall Arney, Jennifer Engstrom, Steve Key.

Fight Captain: Ian Duff

Manhattan Theatre Club’s Bug is playing at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre. Tickets available here. Playing through February 22nd.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

And Her Children, a dynamite, deeply dark vision of our troubling times, is strong, uncomfortable, direct, and brilliant in its presentation. I can not say enough good things about this production. The script, the acting, directing, set, musical accompaniment, and lighting come together to produce the power of what theater can be.

Launching from Dana Loesch‘s defending the NRA after the Parkland shooting, and combining it with the essence of Brecht‘s Mother Courage and Her Children, writers Rosie Glen-Lambert and Hailey McAfee dig deep in addressing not only America’s relationship and devotion with guns and the violence they bring, but the mentality behind where so many stand. This show will not make you comfortable no matter where on that spectrum you land.

Speaking from her job as the public face of the NRA defending the indefensible, Anna Fierling (Hailey McAfee) confronts her role as a mother, what the world we live in does to her children, and what she does for a living to support her family and her sense of self as it defines both selfish and selflessness. It’s not a pretty site, any of it. What Hailey gives us in the role of Anna, is not a charicature, but a fully flushed out person grappling with life as she sees it. Her life as she sees it will challenge you and how you see yours.

What’s great about the script is that there’s no preaching. Ideas are presented and feelings are discussed, laid on the table, and observed. Like our individual conscious’s, we are free to decide what to do with the offerings.

The beginning of the year in New York is inundated with great theater brought to you by Under the Radar (January) and Soho Playhouse’s Fringe Encore Series (January and February) making it nearly impossible to see all of the great, and I really mean great, offerings due to the quantity of offerings (put And Her Children at the top of your list). Fringe Encore is put together by its directors traveling the globe to all the theatrical fringe festivals throughout the world (good gig) and bringing the best of the best to New York for you to see. Every year I see things that blow me away, deeply challenge me, put a smile on my face, and make me happy for what live theater can do.

——-

And Her Children is presented by The Attic Collective and Soho Playhouse. Written by Rosie Glen-Lambert and Hailey McAfee, directed by Rosie Glen-Lambert, and performed by Hailey McAfee.

Violinist is Julia Hoffmann.

Scenic design Raphael Mishler; costume, hair, makeup design Mallory McAfee; lighting design Russell Chow; sound design and composition Padra Crisafulli.

Tickets can be had HERE

Flashing lights are used in the production.

Running time 85 minutes.

title.rendered: Morning Stars: American Classical Orchestra Illuminates with Radiance

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

Music can transcend mere performance and become something approaching revelation. Thursday night at Alice Tully Hall was such an evening—a radiant encounter in which sound itself seemed animated by divine inspiration. The American Classical Orchestra, under the baton of its founder and artistic director, Thomas Crawford, presented “Morning Stars,” a program tracing the luminous ascent of eighteenth-century genius through the works of W. A. Mozart, Boccherini, and Haydn. What emerged was not an antiquarian exercise, but a living affirmation of artistic rectitude: historically informed, intellectually alert, and glittering with expressive purpose.

Crawford’s Illuminating Concert Preview: Scholarship Rendered with Wit and Lucidity

From the moment Crawford stepped before the ensemble, one sensed the particular alchemy that distinguishes an ACO evening. Following a vigorous, superbly articulated reading of Mozart‘s Overture to La finta semplice, he embarked on his signature Concert Preview. This was not bloviation but eloquent exegesis—scholarship rendered with wit, charm, and lucidity. With the ease of a raconteur and the precision of a seasoned pedagogue, Crawford illuminated each work’s provenance, stylistic grammar, expressive intention, amusing anecdotes, and historical contexts, while inviting his players to demonstrate key passages. In doing so, he made audible the syntax of music itself: music not as a decorative surface, but as a disciplined language of emotional meaning. One was reminded of Adorno‘s insistence that genuine musical understanding lies in apprehending a work’s historical truth content. Crawford’s gift is to render such understanding accessible without ever diluting its intellectual gravity.

Conductor Thomas Crawford delivering a concert preview with the American Classical Orchestra in the program Morning Stars, at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Period Instruments and the Pursuit of Authentic Sound

The ACO‘s commitment to historically informed performance practice proved central to the evening’s character. Period instruments—gut strings, wooden winds, and valveless brass produced a sound world of translucent intelligibility and pliant warmth. Textures were transparent yet resonant; cantabile passages breathed with delicacy, while dramatic climaxes carried a pungent, almost astringent bite. This was not antiquarian pedantry, but a hermeneutic recovery of original expressive horizons. Alice Tully Hall‘s warm acoustic became an ideal vessel for this luminous palette, allowing color, articulation, and phrasing to speak with unerring precision. The orchestra’s collective sound suggested not a museum exhibit, but a living language—classical in its proportion, yet freshly articulate in its affect.

Song Hee Lee’s Transcendent Mozart: Youthful Mastery Revealed

The emotional apogee of the evening arrived with soprano Song Hee Lee in Mozart‘s Exsultate, jubilate. From her first phrase, Lee revealed a command at once youthful and consummate. Her technique was immaculate: every melisma unfurled with legato grace, every phrase shaped by breath, intelligence, and instinctive poise. The voice itself—graceful yet capable of thrilling amplitude—dazzled equally in hushed pianissimo and ringing fortissimo. What distinguished the performance, however, was not virtuosity alone, but communion. Lee did not merely execute Mozart’s writing; she inhabited it. The motet’s architecture emerged as luminous joy—pure celebration, lifted on sound. Her vocal pyrotechnics never tipped into exhibitionism; instead, they served an expressive line of rare coherence and radiance. This was not simply a star turn, but the apotheosis of youthful mastery, a moment when technique and meaning became indistinguishable.

Song Hee Lee, Soprano, soloist with the American Classical Orchestra in the program Morning Stars, at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall. Courtesy opus3artists

Boccherini’s Noble Symphony: Aristocratic Poise and Expressive Nuance

If Mozart provided the evening’s spiritual center, Boccherini and Haydn supplied its structural and dramatic arc. Boccherini’s Symphony No. 26 in C minor—still too rarely heard—unfolded with aristocratic poise and expressive nuance. Its varied deployment of solo instruments suggested a composer quietly testing the boundaries of orchestral color, presaging the more overt concertante brilliance to follow. The ACO‘s reading emphasized elegance without blandness: lines were shaped with clarity, inner voices articulated with care, and harmonic tensions allowed to register without excess. It was a portrait of a composer often misunderstood as merely decorative, here revealed as thoughtful, balanced, and subtly inventive.

Haydn’s “Le Matin”: The Crowning Achievement of Concertante Brilliance

The crowning achievement of the evening was Haydn‘s Symphony No. 6 in D major, “Le Matin.” Written during his early years at Esterházy, the work remains a marvel of unfailing variety and imagination. Its opening evocation of dawn—soft sonorities emerging from darkness into light—was rendered with remarkable poise, each instrumental entrance precisely weighted, each phrase breathing naturally within the whole. The symphony’s concertante design became a living tableau of musical character. Concertmaster Aisslinn Nosky brought incisive brilliance and rhetorical clarity; violist Jessica Troy offered a glowing inner voice of rare warmth; cellist Myron Lutzke shaped lines with resonant eloquence; and bassist John Feeney anchored the texture with firm, expressive authority. Their dialogues sparkled with vivacity, wit, and structural coherence. Haydn’s invention—at once playful and architectonic—unfolded as both drama and delight, the orchestra illuminating every turn of phrase with precision and style.

Soprano Song Hee Lee performing Mozart’s Exsultate, jubilate with the American Classical Orchestra in the program Morning Stars, at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Historical Awareness as Expressive Liberation

Crawford’s approach throughout the evening underscored a central principle: historical awareness need not constrain expressive freedom. On the contrary, the ACO‘s performance suggested that fidelity to period practice can liberate the music’s innate rhetoric. Ornamentation was purposeful, articulation finely etched, and tempo relationships conceived with a keen sense of proportion. One heard not merely accuracy, but insight—a reading shaped by what might be called musical hermeneutics, in which sound becomes a medium of meaning rather than surface effect. The result was neither academic nor precious, but bracingly alive.

A Legacy of Excellence: Cultural Stewardship at the Highest Level

Since its founding in 1984, the American Classical Orchestra has established itself as New York‘s preeminent period-instrument ensemble. With principal players drawn from the faculty of Juilliard‘s Historical Performance Program and an educational mission that has reached hundreds of thousands of young listeners through its Classical Music for Kids program, the organization embodies cultural stewardship at the highest level. In an era when classical music is too often treated as either a museum artifact or background decoration, the ACO offers something rarer: performances that unite scholarship, imagination, and expressive truth.

The American Classical Orchestra in the program Morning Stars, at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Authenticity as Revelation: A Concert That Speaks to the Present

“Morning Stars” was such an evening—lucid, radiant, and intellectually alive. Through Crawford’s illuminating guidance, Song Hee Lee‘s transcendent Mozart, and the orchestral playing of distinction and vitality, the concert reaffirmed the enduring power of historically informed performance not as nostalgia, but as revelation. Here, authenticity did not constrain imagination; it released it. And in that release, the music spoke not only of the past, but vividly, urgently, to the present.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Exploring genius, indulging ego, examining personal sacrifice at the alter of art, with a toe firmly immersed in the mud of the river of farce, The Disappear is a clever, with a dash of charm, seriocomedy that comes across as straddling the line of entertainment and an exploration of fallibility. In less capable hands then this stellar cast’s, the show would not have been able to get off the ground. But this rendition flies because of the talent on stage that makes the weaknesses in the script negligible.

In an old country house north of the city near water, the second home of married couple Ben (Hamish Linklater) and Mira (Miriam Silverman), they are currently staying there with their daughter while Ben struggles with his art. He is a film director/screenwriter and she is a heralded novelist. A power couple. In his drive to make himself famous again, he is going through a later than mid-life crises about what makes him whole. He’s decided it is not his family. A young actress (Madeline Brewer) comes in to audition and surprise, surprise, he’s now found his true muse that will finally make his life happy. The couple have slowly grown apart for some time and things are now coming to a head.

This is writer director Erica Schmidt‘s second world premier that Audible has produced at Audible’s Minetta Lane Theatre, the first being Lucy.

The title, The Disappear, refers to a movie that Ben ends up writing and directing. The plot of which is a wife who disappears after the husband says at a party that he’s going to kill her. She disappears, and ghost like, torments him for his cruelty. This plot is reflected in the onstage horrific mess of a relationship that Ben and Mira have and what creativity and art requires of its worshipers, as well as the parallel ending of the movie and this play as the characters take leave of each other.

Concerning the end of the movie, “She fails. She’s human. And he fails her by letting her go.”

Ben is a hyper egotistical unlikable character believing that his dogged pursuit of art is the only thing that makes his life worthwhile and everyone should sacrifice in that pursuit. Living this life with blinders on brings about his own destruction and Hamish relishes this in the playing. His key character flaw of speaking before thinking with no filter whatsoever leaves nothing to like as he continually hurts those around him. If the end justifies the means, his all encompassing pursuit of art is the fault that justifies his meanness. We’re told by Mira and his agent Michael Bloom (Dylan Baker) of his personal greatness, but it seems to be long gone and those laurels have now become browned, crinkled, and dried up.

A pleasant entertainment, especially if you enjoy how good actors can elevate a script.

——-

The Disappear, written and directed by Erica Schmidt, premieres off Broadway at Audible’s Minetta Lane Theatre running to February 15, 2026.

Cast: Dylan Baker, Madeline Brewer, Kelvin Harrison Jr., Hamish Linklater, Anna Mirodin, and Miriam Silverman.

Set design by Brett J. Banakis, costume design by Jennifer Moeller and Miriam Kelleher, lighting design by Cha See, and sound design by Palmer Hefferan.

Tickets can be purchased HERE.

This production contains sexual content, nudity, simulated sex, brief strobe lighting effects, and themes of suicide.

title.rendered: Going Bacharach: The Songs of an Icon

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

Awesome! Brilliant! Going Bacharach: The Songs of an Icon is a review of the timeless song gems of Burt Bacharach.

Burt wrote music for over 70 years before his demise in 2023, writing to the tune of over one thousand songs, over a hundred making their way into the ranks of best sellers. Whether you think you do or you don’t, you know Burt Bacharach’s music as he influenced many musicians, singers, and other composers of his and future generations. His musical creations, many in collaboration with Hal David, are classics in the music world, songs that lean on pop, jazz, rock, and folk, but all ringing with Bacharach’s inimitable style.

At the wonderfully intimate Marjorie S. Deane Little Theater is now playing the world premiere of Going Bacharach: The Songs of an Icon, a marvelous tribute and look back at Bacharach’s body of work. The show was conceived by Jack Lewin and co-created with Will Friedwald, Adrian Galante, and Tedd Firth. The arrangements and orchestrations are by Adrian Galante. Galante is the production’s music director, pianist and clarinetist. He opens the evening with a Bacharach overture that only wets our appetite. Along with his brilliant band, he, Galante, is otherworldly in his virtuosity. Never have I seen a pianist’s entire body thrown into the music. Thrown in with gusto and life. Spectacular! And never have I witnessed the pianist step away from his keyboard to then wow us with his magnificent clarinet accompaniment and dazzling solos!

And this is just the beginning because next out steps our three performers for the evening, Hilary Kole, John Pagano, and Ta-Tynisa Wilson who individually and together light up the stage with their vocal and emotional connection to the songs. They bring their beauty and depth and humor along for the Bacharach ride. Pagano tells us he was a fan since he first heard Bacharach and David’s, “What’s New Pussycat” song that they wrote for the 1965 movie comedy of the same title, originally sung by with that sexy wild style, Tom Jones! The song was on a 45 record that because of scratches, skipped. And wonderfully without warning, Pagano sings what he heard as a kid, the skips and all! A brilliant and a wonderful take on how music used to come to us. Pagano was also part of Bacharach’s band and traveled the world with him for 14 years.

Everyone on the stage has a connection of some sort to the music (even Ta-Tynisa, who when asked to audition didn’t think she knew any of Burt’s songs, but as soon as she heard them made the connection that they had been a part of her life) and the man who effortlessly melded genres together and as a musical chef with many fusions and gave us a sound that will live forever.

The songs you’ll hear: “Always Something There to Remind Me,” “Walk on By,” “Do You Know the Way to San Jose,” “Close to You,” “Raindrops Keep Falling On My Head,” “I’ll Never Fall In Love Again,” “What’s It All About Alfie,” “I’ll Say a Little Prayer For You,” “The Look of Love,” and the list goes on and on. From television, to movies, to musicals, encompassing 21 Grammy nominated songs. When you look at Bacharach’s 70 years of songwriting you are looking at the landscape of American entertainment. The best of it!

But wait, there’s more. Throughout the evening is speckled Bacharach anecdotes and behind the scenes musical peeks of how his music came to be and how he shaped it into the memories that we all cherish.

The set design, the layers of curves and light add wonderfully and without overpowering  the layers of Bacharach’s sound and style. A marvelous evening all around.

Going Bacharach: The Songs of an Icon  is the world of music in our lives on the stage at The Marjorie S. Deane Little Theater and it is a must see, must experience.

Going Bacharach: The Songs of an Icon directed by David Zippel, co-created by Will Friedwald, Adrian Galante, Tedd Firth & Jack Lewin, and conceived by Mr. Lewin.

Cast:vocalists : Hilary Kole, John Pagano, Ta-Tynisa Wilson, and Adrian Galante at the Piano & Clarinet leading a 5 piece band.

Band: Piano/Clarinet Adrian Galante, Keyboard Patrick Firth, Guitar Derek Duleba, Bass Nate Francis and Drums Jakubu Griffin

Creative Team: Director David Zippel, Music Direction Adrian Galante, Scenic Design Christopher and Justin Swader, Costume Design Frank Cazares, Lighting and Sound Design Matt Berman, Stage Management Ian McQueen

Going Bacharach: The Songs of an Icon, is produced by Amas Musical Theatre by special arrangement with Jack Lewin. General Management Consultation is by Visceral Entertainment.

Tickets are $59-$119 and can be purchased at www.goingbacharach.com. VIP Package Upgrades are available for $149. The performance schedule is: Monday at 7:30pm; Wednesday at 2:30pm; Thursday at 7:30pm; Friday at 7:30pm; Saturday at 2:30pm and 7:30pm; and Sunday at 2:30pm.

The Marjorie S. Deane Little Theater  (10 West 64th  Street – between Broadway & CPW)

RUNNING TIME IS APPROXIMATELY 100 MINUTES (including intermission)

TICKETS HERE

The production will play through Sunday, February 15, 2026.

title.rendered: Scott & Flynn – Improvisation with Kevin and Dion

content.rendered:
Scott & Flynn (Kevin Scott and Dion Flynn), OG’s of Improv at The Pit Photo by Steph Jacobson

by Margret Echeverria

There was a time in the mid-ninties, when one could not remove their flannel overshirt in New York City without bumping an elbow into a troupe of improvisational actors.  You could see an improv show any night of the week — and sometimes during the day!  As the New York Theater scene has lost its grit on Broadway almost entirely, independent theaters also tend to book safer acts these days.  But, by the grace of Dionysus, the thrill of witnessing actors in games of total risk is not completely dead.  Last Saturday night, Kevin Scott and Dion Flynn, two OG’s of the improv art form treated an audience at The PIT – the extant People’s Improv Theater – to a single show, just the two of them, for one night only this year.  As the world is dark and feels so very cold right now, I was so grateful to have such a great time in their audience.

The best part about watching these seasoned players is that the scaffolding of the games’ structures was often so hidden that it felt like there were no rules; you know the rules, right?  Yes And, Listen, Focus On The Other Person, etc.  Not once did I see either performer reviewing the protocols in their head before coming up with a new action.  The comedic situations, pulled from whim, flowed easily and escalated to draw rolling laughter from the observers.  Making us even more comfortable was the minimal use of audience members to make the show funnier with clever suggestions or even getting up onto the stage themselves.  The connection between those in the seats and the pros on stage was felt, understood and never violated; we could all relax and enjoy the creative energy between Scott and Flynn that was on fire.  And I’m certain that, if the audience members had wanted to participate more, Scott and Flynn would have known it — telepathically?  When improv works, folks, it feels like magic.

Highlights included Scott’s technique for turning dense ideas like a competition for superior philosophical insights into a college debate spectacle in which he played several characters – judge, arrogant self-assured student, teacher/mentor, coach – to both Flynn’s timid competitor faking confidence and the Event Host asking hard questions of the competitors.  In another scene, Flynn morphed his gender identity to give us a vulnerable woman dealing with an attachment avoidant boyfriend (Scott) by charming him with her wit.  But what fascinated me was the dangerous choice Scott made to not always embody the “Yes And” rule.  Scott defied the norm early in the show and my chest tightened with fear that the scene would fall dead, but Flynn would enthusiastically “Yes the No” and elevate the story to our utter delight.  It happened so many times.  That is incredible talent, Friends.  And I want to shout out that these two actors often invented multiple characters on the stage flowing in and out of their shells often exchanging with one another whom they were personifying while the other actor manifested an additional character without losing us once!  Fantastic.

Rumor has it Scott and Flynn will collaborate again early in 2027.  As I pray that we will all still be alive and free then, I also ask the Divine that these two will grace us with another show in 2026.  In the meantime, I encourage the reader to mark their calendar for January 2027 to keep eyes and ears open for an announcement.  The PIT event calendar can be found here.   You can drop in and check out improv classes and open mic offerings at The PIT, 154 West 29th Street, NYC.
