@graph.description: In the summer of 1978, while watching a performance of A Murder is Announced on the London stage, Margret fell in love with the theatre. Born and raised in Cedar Falls, Iowa, Margret came to New York City in 1994. She was admitted to Newmyn’s Nose Limitless Theatre Limited, an innovative and award winning improvisational company, in the summer of 1995 and eventually became a member of the company’s board. Margret starred in the critically acclaimed short film Jigsaw Venus by Dean Capsalis in 2000 (Best Actress, Buenos Aires International Independent Film Festival) and her film career was begun. She played the adorable Fag Hag (GenX does not find this term offensive at all), Audrey, in both A Four Letter Word (2007) as well as Violet Tendencies (2010), films by Casper Andreas and Jesse Archer. She has a co-starring role in Max Emerson's film, Hooked. Always sentimental about performing for a live audience, Margret penned and performed Orangerie, a one-woman show exploring the subject of finding love while traveling non-traditional avenues, which premiered at the Bowery Poetry Club in November of 2005 and ran through the spring of 2006 to critical acclaim. After Margret’s family survived the death of their son, Gavin, to SIDS in 2011, she penned her last one woman show, Finding Gavin, which premiered in New York City in 2015. She was on the season finale of Law & Order SVU in 2021. Margret studied Acting at Regent’s College in London, Classical Voice and Opera at the Royal Academy of Music in London, and Acting at Sally Johnson Studio here in New York City. She has a BFA in Acting from Rockford University. Margret is also a published poet. She lives in Yonkers, NY with her daughter, Alyson.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

At a rehearsal studio on the seventh floor of the Samuel B. and David Rose building at Lincoln Center, as part of the 2026 Under the Radar Festival, is currently running a one man show entitled Benevolence.

Writer and performer Kevin Matthew Wong takes the audience on a personal journey of his ancestry as part of the Chinese Hakka community. The name Hakka (客家) means “guest families,” which refers to their far reaching migrations as often being guests of where they’ve settled, as well as their welcoming cultural outlook on how to treat strangers. They immigrated throughout Asia as well as establishing communities in Jamaica, the U.S., and Canada.

We all want to know who we are. Sometimes who we are comes searching for us.

Such is Kevin’s journey when he gets a phone call from a group of seniors asking him, because of his theatrical background, to write, guide, and direct a talent show for the upcoming Hakka global conference in two months. Realizing that he knows next to nothing about his ancestry, he is very reluctant to take on this task. This task though, decides that this is the right thing for him as it serendipitously guides him to the oldest Buddhist temple in Canada, finally asking his 100 year old grandmother about her life (we get to see her on film, a delightful woman), and realizing that he is part of something bigger than himself that he never knew he was.

Kevin’s amiable presence on his journey makes this a gentle voyage with a guide that enjoys the exploration as much as the audience. His sharp characterizations of the people he meets along the way bring them to life so as we feel we’ve met them. This is a pleasant evening of discovery into a culture that many of us have never been aware of.

——-

Benevolence is created, directed, and performed by Kevin Matthew Wong.

Set and lighting designer Echo Zhou; Composer and sound designer Chris Ross-Ewart; Head of video and video editor Noel Pendawa; Dramaturg Yizhou Zhang.

The Under the Radar Festival has been presenting since 2005 (with a few pauses) productions that it has gleaned from the four corners of the earth.  It has been a theatrical highlight for the month of January in New York City, and a festival that is known for its consistent quality of performance presentation. This year there are 32 offerings on its schedule and all are intriguing.

Now through January 18th. Tickets can be purchased HERE.

Run time 85 minutes.

The Samuel Rehearsal Studio is located on the 7th floor of the Rose Building on West 65th Street, between Broadway and Amsterdam Avenue. To reach the Rose Building, on the north side of the street, take the stairs, elevator, or escalator from street level to the plaza level lobby just past the movie theater. The theater is accessible from the elevators inside the lobby.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Mario Banushi’s play Mami, now playing at NYU Skirball, is stunningly beautiful in the images that it creates. It draws you in immediately as the house lights dim and stage lights slowly reveal the muted glow of a dimly lit street light and a primitive hut with a soft glow emanating from one bulb lighting the interior. From that first visual it immediately launches into two major milestones of life, the pain of birth, and fading from that into lovingly caring for the aged that is both striking, intimate, and universally personal.

This is an image play as there are no words spoken. This silence is both a blessing and a curse, as it deletes one of our tried and true senses from participating. This audible loss though in turn punctuates and strengthens the sense of sight as it is what we have to rely on to find meaning in what is happening in front of us. This heightened sense then enhances the slow hypnotic images unfolding before us. Lack of speech allows us to spend more time with what we’re seeing, more time with the humanity of intertwined body and soul that Banushi is presenting to us. What it does leave open on the other hand is the opportunity for multiple interpretations about what interaction between the actors and their environment means to you. After theater conversations will be mandatory.

Sotiris Melanos’ set (strikingly lit by Stephanos Droussiotis) is magical in its simplicity and flexibility of presentation. The set is basically minimilistic, but rich in it’s representation of the lives unfolding upon it.

This is a difficult play to describe to you as it defies conventional theatricality and instead relies on the creation of haunting imagery to portray its meaning. Image Theater may be a good description. You will take away impressions of living that may linger with you for the rest of your life.

Mami is the initial offering opening the 2026 Under the Radar Festival. Since 2005 (with a few pauses) the festival has presented theater that has been gleaned from the four corners of the earth.  It has been a theatrical highlight for the month of January in New York City, and a festival that is unrivaled in its consistent quality of performance presentation. This year there are 32 offerings on its schedule and all are  intriguing.

——-

Conceived and directed by Mario Banushi
Performers: Vasiliki Driva / Katerina Kristo, Dimitris Lagos / Nontas Damopoulos, Eftychia Stefanou / Ilia Koukouzeli, Angeliki Stellatou, Fotis Stratigos and Panagiota Υiagli
Set and costume design: Sotiris Melanos
Original music and sound design: Jeph Vanger
Lighting design and associate dramaturg: Stephanos Droussiotis
Artistic collaborators: Aimilios Arapoglou, Thanasis Deligiannis

Use of smoke, sound of fireworks, smell of incense, nudity, and violence. This production is recommended for mature audiences.

This performance is 70 minutes with no intermission.

Mami only runs until January 10th, so get your tickets HERE.

title.rendered: The Eglevsky Ballet: A Triumphant Nutcracker with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

There are evenings in the concert hall when time loosens its grip—when chronology, obligation, and the ordinary architecture of thought quietly dissolve, yielding to something at once more primal and more elevated. Such a moment unfolded on a December night at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts in Brookville, as the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony joined forces with the Eglevsky Ballet to present Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s immortal The Nutcracker. What emerged was not merely a seasonal tradition faithfully renewed, but an artistic convergence in which music, movement, color, and collective imagination fused into a shared experience of wonder—an experience that lingered long after the final note faded.

David Bernard with musicians and members of the ballet troupe moments before the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

Conducted with characteristic élan, structural clarity, and emotional intelligence by David Bernard, the performance affirmed the enduring power of live art to enchant, to console, and to remind us—especially in the depths of winter—why human beings continue to gather in darkened theaters, hearts open, ready to be changed.

A scene from the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

Tchaikovsky’s Score: Inexhaustible Wonder

As Theodor Adorno observed, truly great music reveals new dimensions with each encounter, and The Nutcracker—despite its familiarity—proved inexhaustible. The celesta’s silvery shimmer, the pizzicato delicacy of the Trepak, the sweeping cantabile of the Grand Pas de Deux: all emerged freshly minted, as if heard for the first time.

A scene from the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

The Literary Provenance of an Enchanted Tale

The setting itself contributed immeasurably to the evening’s effect. Tilles Center for the Performing Arts, Long Island’s premier live entertainment venue, remains a vital cultural beacon, both architecturally imposing and acoustically refined. Its 2,200-seat Concert Hall, nestled on the campus of Long Island University in Brookville, offered an ideal frame for this grand-scale collaboration—intimate enough to preserve detail, expansive enough to accommodate spectacle.

For nearly four decades, Tilles Center has welcomed artists of international distinction while serving as a cultural commons for Nassau and Suffolk counties. Its commitment to accessibility, education, and artistic excellence makes it a natural home for Eglevsky Ballet’s annual Nutcracker. This production has become a cherished seasonal ritual for generations of families.

A scene from the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

Tilles Center: Long Island’s Cultural Jewel

For nearly four decades, Tilles Center, as a nonprofit institution, has welcomed 150,000 visitors annually, presenting world-renowned artists across all genres while serving as a vital cultural hub for Nassau and Suffolk counties. The Center’s commitment to making the performing arts accessible to all—from symphonic performances to ballet to children’s programming—makes it the natural home for Eglevsky Ballet’s annual Nutcracker tradition.

A scene from the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

Orchestral Excellence: The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony in Full Flower

The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony, recipient of three First Prize awards from The American Prize Competition in Orchestral Performance, once again justified its reputation for depth, discipline, and expressive generosity. Long admired for its transparent sonority and stylistic integrity, the ensemble played with a refinement that revealed Tchaikovsky’s orchestration in all its shimmering detail.

Under David Bernard’s direction—a conductor aptly dubbed “the Johnny Appleseed of Classical Music”—the score unfolded with a natural sense of breath and proportion. Tempi felt organic, rubato expressive yet never indulgent, and dynamic contrasts were shaped with architectural care. Soft passages hovered as snowfall while climaxes bloomed without heaviness, allowing the music’s inherent lyricism to speak.

A scene from the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

The Winds: A Particular Triumph

Of particular distinction throughout the evening was the ever-powerful wind section, performing exactly as Tchaikovsky intended. The composer, that master orchestrator who understood each instrument’s unique voice with almost supernatural prescience, wrote wind parts of uncommon brilliance for The Nutcracker, and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s principals rose magnificently to the challenge. Principal flutist Kennedy Burgess delivered the Sugar Plum Fairy’s celestial melody with an espressivo quality that seemed to float above the orchestra like morning mist over a still pond. The piccolo work throughout sparkled with bravura, while the oboe, clarinet, and bassoon soloists articulated legato phrases of notable elegance.

The famous Waltz of the Flowers unfolded with rubato that breathed naturally, the harp arpeggios of Sophia Shedd rippling beneath the melody like sunlight on water. Indeed, the entire evening showcased solid playing throughout, with the works’ colors and moods performed with verve and aplomb—a tour de force of orchestral collaboration.

New York City Ballet principal dancers Miriam Miller as the Sugar Plum Fairy and Tyler Angle as her Cavalier in a scene from the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

Dance of the Highest Order: Principal Dancers from the New York City Ballet

The Sugar Plum Fairy and Her Cavalier

The crown jewels of this vast production included, without question, the guest appearances by New York City Ballet principal dancers Miriam Miller as the Sugar Plum Fairy and Tyler Angle as her Cavalier. Their performance of the Pas de Deux from George Balanchine’s The Nutcracker®—presented by arrangement with The George Balanchine Trust and produced in accordance with the Balanchine Style® and Balanchine Technique® Service standards—was nothing short of breathtaking.

Ms. Miller, who ascended to the rank of principal dancer at NYCB just this January 2025, brought to the Sugar Plum Fairy a luminous quality that seemed almost otherworldly. Her port de bras flowed with liquid grace, each arabesque held with the kind of serene stillness that speaks to complete mastery of one’s instrument. There was, in her dancing, that rare quality which the great ballet critic Arlene Croce once described as the ability to make virtuosity appear effortless—to transform technical mastery into pure poetry.

A scene from the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

Mr. Angle, a principal since October 2009 and a veteran of countless Nutcracker performances at Lincoln Center, partnered Ms. Miller with the gallantry and technical assurance that have made him one of NYCB’s most valued danseurs nobles. His lifts were secure yet seemingly weightless, his tours en l’air crisp and landed with feline precision. Together, they embodied that Balanchinian ideal of partnership—two individuals moving as one, each enhancing the other’s artistry through perfect symbiosis.

A Grand Production: The Eglevsky Ballet’s New Vision

Peter LeBreton Merz’s Fresh Choreography

The new choreography by Artistic Director Peter LeBreton Merz brought fresh energy to this beloved classic while honoring its traditions. Mr. Merz, whose distinguished career spans the Academy at Ballet West, Point Park University, and the USA International Ballet Competition, has created a production that speaks to contemporary sensibilities while preserving the work’s essential enchantment. His reimagining of the Act II divertissements—incorporating global holiday traditions from the Good Luck Grapes of Spain to the Dongzhi celebration of China—demonstrates a thoughtful expansion of the ballet’s cultural horizons.

Choreographer and Artistic Director Peter LeBreton Merz and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

The Full Company: A Stage Alive with Movement

The scale of this production must be acknowledged: here was a company of dancers, magnificent scenery, period costuming, and a symphony orchestra—the kind of grand theatrical undertaking that has become all too rare in our economically constrained artistic landscape. The Eglevsky Ballet, founded in 1961 by legendary New York City Ballet principal dancer André Eglevsky, demonstrated throughout the evening why it has remained Long Island’s premier ballet company for over sixty years.

The company dancers performed with notable dedication. Bella Radolovic, in her eighth season with Eglevsky, brought youthful wonder to Clara, while Giuliano Ruocco danced the Nutcracker Prince with athletic grace. The supporting cast—including Brett Dalis as both the Harlequin Doll and Rat King, Courtney Jordan as Frau Drosselmeyer, and the luminous Ayne Kim as Dew Drop—contributed performances of consistent quality and commitment.

The Waltz of the Snowflakes in Act I, with its corps of sixteen dancers moving in unison patterns of crystalline precision, demonstrated Répétiteur Courtney Jordan‘s meticulous rehearsal direction. The Flowers of Act II, led by Claire Higgins and Caroline Jonassen, unfolded with the legato grace that Tchaikovsky’s sweeping waltz demands.

Conductor David Barnard in the forefront during curtain calls at the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

Tchaikovsky’s Masterpiece: A Score of Inexhaustible Riches

Truly great music resists exhaustion. It does not yield its meaning all at once, nor does familiarity diminish its force; rather, each encounter discloses new internal relationships, fresh emotional weather, newly perceived truths. The Nutcracker—despite its omnipresence during the holiday season—proved once again the accuracy of this insight. What lesser works risk becoming background ritual, Tchaikovsky’s score continually reclaims as living experience.

Completed in 1892, the music reveals a composer at the height of his imaginative powers, deploying orchestral color with a specificity that feels almost sentient. The celesta’s otherworldly shimmer for the Sugar Plum Fairy—an instrument so novel that Tchaikovsky famously concealed its use until the premiere—still sounds like a message from another realm. The pizzicato delicacy of the Trepak, the long-breathed cantabile of the Grand Pas de Deux, the glowing warmth of the waltzes: each passage seems to know precisely how memory works, how wonder forms, how joy takes hold before the mind can interfere.

A scene from the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

Adorno warned that art loses its force when it becomes merely consumable. Yet The Nutcracker survives precisely because it does the opposite: it reawakens perception. Heard in the context of live performance—embodied by dancers, shaped by breath, suspended in silence—it restores what modern life so often dulls: attentiveness, emotional openness, and the capacity for unguarded delight.

The original 1892 production, choreographed by Lev Ivanov to Petipa’s scenario at the Imperial Mariinsky Theatre in St. Petersburg, launched a tradition that would eventually conquer the Western world. George Balanchine’s 1954 production for New York City Ballet transformed the work into an American institution, and it is fitting that his Pas de Deux graced this Long Island production.

An Evening of Pure Enchantment

A performance that generated unmistakable warmth was received by a full house, with smiles radiating throughout the hall—children and adults alike visibly caught in its spell. What unfolded was not simply well executed; it was deeply felt. The dancing, music, and stagecraft worked in quiet unanimity to stir something elemental, touching hearts and igniting imaginations with a joy that felt both immediate and strangely profound.

In moments of authentic artistic experience, one may briefly perceive reality not as something fixed, but as something fluid—its rhythms, its contours, its emotional tides suddenly made visible. Such experiences do not argue or explain; they reveal. And so it was in that darkened theater, as Tchaikovsky’s final bars dissolved into a hushed, almost sacred silence—an intake of collective breath—before the spell finally released itself in sustained, grateful applause.

A scene from the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

The evening concluded, as all great Nutcrackers must, with Clara’s return from her journey—whether dream or awakening—surrounded by warmth, love, and the glow of something newly discovered. It is a Christmas Eve she will never forget, the program book reminds us. Nor, one suspects, will anyone who shared in this luminous performance.

In moments like these, art does not merely decorate the season—it reminds us that music and movement are ways of knowing, teaching us how to feel time, how to trust wonder, and how to recognize ourselves, briefly and joyfully, in sound and motion.

The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony: A Legacy of Excellence

The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony, critically acclaimed by The New York Times, Gramophone, and WQXR, continues its mission of bringing artistic excellence and innovation to audiences in New York City and worldwide. Through its partnership with InsideOut Concerts, Inc.—David Bernard’s innovative approach to building new audiences for classical music—the orchestra has pioneered immersive concert experiences that place audience members among the musicians.

The collaboration with Eglevsky Ballet represents yet another dimension of the orchestra’s community engagement, demonstrating that music and ballet, sound and motion, pillars of the arts, remain vibrantly alive on Long Island.

A view from the Orchestra Pit of the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

Eglevsky Ballet: Programs and Contact Information

Eglevsky Ballet, Long Island’s premier ballet academy and the official ballet company of the Tilles Center, offers comprehensive dance training for aspiring dancers of all ages at its state-of-the-art 12,000-square-foot facility in Bethpage.

From the beloved Kinderdance Program introducing children as young as three to the joy of movement, through the Children’s Division (First Steps, Pre-Primary, and Pre-Ballet), the Lower School (Levels I–V), and the rigorous Pre-Professional Training Program (PTP I, II, and III) preparing serious students for professional careers, Eglevsky Ballet nurtures dancers at every stage of their journey.

Curtain calls at the Eglevsky Ballet production of The Nutcracker at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony and Conductor David Bernard. Courtesy eglevskyballet.org

The academy also offers an Adult Division for those discovering or returning to ballet, Summer Intensives for ages 7–20, master classes with nationally and internationally renowned educators, and a free ballet program for boys ages 6–10. Former students have gone on to dance with prestigious companies including American Ballet Theatre, New York City Ballet, Carolina Ballet, and Collage Dance Collective.

In addition to training, Eglevsky Ballet presents its annual production of The Nutcracker—the most significant and only professional production on Long Island—and a Spring Workshop performance at Adelphi University.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Taylor Mac’s Holiday Sauce was a holiday pageant with teeth.

I entered New York City’s historic Town Hall to spend an evening with an artistic genius: one who would drop us into a cauldron: queer or not, stir us with laughter and spirit separated from and relieving us of the clashing family, hectic gatherings and gift-giving, and stressing over what to wear to Christmas parties. I had been impressed with Mac’s unapologetic approach in his performances and orchestrations over the past few years.

Cue Taylor Mac stunning us with an entrance as a banana split—which was about as hard to remove, unrehearsed as you can imagine—hilariously—center stage.

I expected an absurd spectacle of freaky and grotesque humor. I anticipated the campy, outlandishly creative, and sardonic renditions of Christmas classics and original songs. But a deeper trauma-turned-loathing bled through much of the evening.

As the audience was asked to stand to join in Mac’s rendition of “O Holy Night,” moving our bodies in ways we all found funny: fisting, as we caroled together “O, Holy.” Now, imagine a room of people dropping to their knees—or the closest they could get to the floor in a packed theater—as “fall to your knees” was belted from the stage, the balcony, the orchestra. When the song references the birth of Christ, Mac prompted us to instead sing our praises to nature and his mentor and drag mother, Mother Flawless Sabrina.

I leaned over to my friend, half joking—half serious: Are we in the middle of a cult?

Mac’s performance was ultimately performed for this queen, who inspired and protected him through formative years in his career; his mantra of the evening, “When the sun gives less, the heart gives more,” aligned with his celebration of the winter solstice.

Mac expressed a deep, underlying bitterness: the way his resentment of Christianity taking over winter solstice filled the space and tampered with my fun.

The true moment of audience participation was when a giant blow-up banana was released into the audience, and we all hit it, soaring across the orchestra. My friend went wild over this, extending himself just to touch that banana twice.

His band (lead by Matt Ray) rocked the entire night through unfiltered chaos. MissHis Claus and Mr. Claus (strap-on included) were our first guests to the party.

Baby Jesus (Tigger-James Ferguson) was rolled out wearing a diaper, soon pulled down—an audience member spanked him with palms.

Machine Dazzle, bristled down the aisle as a decked-out, towering tree.

Photo Credit: Little Fang

Ari Shapiro made a surprise appearance as he performed a Yiddish song, Keler Fun Ash. It was calming, weighty: a sincere hymn that made us pause and linger in the moment. Blues singers from the band—one being Thornetta Dais—sang songs rooted in God, interestingly contrasting Mac’s tone.

Cue Mac dressed as a carousel, playing a ukulele, singing a comedic diddy about going to grandma’s for Christmas. It quickly turns dark. I’m simultaneously cackling laughter while my chest tightens; the sharp imagery—the narrative—is real, and it’s distressing. But this song is the most prominent of the night—it captures the pain in that absurd and amusing way only Mac can pull off. THIS is what I wanted the whole night.

Photo Credit: Kendra Jones

This evening was honestly a lot to unpack: the dialogue stole space for genius humor. I wanted to be split in both laughter and confusion of what the heck was happening up there. Instead, we were there to join in on the hate of the Christian holiday, how it stole the light from the pagan holidays. Frankly, I didn’t need to hear any references towards the history of Christianity to understand that Mac was not celebrating God or enduring Christmas traditions.

Maybe this is Mac coping with the season, and I’m sure many others found comfort through this performance. I was reminded that while I was repelled by the bitterness, this was a drag concert of personal narrative. Holiday Sauce is about the comfort we find in our found family and our art.

Taylor Mac’s Holiday Sauce is produced by Pomegranate Arts and is part of the 2025-2026 Season of The Town Hall Presents, celebrating Black Brilliance, Queer Icons, Girlhood, Animated Splendor, and Spiritual Inspirations. It was performed at the Town Hall, New York City.

Written and performed by Taylor Mac. Co-directed by Niegel Smith.

Featuring: Steffanie Christi’an (Vocals), Machine Dazzle (Costume Designer/Ensemble), Thornetta Davis (Vocals), El Beh (Cello), Glenn Marla (Featured Performer), Dusty Childers (Featured Performer), Viva Deconcini (Guitar), Antoine Drye (Trumpet), Greg Glassman (Trumpet), J Walter Hawkes (Trombone), Skye Steele (Violin), Joel E. Mateo (Drums), Danton Boller (Drums).

Music, pageantry and band led by longtime collaborator, Matt Ray.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

This is a play that you should see because it has affected you.  Whether you know it or not.

Meg Crane invented the first at-home-pregnancy test in 1968.  Called “Predictor.” On the day I saw the show Crane, normally played by Caitlin Jinnunen, was played by the understudy Lauren Molina who did a brilliant job in spite of lugging around a script.

Meg Crane’s invention “Predictor” was inventer in 1967, but not approved by the FDA until 1976.

Got that?

Crane’s contribution to this invention was played down by the men running things in the pharmaceutical world.  Surprise.  So much so that neither you nor I know about Crane.

Until now.

What this play details is Crane’s story – which is not pretty – as she battered her way into the inner sanctums of a company called Orgonon.  There are a lot of gaps in this script, one of which is how she got hired as a graphic designer and then not given the chance to ply her craft.  It was only when she got a tour into the inner sanctum where women’s urine samples were analyzed and the results known within hours.  Those results were not given to the woman directly, of course, but sent to the doctors.  It could take upwards of a few weeks for the results to be given to the woman.  Not clear on why – it was just a fact.  This fact made NO sense to Crane.

This procedure was, however, SOP in the day, ( think “Madmen.”) including everyone except the women in question, giving those included in the food chain a job (this was AFTER the method of injecting rabbits with the urine and then killing them to obtain the results…).  When Meg Crane did the math and saw how simple the process was, and that it could indeed been performed by ANY woman, she was threatening to topple an entire male hierarchy.

This was not her intention.  Her intention was to help women have control of their bodies.

Oops – what WAS she thinking???

It is also not clear how it happened that Crane signed over her rights.  That it was a power grab is clear.  But the details could have been clearer – for me.  As it was, the rest of the audience was  completely on board.  When Crane was given the signature page to sign over her rights, one woman whispered in a loud voice, “Don’t do it!”

So despite my desire for fewer gaps in the story – the story itself hits home.  This is due in no small part to the cast.  As I mentioned, Laura Molina ably handled the role of Meg Crane.  This means that the Standby Adrienne Wells was jettisoned into the role of Chorus #2.  The two actors were seamless, as was the rest of the cast who had to modify their movements to adjust for and support these two actors.

Unfortunately the characters, with the exception of Meg Crane, are all labeled as “Chorus”.  And the program (only available with a QR Code) has photos of the cast that are grayed out.  So all I can tell you is this ensemble of Jes Washington, April Ortiz, John Leonard Thompson, Eric Tabach, Nick Piacente, Adrienne Wells, and Jose Maria Aguilawas perfect in every way – and believe me they have costume changes and character shifts that make your head spin.

A final note to the understudy announcement: there was none.  It took me awhile to figure out that the pile of papers Meg Crane was carrying was a script.  When I mentioned this to the house manager at intermission he pointed to the small sign at his counter and another one on the side of the doorway.  I reminded him that people don’t read and that an announcement would have been helpful.   He was very kind and assured me that the signs were enough.

I am officially old school.

Support this play.  It needs a few revisions, but the story is critical and should be part of our well-known history.  In the 1960’s married women could not get a credit card in their own name.  Female flight attendants could not be married.  Abortion was illegal.  Birth control was made legal in 1965.

And while all this was going on, Meg Crane was pursuing her goal of a home pregnancy test.  Have a look HERE.

It took ten  years, but Meg Crane changed lives and continues to do so.

Predictor, written by Jennifer Blackmer; directed by Alex Keegan

WITH Caitlin Kinnunen, Jes Washington, Lauren Molina, April Ortiz, John Leonard Thompson, Eric
Tabach, Nick Piacente, Adrienne Wells, and Jose Maria Aguila

The creative team includes Scenic Design by Cat Raynor, Costume Design by
Alicia Austin, Lighting Design by Zach Blane, Sound Design by Daniela Hart, Noel Nichols, and
Bailey Trierweiler

The AMT Theater (354 W 45th St, New York, NY 10036), December 6-January 18.  TICKETS HERE

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: Musica Sacra: A Luminous Evening of Sacred Splendor

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

There are evenings when the stars align—when venue, ensemble, and repertoire conspire to create something ineffable, something that transcends mere performance and enters the realm of the transcendent. Such was the case on Wednesday evening when Musica Sacra, New York’s longest continuously performing professional chorus, graced the hallowed stage of Carnegie Hall’s Isaac Stern Auditorium with their annual “Classics for Christmas” program. Indeed, this venerable hall—with its superb provenance and acoustics that seem to have been designed by angels themselves—provided the apposite setting for an evening of musical magnificence.

Under the luminous baton of Music Director and Impresario Kent Tritle—whom The New York Times has aptly called “the brightest star in New York’s choral music world”—the ensemble delivered a performance that was, in equal measure, intellectually rigorous and deeply moving. Moreover, Tritle’s expressive, enthusiastic conducting throughout the evening demonstrated why he remains the preeminent force in American choral music.

Maestro Kent Tritle with the Chorus and Orchestra of Musica Sacra in Classics for Christmas at Carnegie Hall. Photo by Brian Hatton

Bach’s “Gloria in excelsis”: A Fanfare of Celestial Joy

The program opened with Johann Sebastian Bach’s magnificent “Gloria in excelsis” from his Mass in B Minor—a work of such polyphonic intricacy that it demands nothing less than perfection from its performers. Accordingly, the Musica Sacra Chorus and Orchestra rose magnificently to the occasion. The balance between choir and orchestra was exemplary and elegant; the sixteen independent vocal and instrumental parts danced together in what the program notes correctly described as “a joyous triple-meter fanfare.” Here was Bach’s brilliant oeuvre rendered with luminous clarity, immediately establishing the evening’s tone of celebratory excellence.

Thompson’s “Alleluia”: The Choir’s Sublime A Cappella Prowess

What followed was a most exquisite demonstration of the choir’s remarkable capabilities. Randall Thompson’s Alleluia—that “fanfare for voices” born of wartime contemplation—was performed a cappella with such elegance and pathos that one felt transported. As the philosopher Susanne Langer once observed, “Music is the tonal analogue of emotive life,” and nowhere was this more evident than in the choir’s gorgeous gradual build to the work’s apex and denouement. The pitch was impeccable, the blend seamless, and the musicality profound—a testament to the finely crafted skills that distinguish this ensemble.

Kathryn Lewek, Soprano, guest artist with the Chorus and Orchestra of Musica Sacra in Classics for Christmas at Carnegie Hall. Courtesy kathrynlewek.com

Corelli’s “Christmas Concerto”: The Doctrine of Affections Made Manifest

Subsequently, Arcangelo Corelli’s Concerto Grosso in G Minor, Op. 6, No. 8—the celebrated “Christmas Concerto”—demonstrated the strings’ splendid sonority. Performed by strings and continuo (organ), this glorious, well-crafted work beautifully embodied in all its manifestations the Affektenlehre (doctrine of affections) of the Baroque era. Special recognition must be given to the concertmaster, principal second violin, and principal cello, whose interplay masterfully evoked the pastoral sounds of Italian shepherds on that first Christmas night.

Soprano Kathryn Lewek: A Voice of Crystalline Magnificence

The evening’s vocal centerpiece was undoubtedly the Scena from Handel’s Messiah, featuring the ecstatically marvelous soprano Kathryn Lewek. To say Lewek’s performance was mesmerizing would be an understatement. Her soaring, gorgeous intones were crafted and performed with such grace and virtuosity that one recalled The New York Times‘ assessment: “singing like Lewek’s is what the magic of opera is all about.”

Soprano Kathryn Lewek with Kent Tritle and the Chorus and Orchestra of Musica Sacra in Classics for Christmas at Carnegie Hall. Photo by Brian Hatton

Her tone and sonority were pure, her expressive powers formidable, and her melismatic passages in “Rejoice Greatly” were performed seemingly without effort—a testament to her remarkable facility and style. Indeed, this is an artist whose sumptuous range and crystalline purity remind us why we attend live performances: to witness the ineffable made audible.

From Poulenc to Paish: A Panoply of Contemplative Beauty

Francis Poulenc’s O magnum mysterium, performed a cappella, offered a marvelously captivating change in musical styles—a testament to Tritle’s gift for selecting music from varied eras that fit perfectly within a unified thematic arc. Furthermore, Helena Paish’s “While Mary Slept”—composed when this Scottish prodigy was merely eighteen years old—featured the exquisite voices of Adrienne Lotto (soprano) and Clifton Massey (countertenor). This haunting lullaby demonstrated Tritle’s commitment to bringing new works to the forefront, creating a panoply of sonic landscapes that embrace celebration, family, love, generosity, and thankfulness.

Mariko Anraku, Harp, guest artist with the Chorus and Orchestra of Musica Sacra in Classics for Christmas at Carnegie Hall. Courtesy @aiashow on Instagram

Harpist Mariko Anraku: Otherworldly Elegance

The second concerto of the evening brought to the stage the incomparable Mariko Anraku, associate principal harpist of the Metropolitan Opera Orchestra. In Handel’s Harp Concerto in B-flat Major, Anraku expressed an exquisite, effervescent, otherworldly beauty that fully justified The New York Times‘ description of her as “a masterful artist of intelligence and wit.” Her fingers seemed to coax light from the strings, transforming the Baroque dance forms into something at once ancient and utterly contemporary.

L-R: Maestro Kent Tritle, Guest Conductor Michael Sheetz, Harpist Mariko Anraku, Soprano Kathryn Lewek, and the Chorus and Orchestra of Musica Sacra in Classics for Christmas at Carnegie Hall. Photo by Brian Hatton

A Heart-Rendering Finale: From Adam to Handel

Adolphe Adam’s beloved Cantique de Noël, beautifully arranged by K. Scott Warren and conducted by Associate Music Director Michael Sheetz, featured Lewek once again in a marvelous, moving rendition of this familiar carol. Rachmaninoff’s magnificent “Bogoroditse Devo” from his “All-Night Vigil”, performed a cappella, provided a beautiful transition to the evening’s triumphant conclusion: Handel’s “Worthy is the Lamb” from Messiah.

The audience rose with thunderous applause, prompting an encore of the “Hallelujah” chorus—and everyone stood, just as King George II reportedly did so long ago. Marvelous, moving, inspiring!

An Ensemble Without Peer

In the final analysis, this concert affirmed what devotees of Musica Sacra have long known: this is an ensemble of extraordinary virtuosity, impeccable artistry, seamless skills, expressivity, and profound musicality. Under Kent Tritle’s visionary leadership, they continue to set the standard for professional choral performance in America. As Virginia Woolf once noted in her extended essay A Room of One’s Own (1929), “One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well.” In our context, one cannot live fully without experiencing music of this stature.

Maestro Kent Tritle conducting tonight’s encore, Handel’s “Hallelujah” chorus with the Chorus and Orchestra of Musica Sacra in Classics for Christmas at Carnegie Hall. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Phone: 862-352-9509

Upcoming: “Oquin and Shaw” featuring the world premiere of Wayne Oquin’s On the Words of Walt Whitman — featuring soprano Susanna Phillips and baritone John Moore, March 11, 2026, St. Bartholomew’s Church, NYC

excerpt.rendered: Musica Sacra’s “Classics for Christmas” at Carnegie Hall offers a transcendent musical experience that celebrates the season’s joy and contemplation. Under Kent Tritle’s masterful direction, with luminous performances by Kathryn Lewek and Mariko Anraku, this concert reminds us why live sacred music remains essential. Seek out Musica Sacra’s upcoming season—your soul will thank you.

Bt Tulis McCall

Sidney Myer is a cross between a mensch and an elf.  At over 6 feet tall, with rosy cheeks, a curly mop of hair and an actual twinkle in his eye, Myer is an inside joke personified.  From the second he steps onstage you want to buy whatever he is selling.  His music selection is eclectic in the extreme.  Most of the number are unfamiliar to us, but Myer’s delivery makes us think we have heard them before. “I May Never Go Home Anymore” (Ralph Arthur Roberts & Jack Brooks) was originated by Marlene Dietrich in 1958, but Myer makes us think it is just for us in the room.

Many of Myer’s choices could be considered camp, but there is a kind of innocence combined with a touch of daring that infuses his delivery.  “I Am Your Man” (Bonnie Lee Sanders & Ellen Schwartz is followed by a dated and sentimental “That’s Him” from “One Touch Of Venus” (Kurt Weill/ Ogden Nash) that Myer first heard sung by Mary Martin 50 or so years ago.  It never entered his mind that it would be okay and accepted for him to sing.  Lyrics wander through the forest of love, picking simple sweet images – like how you feel when your heart is gone, or how you could pick him out of a crowd of millions,  or how you feel about a hat created just for you, or how you feel about fireflies glimmer – COMPLETE schmaltz up and down.  But in Myer’s hands these become sweet Cupid’s arrows that we cannot avoid.

The evening is not all sentiment.  Myer’s parody of “Santa Baby” presents us a cornucopia of Jewish requests from brisket to latkes to bagels with a schmeer.  And “A New Year’s Eve Love Song” (Joshua Cohen)  is a list of every place a to which a person would travel for a lover EXCEPT go to Times Square on New Year’s Eve.  It is a too true song that wraps us up in the smug feeling of being real New Yorkers and not tourists.  Feh on tourists.

Myer breaks our hearts more than once – “The Kerry Dance” (by James Lynam Molloy – written in the 1800’s),  “Namely You” (Gene DePaul & Johnny Mercer)  and gives a nod to the present state of affairs by encouraging us to “Just Keep Holdin’ On” (Alan Barcus).  And we get the old chestnuts that we have come to expect, and these are delivered as if for the first time.

There is an old fashioned quality to Sidney Myer.  He is a story teller whose medium is music.  He is devoted to spreading love because that is his nature.  He has been the impresario of Don’t Tell Mama for decades.  I myself have been on the receiving end of his generosity more than once.  This purity combined with a touch of being sly enough to get out ahead of his audience that clobbers us.  We are, after all, New Yorkers who take a certain pleasure in being jaded, but Sidney sprinkles his Magic all over us before we have a chance to refuse.

An evening with Sidney Myers is an evening of enchantment.   Period.

There are a few more shows this week – mostly sold out.  But don’t give up.  Go online or even call 212-995-0900.  Or just show up and see if there are any no-shows.  (Don’t tell anyone I said that.)

Sidney Myer Rides Again! – Musical Director: Tracy Stark, Bass: Skip Ward, Drums: David Silliman

Tues Dec 23, Sat Dec 27 and Mon Dec 29, all at 7pm $25 cover and $20 minimum. and A SPECIAL NEW YEARS SHOW With a music charge at a heart-warming $50 per person and a $75 food and drink minimum

Pangea, 178 Second Avenue (between 11th & 12th Streets) 212-995-0900.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

What if  you took the story of Ann Frank – that most of us read at least once – and turned it inside out.  Instead of focusing on two Jewish families who hid in an Amsterdam attic for two years during WWII,  you just started tossing around “What if’s” like ping pong balls?  What if you threw everyone’s sexual identities and preferences up in the air and let everyone grab what they could get their hand on.  Just for starters.  What if?

And what if you added some wild and thrilling music with lyrics that made people laugh so hard they had to hush themselves so they could hear the next line?

And what if you collected a cast that could sing the Be-Jesus out of anything.

Well, WHAT IF has won the lottery and is now in residence at  a tiny east side theater, and the smart money says that you will want to get your but over to Asylum NYC (123 East 24th Street, NYC). The show, which initially announced a three-week run, is now adding its fourth month of performances, through December 28.

Inspired by a viral Twitter thread that asked, “Did Anne Frank ever acknowledge her white privilege?”, “Slam Frank” not only answers that question, it multiplies it like a gyroscopic adventure.   Boiled down to its bones, this is a group of people saying, “What About Me?” “What about all my weird bits? Just because there is a war on (not to much mention of that here) doesn’t mean I don’t want and think and yearn and dream.  Doesn’t mean I won’t question every teeny weeny thing that floats under my nose.”

Anne (the jubilant Olivia Bernábe) is perfectly kitted out (a special nod to Sarah Lockwood for creating costumes that suited each character brilliantly) in her plaid 1940’s school girl skirt and suspenders that match the diary she will never release. Anne is at the center of the tsunami we do not see coming.

Olivia Bernábe as Anne; Photo by Jasper Lewis

She is filled with teenage EVERYTHING and her parents are not much help.  Her mother Edith (Austen Horne) has had her last nerve trampled on and is about to create a black feminist movement all on her own.  Anne’s father Otto (Rocky Paterra) has the kind of OCD that compels him to catalog his many afflictions.  Over and over and over again. Everyone’s got something.  And NOTHING goes unnoticed by Anne.

The twists and turns in this story remind me of the old wooden roller-coasters that made you think the first steep hill and subsequent drop were the main event.  Little did you realize that you would be tossed and tumbled over and over again until the train finally pulled into the station and poured you out.

You see none of this story coming, no matter how much you try.  And that is the point isn’t it?

Considering that  this show is now in the fourth month of a previously planned three week run, this writer assumes that a move is in the works.  Another reason to see it now so you can say “I saw the original downtown”.  A new venue will give them a larger audience, and it can also provide time for some serious rewrites.

Sinensky and Fox have overwritten this story – we do that when we are uncertain as to whether or not we are being clear.  Now that they know – they can afford to strip away the unneeded text and peel the songs down to the minimum.

These terrific actors will carry less and deliver more.  That is the magic.

Looking forward to the next incarnation.  YOU on the other hand, don’t have to wait that long.

SLAM FRANK book by Joel Sinensky, score by Andrew Fox, directed by Sam LaFrage.

Olivia Bernábe as Anita (Anne), Andrew Fox as Mr. Van Daan, Alex Lewis as Peter, Anya van Hoogstraten as Margot, Austen Horne as Edith, Rocky Paterra as Otto, Jaz Zepatos as Mrs. Van Daan, and Walker Stovall as the Assistant Stage Manager. Covering the company are Kris Bramson, Peter Kendall, and Crystal Stewart.

The creative team includes Associate Director Emily Abrams, Music Director Alex Harrington, Choreographer Nico DeJesus, Assistant Choreographer Arianne Meneses, Costume Designer Sarah Lockwood, Set and Props Designer CJ Howard, Lighting and Live Video Streaming Designer Zach Lobel, and Projections Designer Nicholas Ferrari

Performances are at Asylum NYC (123 East 24th Street, New York City) through December 28; Tuesday – Sunday at 7 pm; Saturdays and Sundays at 2:00 pm. Tickets are $60–$120 at SlamFrankMusical.com, with $20 standby tickets available in person at showtime, subject to availability.

@graph.name: Tulis McCall
@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

In Tartuffe at the New York Theatre Workshop, Lucas Hnath is serving up satire in a colorful reinterpretation of an ever relevant tale of religious hypocrisy and human fallibility.  Told in verse but in  modern vernacular, peppered with epithets that feel out of place, even forced,  the play is nonetheless set in its original century, with beautiful period costumes and set.

The story, in brief, is of Tartuffe (literally the ‘imposter’) (Matthew Broderick), a man of false piety and nefarious aims, who has managed to worm his way into the household of the wealthy dingbat Orgon (David Cross).  So infatuated is he with Tartuffe, Orgon falls into the trap of mindless religious zeal, slowly ceding Tartuffe more power over his family, his money and his life.  Meanwhile Tartuffe is chasing every skirt he sees.

And oh, what skirts!  Enver Chakartash‘s detailed, whimsical costumes delight in the era of the panier and knee breeches.  Invigorated with heightened color, they are a delicous treat, like ‘petit fours’ in clothing form.  Chakartash’s designs are characters unto themselves, complemented pefectly by Robert Pickens wig design.  A candy pink ruffled underskirt and flowered panier perfectly reflects the candy coated character of Orgon’ hapless daughter Mariane (Emily Davis).   With her ringlets and look of eternal confusion and despair, Mariane is like a china doll come to life.  As her mother Elmire (Amber Gray), in her own delightfully flowered panier gown, is a far more able woman.  She despairs as her husband falls ever the more prey to Tartuffe’s influence, and her plot to expose Tartuffe’s hypocrisy is cunning (if doomed to failure).

For his part, Orgon is the perfect mark.  Self-absorbed and, let’s face it, pretty dim, he willingly twists any conversation or complaint into justification for Tartuffe’s behavior.  Attired in head-to-toe lavish gold brocade, with a side order of gold brocade, he is like a 17th century European buddha without the capacity for self-reflection.  David Cross carries this role brilliantly, with perfect timing and subtlety that give his bewildering ideation an odd kind of heft. All with the lightest of touches.

Bianca del Rio, as Orgon’s domineering mother Madame Pernelle, sweeps onto stage, breathing life into her scenes as she moves and speaks more directly than the other characters, brooking no contradiction.  The contrast between her agency and the almost frozen quality of the other characters feels intentional, as Madame Pernelle is more a sardonic narrator  of the action than a participant, clarifying the relationships among them and tidying up plot points in a self-assured bow.  Yes, like the others she speaks in verse, but unlike them she is not trapped in it.

Yet it is Matthew Broderick, as Tartuffe, the ever innocent yet persistent sotto voce Svengali who steals the show.  In an intelligent, careful, sly performance, Broderick presents a mighty character in deceptively reasonable form.  He’s so stable, even when you know he’s being creepy.  ‘Barkus is Willing’ meets Uriah Heap.  Broderick somehow slithers without slithering.  And he’s funny as hell.  Honestly he’s so funny it’s hard to be mad at him, much as you long for his comeuppance.

Director Sarah Benson keeps the farce moving in a sprightly pace that is precise yet unencumbered.  The actors pick up their cues, making momentary ‘takes’ all the more effective.  This energy buoys the verse.  As a style, verse can be static, as it so frequently proceeds in a roundabout fashion.  This does give Tartuffe’s straightforward impudence a quiet punch.

In the end, though, two hours of verse does begin to wear thin.  Clever, yes, but a difficult flex to maintain for a long period of time.  Two other elements that, frankly, annoyed me are the jarring, industrial honking alarm that accompanies the scene changes, accomplishing God knows what, and the rather distaff closing musical number, which comes out of nowhere.  It blunts the effect of the play’s conclusion.  Nevertheless, Tartuffe is a clever show with an excellent cast and high production values, and some moments of true hilarity.

Tartuffe, written by Molière, adapted by Lucas Hnath; choreographed by Raja Feather Kelly and directed by Sarah Benson.

With: Matthew Broderick, David Cross, Emily Davis, Bianca del Rio, Amber Gray, Ryan J. Haddad, Francis Jue, Lisa Kron, Ikechukwu Ufomadu

Scenic design by dots; costume design by  Enver Chakartash, lighting design by Stacey Derosier, sound design by Peter Mills Weiss, hair and wig design by Robert Pickens and makeup design by Katie Gell.

At the New York Theatre Workshop (79 E 4th Street, New York, 10003) through January 24, 2026.  Buy tickets HERE or go to www.nytw.org.

In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

title.rendered: The Nutcracker: A Magical Family InsideOut Concert Experience with Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

content.rendered:
There are moments in life where dreams take flight and sugar plums dance upon the air. It is then that music transcends the merely beautiful and achieves something approaching the miraculous—when an orchestra, a conductor, and an audience breathe together in perfect communion. The world beyond the concert hall simply ceases to exist.

Such was the enchantment wrought by the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony under the luminous baton of David Bernard in their presentation of The Nutcracker: The Family InsideOut Concerts® Experience at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in New York City.

David Bernard introducing InsideOut Nutcracker with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in NYC. Photo by Edward Kliszus

A Conductor’s Gift: The Art of Musical Storytelling

Maestro Bernard, that rare amalgam of scholar, showman, and poet, possesses what one might call the pedagogical temperament of Leonard Bernstein combined with the interpretive depth of the great European tradition. Conducting the entire ballet from memory—a feat that speaks to both his formidable intellect and his profound internalization of this beloved score—he moved between podium and audience with the ease of a master storyteller, his introductory remarks preceding each section transforming what could have been mere musical illustration into a genuine Gesamtkunstwerk—Tchaikovsky’s total work of art that engaged hearts and minds alike.

A view from the woodwind section of Ballet Dancer Savanah Quiner in a scene from InsideOut Nutcracker with David Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in NYC. Courtesy PACS

The tale itself, as Bernard reminded his rapt audience, springs from darker roots than the confectionery delights of the ballet might suggest. E. T. A. Hoffmann’s original 1816 fairy tale, The Nutcracker and the Mouse King, presented a Gothic fantasy of considerable psychological complexity—a Märchen in which the boundaries between waking life and dream dissolve into something strange and wonderful.

Yet the ballet we cherish today emerged from a gentler French adaptation by Alexandre Dumas entitled The Story of a Nutcracker, which softened Hoffmann’s shadows while preserving the essential magic. This French confection served as the narrative framework for Marius Petipa and his assistant, Lev Ivanov, to construct their choreographic masterpiece for the Imperial Mariinsky Theatre in Saint Petersburg, where it premiered in December 1892.

Splendid visual art of a scene from The Nutcracker with Conductor David Bernard, Ballet Dancer Savannah Quiner, and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in NYC. Courtesy PACS

Orchestral Excellence: The Winds Sing, The Strings Soar

The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony—three-time First Prize Winner of The American Prize Competition in Orchestral Performance—demonstrated precisely why critics have proclaimed their performances “triumphant, polished, exquisite, with the depth and fervor of the old school European orchestras.” Founded in 1999 and nurtured by Bernard’s visionary leadership, this ensemble has achieved a remarkable synthesis of technical polish and interpretive vitality.

The orchestral playing throughout the afternoon was nothing short of bravura—solid, assured, and brimming with the colors and moods that Tchaikovsky painted with such orchestral brilliance. The ever-powerful winds, written with that characteristic Tchaikovskian espressivo, sang forth with noble authority. The flute solos possessed an otherworldly shimmer, whilst the piccolo’s crystalline arabesques in the “Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy” sparkled like frost upon a winter window. The woodwind choir achieved a pianissimo of gossamer delicacy in the “Waltz of the Snowflakes,” creating that sense of frozen enchantment that Tchaikovsky surely envisioned.

Particularly noteworthy was the orchestra’s handling of the famous celesta passages—that instrument which Tchaikovsky discovered during a Parisian sojourn and immediately recognized as the perfect “voice” of the Sugar Plum Fairy. The bell-like tones floated above the ensemble with ethereal purity, achieving what might be termed a timbral transcendence.

Tchaikovsky by Reutlinger (1888). Émile Reutlinger, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Terpsichorean Delights: The Dancers Who Enchanted

Ballet and music intertwined most gloriously through the participation of exceptional dance artists who brought visual poetry to Tchaikovsky’s sonic canvas. Savannah Quiner, a luminous talent from the American Repertory Ballet, performed the “Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy” and the role of Clara with exquisite legato movement and ethereal grace. Her port de bras possessed that rare quality of seeming to continue infinitely beyond the physical gesture—I might describe it as movement that shimmers and ripples like light upon water.

The dancers from Eglevsky Ballet—that venerable Long Island institution founded by legendary New York City Ballet principal dancer André Eglevsky over fifty years ago—brought professional élan to the “Marzipan/Merlitons” divertissement. Charlotte Jonassen, Josette Gerber, Eleanor Han, Ella Zhu, and Gabriella Renosis performed with disciplined artistry and joyful abandon, their synchronized movements creating visual counterpoint to the flutes’ delicate melodies. These young artists embody the finest traditions of classical training, demonstrating that the pedagogical legacy of the great Russian ballet masters continues to flourish on American soil.

Nutcracker. Image by Enrique from Pixabay

The InsideOut Experience: Innovation Meets Tradition

What distinguishes Bernard’s approach—indeed, what has earned him recognition as “the Johnny Appleseed of Classical Music”—is his revolutionary InsideOut Concerts® format, in which audiences are seated among the musicians. This patented innovation dissolves the traditional barrier between performer and listener, creating an immersive experience of extraordinary intimacy. As WQXR, Newsday, and Classical World have attested, this format offers “an unsurpassed experience and level of engagement for audiences of all ages.”

Featured Dancers assembling pre-performance with InsideOut Nutcracker with David Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in NYC. Courtesy PACS.

The full house—parents and children alike, many of the latter dressed in festive holiday garb—responded to each introduction with enthusiastic warmth. But the true coup de théâtre arrived during the closing “Waltz of the Flowers,” when children were invited to the front of the hall. There, at the podium itself, Bernard showed each young aspirant how to conduct the orchestra in this most famous of waltzes. The sight of small arms waving earnestly while the orchestra responded with professional courtesy and genuine affection was enough to melt the most cynical heart. Images from a ballet performance projected on a large screen accompanied the musical journey, creating a multimedia experience that genuinely touched hearts and minds in its delight and sheer enjoyment.

Savannah Quiner, Dancer. Photo by Rachel Neville

A Living Tradition: The Enduring Magic of Tchaikovsky

There was no end to the smiles of children and adults alike. Bernard’s animated, inspired introductions created that most precious of musical phenomena: genuine gemütlichkeit, a communal warmth that made strangers into fellow travelers in Tchaikovsky’s magical realm. Since the San Francisco Ballet began staging annual performances in America in the 1940s, The Nutcracker has become synonymous with the holiday season. This tradition now accounts for approximately 40% of the yearly ticket revenue of major American ballet companies.

Yet traditions endure not through mere repetition but through constant renewal. In the hands of Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony, Tchaikovsky’s score—which the composer himself once disparaged as “infinitely worse than Sleeping Beauty“—achieves its rightful status as one of the supreme achievements of the balletic repertoire. The orchestration glitters; the melodies soar; and for one magical afternoon at the DiMenna Center, the Land of Sweets became as real as the streets of Manhattan beyond its doors.

Maestro David David Bernard engaging with the audience at an InsideOut Concert with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music In New York City. Photo Courtesy Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

Park Avenue Chamber Symphony Contact Information

Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

Tickets: Eventbrite Season Events
Venue: DiMenna Center for Classical Music, 450 West 37th Street, New York, NY 10018
Email: info@chambersymphony.com

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Back in  2015 this website reviewed “Marjorie Prime.” whose cast featured Noah Bean, Lisa Emery, Stephen Root and Lois Smith.

Ten  years later the same story (with a few adjustments)  is being told with Danny Burstein, Christopher Lowell, Cynthia Nixon, and June Squibb

Back in 2015 AI was a thing of our imaginations.  A science fiction.  A Star Trek episode.

Not so much today.  This changes the perspective dramatically.  The chickens come home to roost in our front yard while we watch.

In 2025, the idea of a beloved person morphed into a 3 dimensional being who is as capable as we wish them to be – they only learn what they are told about the person whose Prime they are – this play may finally be hitting too close to home.  Thank goodness these actors are able to pick up the slack and then some.

Marjorie (Squibb), a mere 85 years old, is living with her daughter Tess (Nixon) and Tess’ husband Jon (Burstein).  The children have all flown and are rarely mentioned unless to use as a marker of time passing.  One, the most painful, is not mentioned at all until it becomes a breaking point.

You see, this family has welcomed a Prime, and AI generated computer that is Walter (Lowell), Tess’s father and Marjorie’s husband who has been dead for many years.  Walter Prime’s purpose is to help Marjorie thrive rather than just exist.  Marjorie had some hand in his appearance and age.  When we meet them they are well into their relationship, and the parameters become clear.  Walter’s behavior depends on what it is told.  Facts are assimilated – like the night they got engaged – and they are shared as actual memories that help the family deal with the loved one’s absence.

While odd, this seems amicable until Tess begins to melt down.  In this sparse residence  – not a photo or a painting on the wall, water is the only beverage, curtains are never fully opened – there is no way to avoid what is not a real person who is living with them.  Jon is bearing the weight of the real life and tragedies that lay dormant.

Danny Burstein, Cynthia Nixon; Photo by Joan Marcus

The story is fluid.   Once we understand what the beginning situation is, it changes like a breeze and Walter Prime disappears.  He is replaced by Marjorie Prime who is at the very beginning of her tenure.  Tess feels painted into a corner and questions the very value of the Primes.  Why do we insist on keeping everyone alive, she asks.

Jordan Harrison never tries o answer this question, which is a strong stance to take.  Instead he lets the circumstances creep up on us until the Primes are forced to reassure one another.

It is a bleak tale ably handled by this very fine cast.  This is a seamless ensemble, switching partners and dance steps without a flicker of uncertainty.  The gamut of emotions is pulled through the path of this family’s life like a cloth with an ancestral scent.  We follow.  These people, and their Primes, are not so much thinking about ramifications as they are surviving each revelation that every bend in the road reveals.  And the Primes, because they are reflections of the humans who created them, end up eternally eternal.

Marjorie Prime is a sobering piece knocking on our door.  It has all the time in the world to wait us out.

MARJORIE PRIME  by Jordan Harrison, directed by Anne Kauffman

WITH Danny Burstein, Christopher Lowell, Cynthia Nixon, and June Squibb

Scenic design by Lee Jellinek, costume design by Márion Talán de la Rosa, lighting design by Ben Stanton, and sound design and original music by Daniel Kluger.

Through February 15 At Second Stage Hayes Theater (240 West 44th Street) TICKETS HERE

@graph.name: Tulis McCall
@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

When you enter the So”HOHO” Playhouse downstairs’ pub you enter into a wonderfully colorful Christmas forest! A forest of ribbons and baubles and sparkles and oversized Edelweiss flowers, and celebratory hats for all. You enter, Edelweiss,  a celebration. Go early to get a drink at the bar and mingle with your fellow holiday travelers.

It’s the day before Christmas and Santa, our Santa, the one we all know and love, has done something no one ever expected. He died. YES! The man whom we all believed to be immortal, and I am pretty sure he believed it as well or else he would have watched his food intake a little more carefully, is DEAD. And all of the North Pole is in CHAOS. A few of the elves and one of Santa’s reindeers (all part of the North Pole Botany Club) have brought us together to mourn, to talk about our feelings, and figure out what comes next. At this point they only see the end of everything. How can Christmas, with its yuletide caroling, presents, feasts of food and fun, continue without its creator??

How??!!!!

One by one our hosts sing Christmas songs of cheer to lift our spirits and ease our pain. The songs do lift us up, with laughter as they are clever and absurd with Christmas inside jokes. Jessica the Reindeer (Mimi Scardulla), instead of singing to lift us up, does an improvisational dance to let go of her deep, deep pain. The dance you can imagine is brilliantly comedic in its sincerity. The evening turns into a party, and not to celebrate Santa Claus as the elves and reindeer initially thought but to celebrate us and the spirit of Christmas.

Photo By Marcus Middleton

We all have become at one time or another the spirit of Santa, giving gifts to our friends and family, giving money to our favorite charities, wishing strangers Happy Holidays! It is the spirit of Christmas to wish all a good day, a better future, filled with love and joy.

This is On the Rocks Theatre Company’s beloved production that with it’s a lively witty humor and understanding that we all carry the Christmas Spirit is a great way to ring in the Holiday season.

Remember, come early, grab your seat, your Christmas hat, and a drink! And yes there will be classics for you to sing along with including the brilliant Bing Crosby David Bowie duet and songs from the Sound of Music – Santa’s favorite musical.

Edelweiss written by Christopher Ford & Dakota Rose with Original Music by Andrew R. Butler, Directed by Dakota Rose, Music Direction by Ellen Winter & Choreography by Chloe Kernaghan

With: Andrew R. Butler, Shannon Holt, Rebeca Miller, Derek Smith, MiMi Scardulla and Ellen Winter

Creative Team: Set Design by Christopher Ford & Dakota Rose; Costume Design by Christopher Ford; Lighting Design by Kate McGee, Stage Managed by Teagan deGroen* & Produced by Kristy Bodall

Running Time: 40 minutes with no intermission

Soho Playhouse 15 Vandam St, New York, NY 10013

Tickets HERE
